title: Detroit Lions Updated 2026 Week 7 Depth Chart
full_text:
The Detroit Lions have a big opportunity for a statement win on Sunday.
Coming off their bye week, the Lions are set to take on the Green Bay Packers with a chance to make some headway in the NFC North division. All four teams in the division currently have a winning record, and with Sunday being Detroit's first divisional game of the year, it's an opportunity to position themselves to compete for their third crown in four years.
Detroit could be getting a boost on both sides of the ball, with center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch both getting activated off of injury lists for Sunday's game. The expectation currently is that both players will start.
Here is an updated look at the Lions' depth chart heading into their showdown with the Packers .
Starter: Jared Goff. Backup: Josh Dobbs
Goff has the opportunity to continue what has been one of the cleanest stretches of his career, as he remains without a turnover through the team's first five games of the year. He is 7-4 career against the Packers, throwing 19 touchdowns against five interceptions in those games.
Starter: Jahmyr Gibbs. Backup: Sione Vaki. Reserve: Jacob Saylors. Inactive: Isiah Pacheco (Injured reserve).
The Lions will look to get Gibbs going after he was held in check in two games against Green Bay last year. Green Bay will be without two starting linebackers in Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper, and the Lions could look to utilize Gibbs to exploit this.
Behind him, Vaki is established as the second running back. He continues to improve in the pass-protection element of the game, which is an important part of his role.
Starters: Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Isaac TeSlaa. Backups: DeAndre Carter, Tay Martin. Injured: Tom Kennedy (Injured reserve), Kendrick Law (Injured reserve).
The Lions will continue to have their top receivers available, but they are still light on depth heading into Sunday's game. Carter is added to the mix after the season-ending injury to Tom Kennedy, while Martin remains a contributor exclusively on special teams.
Starter: Sam LaPorta. Backup: Brock Wright. Reserves: Tyler Conklin, Jackson Meeks.
The contract situation surrounding Sam LaPorta has caused something of a firestorm over the last couple of weeks, but he continues to produce at a high level for the offense. Coming out of the bye week, LaPorta could be another option to exploit the Packers' inexperience at linebacker.
Detroit has alternated between Conklin and Meeks as the third tight end, and as a result it's uncertain which of the two they will take active into Sunday's game.
Starters: Penei Sewell (left), Blake Miller (right). Backup: Larry Borom. Inactive: Gio Manu (Non-Football injury).
The Lions will lean on Sewell and Miller to handle business up front heading into their first divisional contest of the season. In four starts, the rookie Miller has earned a Pro Football Focus offensive grade of 67.1 and allowed nine total pressure and no sacks.
Starters: Christian Mahogany (left), Tate Ratledge (right). Backups: Juice Scruggs, Miles Frazier. Inactive: Ben Bartch (Injured reserve)
The guard position is one of the most intriguing spots on Detroit's depth chart this week. With Cade Mays returning, the Lions are making a change at center and as a result Scruggs could see some time at guard.
Scruggs is one of the top-performing centers through Detroit's first five games, and because of that the Lions could look to get him involved on the interior. However, Mahogany and Ratledge are both playing well and as a result neither need to be replaced.
Starter: Cade Mays. Backup: Juice Scruggs. Reserve: Seth McLaughlin
The Lions' offensive line has performed well in Mays' absence, and now he will join them as the starter at center after being activated off of injured reserve. It will be his debut with the team after signing a three-year deal in free agency this year.
Scruggs will be the backup, and likely the first option off the bench if any of the three interior linemen were to go down.
Starters: Alim McNeill, Tyleik Williams. Backups: Skyler Gill-Howard, Levi Onwuzurike. Reserve: Mekhi Wingo.
The Lions have developed a nice rotation amidst its interior defensive line. Williams and Gill-Howard have complimented each other nicely, giving the Lions an answer for both the run and the pass. McNeill has been exceptional, recording 23 pressures which ranks second on the team.
Starters: Aidan Hutchinson, D.J. Wonnum. Backups: Tyler Lacy, Derrick Moore. Reserves: Eric O'Neill, Ahmed Hassanein. Inactive: Payton Turner (Injured reserve).
The Lions have been able to get plenty of pass-rush production this year, as they lead the league in sacks. Against a Packers' offense that has been reliant on the big play through the air, getting heat on Jordan Love could be a difference-making factor in whether or not they earn a win.
Starters: Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez. Backups: Trevor Nowaske, Jimmy Rolder, Amen Ogbongbemiga. Inactive: Devin White (Injured reserve), Damone Clark (Injured reserve).
The Lions lost White to a forearm injury that has resulted in an IR stint, which will lead to more opportunities for Malcolm Rodriguez. It could also create more snaps for Rolder, who has logged defensive snaps in just one of the first five regular season games.
Starters: D.J. Reed, Roger McCreary. Backups: Ennis Rakestraw, Rock Ya-Sin. Reserves: Keith Abney II, Khalil Dorsey
The Lions rolled with McCreary as the boundary corner against the Cardinals, and even with Ya-Sin expected to play on Sunday they should stick with McCreary. He had six passes defensed, which was the most by a Lions defender in one game this season.
Rakestraw should see some time. Meanwhile, Abney is an interesting spot. He started at safety against Arizona, but with Brian Branch returning could be in the mix to play some at cornerback.
Starters: Brian Branch, Chuck Clark. Backups: Keith Abney II, Christian Izien. Reserve: Bishop Fitzgerald. Inactive: Kerby Joseph (Physically Unable to Perform), Thomas Harper (Injured reserve), Avonte Maddox (Injured reserve).
Branch was officially activated and taken off of the injury report on Sunday, so his highly anticipated return will be on Sunday. Even if he's not the same game-breaking player he was prior to the injury right away, his presence alone will give them some stability.
Clark is the front-runner to play beside him, though Abney did show some intriguing ability in his audition at safety against the Cardinals. Fitzgerald has yet to be active since being claimed off Pittsburgh's practice squad nearly a month ago, and with Branch returning that may not change.
Kicker: Jake Bates. Punter: Jack Fox. Long-snapper: Hogan Hatten. Kick returners: Jacob Saylors, DeAndre Carter. Punt returner: DeAndre Carter.
The addition of Carter is an intriguing one. He's currently the NFL's active leader in returns, and is on his 12th team in 12 years. He should have an extended leash to handle the return duties, and could bring a spark to the return game after Kennedy had some success in Week 5 prior to his injury.
Interestingly enough, Carter made his official debut in 2018 for the Philadelphia Eagles where current Lions special teams coordinator Dave Fipp was in that role at the time. Now, the two will reunite with hopes of sparking Detroit's return game.
Sports journalist who has covered the Detroit Lions the past three NFL seasons. Christian brings expert analysis, insights and an ability to fairly assess how the team is performing in a tough NFC North division.

title: Packers Report Card After Silly Mistakes Killed Them Against Lions
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers have lost a lot of games like the one they did in Detroit on Sunday afternoon.
They play just well enough to stay in the game, make a few big plays to help you realize their tantalizing potential but, ultimately, fall short at the end.
Why? Because they make too many silly mistakes and don’t put themselves in the best position to succeed.
Let’s dive right into the weekly report card from Green Bay’s 20-17 loss to the Lions.
Drops. The story of Green Bay’s season. Jordan Love tried his best to erase some of the mistakes that the Packers made, as all great quarterbacks do.
An egregious intentional grounding could have been erased if Bo Melton had made a catch on a ball that hit him in both hands. Instead, it was dropped, forcing a third-and-21.
Following Keisean Nixon’s heroic fourth-down stop on defense, Love threw a dime to Josh Jacobs in the corner of the end zone that would have given the Packers a 23-17 lead late in the fourth quarter with the extra point pending.
Jacobs was unable to make the catch.
Love was essentially given the entire game by Matt LaFleur and asked to win it.
He was not perfect. His one interception was, in essence, an arm punt. He nearly threw another in the red zone on what was supposed to be a throwaway. Apart from those plays, however, Love has continued to rise to the occasion while those around him falter.
Love may never put up the gaudy numbers that some premier quarterbacks do. He’s someone you have to watch every week to appreciate how good he is.
He’s continued to roll with the punches behind a bad offensive line, the worst run game in football and a receiving corps that leads the NFL in drops.
As a result, he’s asked to play Superman more than the Packers would probably like him to.
Unfortunately for the Packers, they’ve asked their quarterback to play Superman for the better part of the last 15 years. Asking one man to carry the entire franchise often leads that franchise to crumble in the biggest moments.
That’s what happened to Green Bay on Sunday.
Josh Jacobs was back, albeit on a snap count. There was not much of a difference for Green Bay’s run game. Jacobs carried the ball 11 times for 36 yards. MarShawn Lloyd and Savion Williams were the only other ball-carriers, combining for 24 yards on eight carries. The longest run was a 10-yard burst from Jacobs that felt like it was a 30-yard-run in the moment simply because of how inept the Packers have been on the ground.
Perhaps things will get better as Jacobs gets more acclimated after his six-game absence and is able to handle a full workload.
It’s clear, however, he’s not going to save the Packers’ run game all by himself. The group in front of him needs to start figuring some things out.
Simply put, 19 carries for 60 yards wasn’t good enough – and won’t be good enough as the games get bigger down the stretch of the season.
Is Micah Parsons back yet?
Obviously, the answer is no, but the Packers’ four-man rush was unable to get anything generated against Jared Goff for most of the day. When Goff is comfortable in the pocket, he can dice up any defense. That’s what he did with relative ease for significant portions of the game.
He finished the day with 303 passing yards, 153 of which went to his top target, Amon-Ra St. Brown. Another 91 yards and two touchdowns went to Jameson Williams. They both had two catches of 24-plus yards.
Goff was sacked just once on a bit of an odd play where Anthony Campbell stripped Goff before he fell on the ball. He was pressured on only three of 33 dropbacks, according to PFF.
For the first time since the Packers played Atlanta, they did not record an interception. Brandon Cisse had one wiped out thanks to a pass interference penalty that was called on him. Evan Williams had one hit him in both hands, but he dropped it.
Goff gave the Packers opportunities, but they did not capitalize. They did do a good job situationally, specifically Cisse with a two-play sequence that included a pass breakup and shoving Williams out of bounds to secure a fourth-down stop.
To hold the Lions’ high-flying offense to just 20 points is impressive, which pulls the final grade up.
With Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper out of the lineup, it would have been easy to foresee Jahmyr Gibbs running wild against Green Bay’s run defense.
Quite the opposite took place. There were some instances when Gibbs got going, but he was largely held in check. He finished with 29 carries for 116 yards, but two of his biggest runs of the day came on at least one play in which the Packers were trying to let him score.
Against a back as good as Gibbs, any team will sign up for that.
The biggest play of the game for Green Bay’s defense came on the ground. With the Lions facing a fourth-and-1 from their 24 with about 5 minutes remaining, Keisean Nixon made what could have been the game-winning play with a TFL to give the Packers possession.
It did not turn out that way, but this group was solid as they’ve been for most of the season save for one nightmare against Bijan Robinson.
For everything that went wrong, if the kicker simply would have made his kicks, the Packers would have won the game in regulation. If the kicker would have made one of the two kicks he shanked, the Packers would have had a shot to win in overtime.
Trey Smack has been up-and-down all season, but his performance against the Lions will be one to forget.
Smack missed field goals of 26 and 35 yards. One was officially blocked, but that cannot happen. Smack has missed five kicks in the last three weeks. The Packers are standing by him, but it’s going to be interesting to see how much tolerance there is for a rookie kicker for a team that cannot afford to leave points on the field in big games.
Smack is not the only person at fault for why the Packers lost, but he played a huge role in it. Missing two chip-shot field goals in a dome is inexcusable. In a league in which kickers are better than ever, it’s a wonder how the Packers have not figured out a way to replace the ever-reliable Mason Crosby since allowing him to leave following the 2022 season.
It’s not Travis Glover’s fault. He was asked to do something he never should have been asked to do.
Kevin Zeitler said on Friday that he was ready to play if the Packers called on him. Instead of starting him, the Packers made him a healthy scratch in favor of Glover, who has been the starter since Zeitler signed with the team in late September.
According to PFF’s initial charting, Glover gave up seven pressures against Alim McNeil and the Detroit interior defensive line. The most he’d given up in a game to date was three. He nearly doubled his output in just one performance.
The only way the Lions were going to be able to slow down the Packers’ offense was if their front wrecked the game for Green Bay.
It’s unclear who is in charge of the decision of who to start. Whether it’s Matt LaFleur, Adam Stenavich, Luke Butkus or some combination of the three, there needs to be a come-to-Jesus moment in regards to this offensive line.
In the biggest game of the season to date, the Packers did not put their best foot forward. They did not put their best players on the field. That’s inexcusable. The coaching staff has bungled so many decisions on the offensive line during their tenure to where they do not have the benefit of the doubt that perhaps their evaluation of Glover being a better option than Zeitler is correct.
If Zeitler is ready, he not only needs to be active on Thursday against Carolina but standing next to Anthony Belton as the team’s starting right guard.
Aside from that decision, LaFleur would not comment on the officials after the game. Whether or not he’s correct in that regard does not really matter. LaFleur said it best in that it will not change anything.
His aggressiveness early in the game was the correct decision in my estimation, the players just did not execute.
That has been a significant problem in a lot of the big games…

title: Matt LaFleur Nailed It, But Will Anything Change for Packers After Loss to Lions?
full_text:
DETROIT – The Detroit Lions beat the Green Bay Packers.
The officials beat the Green Bay Packers.
And the Green Bay Packers beat the Green Bay Packers.
It was the trifecta, with there being some symmetry in Green Bay losing by three points, 20-17, to the rival Lions. The Packers’ three-game winning streak was snapped as they fell into last place in the NFC North by blowing a game they should have won, no matter the officiating incompetence.
“We got to grow up fast,” coach Matt LaFleur said.
It was the usual mish-mash of swill for the Packers, who can be kicking butt in one moment and then be kicking themselves in the shins a moment later.
The Packers were guilty of eight penalties for 81 yards.
They went 1-of-4 in the red zone.
They missed two field goals.
They couldn’t block in the run game and gave up too much pressure in the pass game.
Otherwise, as the saying goes, how was the play, Mrs. Lincoln?
Pro Football Focus charged the Packers with only two drops, including one by Josh Jacobs in the end zone with 3:30 to play. It just seemed like more.
“I feel like a game like today, we left a lot of points out there,” quarterback Jordan Love said. “We didn’t finish in the red zone. We didn’t finish with kicks. It’s disappointing. We left a lot of points out there. We did a decent job moving the ball, and we’ve got to look at it, but we’ve got to do a better job finishing.
“To score 17 points in a game we should have scored a lot more, is disappointing, so definitely the red zone area is something we’ve got to clean up. On special teams, we’ve got to be able to finish those kicks, but we left a lot of points out there.”
Love has to play like an MVP for the Packers to have a chance on offense. And even that’s not enough at times to overcome the maddening cauldron of mediocrity.
At times, Love has to run for his life and turn nothing into something. At other times, Love throws a dime but his receivers either drop the ball or fail to make a contested catch.
Love would never in a million years publicly blame a specific teammate, but his frustration was evident after the game.
“At the end of the day, it comes down to throwing and catching the ball, and we’ve got to make plays,” he said. “I talk about it all the time. When it’s Sunday and the lights are bright, we’ve got to be able to go out there and make plays, and that is the difference in winning and losing.
“If we don’t make the plays, this is what’s going to happen. We’ve got to do a better job of finding ways to do that and it’s one of those things where we’ve got to keep going, keep attacking. Yeah, we’ve got to do a much better job of just executing, throwing and catching and making plays.”
The Packers have not had a good red-zone offense this season. This should have been the game to get in gear, though. The Lions entered the game ranked 30th in red-zone defense. In goal-to-go situations, they hadn’t recorded a single stop all season.
Instead, Green Bay went 1-of-4 in the red zone and 0-for-1 in goal-to-go.
“We got to finish plays,” LaFleur said. “Certainly, there’s some play calls that I wish we had back, and then we got to finish some plays. And I think usually the better red zone teams typically can run the ball in the red zone, and then you put yourself in more manageable situations. I got to go back and look at it, but it still doesn’t feel as effective as I think it needs to be.”
The return of Josh Jacobs helped a bit overall as he was able to find some hard-charging yards the other backs had failed to get. Still, the Packers finished with 19 carries for 60 yards – right at their league-worst average. On first-and-goal at the 6 on the opening possession, Jacobs carried the ball twice for 3 yards. After that, it was mostly pass, pass and pass some more.
Their last trip in the red zone ended with Jacobs’ critical drop.
“It just comes down to finding ways to score points,” Love said. “I think you’ve got to have a run game to be able to do that and we’ll keep looking at what we can do to improve that. but it just comes down to throwing and catching and we didn’t do a good enough job of that today.”
The expectation was there would be some growing pains with rookie kicker Trey Smack. On Sunday, the pain was the agony of defeat. He missed two easy kicks against the Lions, including a 26-yarder on the opening possession and a 35-yarder on the final possession after Jacobs’ dropped touchdown.
What was more unbelievable on the first miss? The absolutely inexcusable delay-of-game penalty that nullified his 21-yard field goal or that he missed from 26 with the perfect conditions that come in an indoor stadium? Entering Sunday, there had been only one missed field goal of shorter than 30 yards all season.
Then came the miss at the end of the game after Jacobs’ dropped touchdown. The ball was tipped; at that distance, the kick must have been low. Instead of leading 20-17, the Lions drove to a walk-off field goal.
“The sun rises every morning and it’s not going to stop for me,” Smack said after the game.
LaFleur said he’d stick with Smack as the kicker.
“Trey’s a guy that I think he’s proved that he can do it and I know he can do it,” LaFleur said. “We got to wipe this one clean and got to move on and hopefully we can be a little bit better.”
How about a lot of bit better?
Even though they are in last place in the NFC North, the Packers are still the No. 7 team in the NFC playoff race.
But, really, the Packers are just another of the NFL’s mediocre teams. They are good enough to beat most teams but bad enough to be beaten by anyone. Or, as was the case on Sunday, when the team’s fate was sealed on Karl Brooks’ offside penalty on third-and-5, they can beat themselves on any given Sunday.
“I think we’ve been building some momentum,” LaFleur said. “I think our defense is balling out, doing a lot of great things. That’s a really good offense. I think you hold them to 20 points, you have an opportunity to win the game. Obviously, offensively, we got to score points in the red zone – didn’t do that. Missed a couple kicks, still have too many drops.
“But then there’s some things defensively we got to do better, too, in regards to just the offsides penalties are killer and especially in situations where you know they’re going to hard count and we continue to have these repeated mistakes and we can’t do it. We got to learn from it. We got to grow up. We got to grow up fast.”
But are they capable? After winning nine games in 2024 and nine games in 2025, is it any wonder they are on pace for about nine wins in 2026? Is there any real reason to believe that a team that’s played mistake-filled football through seven games will get its act together for the final 10 games?
Xavier McKinney called the officiating "bullshit" (and more) after the Packers lost to the Lions today. He's absolutely right. Of course, the Packers did plenty of things to lose the game. But the refs are "kind of f***ing up the games."⬇️ https://t.co/IJdIl1WAMe

title: Packers’ Xavier McKinney Calls Officiating ‘Bull****’ – And He’s Right
full_text:
DETROIT – Green Bay Packers safety Xavier McKinney had the perfect word in mind to describe the officiating in Sunday’s 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions.
He’s right. This is my 19th season on the Packers beat. I’ve never written a blame-the-refs story because blaming the referees is only something that losers do. But on Sunday, in a critical game against a division rival that could have wide-ranging ramifications by the end of the season, the Packers got the raw end of the deal on practically every important call.
So, it’s no wonder why McKinney – as calmly as possible – put the officials on blast after his team’s three-game winning streak was snapped and it fell to last place in the powerful NFC North.
“I don’t know how the NFL’s going to treat it but I’m not a big fan of the refs right now,” McKinney said. “I don’t think it’s great officiating, if I’m being completely honest. I think it’s bull**** a lot of the times. I think there are drives where they make calls that don’t even make any sense.”
McKinney offered one example. On second-and-11 midway through the third quarter, Jared Goff completed a short pass to Amon-Ra St. Brown. St. Brown was wrapped up by Isaiah McDuffie and taken down, but St. Brown acted as if he wasn’t down so kept going.
Devonte Wyatt tackled St. Brown, who wound up tripping up the umpire, Terry Killens Jr. Killens from his back threw a penalty on Wyatt for unnecessary roughness.
“The runner was still running and we didn’t hear a whistle,” McKinney continued. “We tried to get him down and then their player hit the ref and he falls, he gets mad on the ground, and he just throws the flag. He don’t even know who hit him.”
In a pool report, referee Alex Moore – incredibly – had this to say.
“We ruled that the play was over. I can’t honestly hear if there was a whistle or not, but the tackler made the tackle, the play was over. Then, there was an additional action, and he basically tackled him again with force after the play was over.”
So, the referee didn’t hear the whistle. St. Brown obviously didn’t hear the whistle. But the Packers’ defenders must have heard the whistle so, therefore, a penalty flag was thrown.
Not to coach Matt LaFleur.
“There was no whistle blown and the guy continued to run and our guy didn’t hear a whistle, he continued to play, too, and then we get called for a penalty,” LaFleur said. “So, I don’t know. They were trying to tell me the play was obviously dead. I’m like, ‘How do you know if you don’t hear a whistle?’ So, I don’t know if you guys heard a whistle, I did not hear a whistle.”
Wyatt said he didn’t hear the whistle.
“If you asked me right now, I’d do the same thing 100 times over,” he said. “So, that’s the refs. They got to figure out what they need to do because I definitely did my job.”
Of course, Wyatt made the tackle. Because what if he didn’t? LaFleur tells his players to play through the “echo of the whistle.” In this case, there was no echo to hear.
“What if he would’ve got up and ran for a touchdown? Then everybody would be looking at D-Wy like, ‘You let him go’. I feel like I did the right thing. Flag or not, I feel like I did the right thing.”
So, instead of third-and-7, the Lions got a first down and, one play later, scored the go-ahead touchdown.
Then, on the first play of the fourth quarter, Jordan Love was flagged for intentional grounding, even though Love’s pass was right on line to tight end Tucker Kraft.
“So, we ruled that although the quarterback was outside of the tackle box, the pass did not make it to the line of scrimmage,” Moore said. “So, that’s where the intentional grounding came in.”
The ball fell short of the destination because Love was taken to the turf, though the officials were correct in that the ball landed behind the line of scrimmage.
“Yeah, you know, it was said that the ball was short of the line of scrimmage,” Love said. “I thought we had a receiver right there in the area. It is what it is.”
Meanwhile, the Packers came into the game with six penalties for roughing the passer against zero for their opponents. That swelled to 8-0 on Sunday.
First, with about 4 minutes left in the third quarter, Brenton Cox shoved Lions quarterback Jared Goff right in the midsection. It appeared he tried to catch him. It wasn’t as weak of a call as the one on Lukas Van Ness last week, but it wasn’t far behind.
“I’m confused, too,” Wyatt said. “I guess we’re supposed to, just, I don’t know. I can’t even tell you.”
Finally, with less than 3 minutes to go in the game, defensive tackle Karl Brooks was flagged for roughing when he hit Goff immediately after the pass. Goff pointed at Moore for the flag and got it on command, much to Brooks’ dismay.
“So, it just be bull**** that’s going on, bull**** calls, and I can’t really tell you because sometimes we’re not seeing the same calls for our quarterback, we’re not seeing the same calls for our offensive guys,” McKinney said.
“I just don’t really understand. It really don’t matter if it’s home or away, it’s kind of been consistent throughout the year. Obviously, it’s not to make it as an excuse but I just say it got to go both ways, man. That’s all I’ll say.”
McKinney had more to say, though. And he doesn’t care about the fine that’s probably going to come.
Asked if he thought the Packers had a stolen from him, he said:
“For sure. At critical moments in the game – like, these are critical drives,” he said. “It’s annoying even talking about it because these are critical drives throughout the game and we might have a drive where we’re getting stops but you’re calling penalties and it’s like, this is not a penalty. To me, it just don’t really make any sense and it’s killing our momentum, it’s killing our drives and it’s kind of f***ing up the games, if I’m being honest.”
The NFL has a major officiating problem. That’s been clear for years. But an industry that’s worth billions and is awash in gambling money needs to do better given there’s so much at stake.
“It is what it is, man,” McKinney said. “They’re going to fine you for anything at this point in this league, so that’s what I know. I would rather get fined and try to help my team out because I see what’s going on and it’s killing us. We all see it. We all see what’s going on. Everyone sees what’s going on, the fans see what’s going on, we see what’s going on when we’re out there.
“I’m looking at the plays and I’m like, ‘Hold up, why are they calling this? It don’t even make any sense.’ And then the fact you’re not even reviewing what you’re calling. You’re just calling it and you’re seeing it and even they’re looking at it, like, ‘OK, that’s not a …’ I’m asking the other refs, and they’re like, ‘Oh, I’m not over there.’  It’s a lot of sh** that doesn’t make sense right now. But, at the end of the day, we’ve still got to find a way to go there and win these games. It’s making it a little bit harder when the officiating is that way, if I’m being honest.”
Good for McKinney for pointing out the, well, bull**** from a league that cares about nothing more than making money, the teams, the players, the outcome of games and the public be damned.

title: Packers Winners and Losers: Trey Smack Leads Negative List After Loss to Lions
full_text:
The Green Bay Packers trailed the Detroit Lions 17-14 in the fourth quarter after a wild first half somehow saw the scoreboard only read 10-7 in Detroit’s favor.
The fourth quarter was going to decide Green Bay’s fate. As has been the case too often in big games for the Packers, missed opportunities sealed their fate.
An offsides penalty on Karl Brooks allowed the Lions to run the clock all the way down to kick a field goal as time expired in what was just the final missed opportunity.
More on that in our weekly winners and losers, starting with the biggest culprit.
Missing a 26-yard field goal is almost impossible for an NFL kicker, but Smack found a way to do so on Sunday, and it may have affected the rest of the game considering how aggressive Matt LaFleur was on fourth downs in field-goal range.
Smack has been excellent from beyond 50 yards this season. He’s struggled on kicks that are traditionally called chip shots.
He is similar to that of Ronnie Bass from the movie Remember the Titans .
Trey Smack can't hit the 26-yard field goal 😬 pic.twitter.com/k1GbPnpxrz
He can throw it a mile, but he can’t pitch it 3 yards.
Smack made a 43-yard field goal with 7:10 left in the game.
As further proof of his ability to ride the roller coaster, Smack missed a 35-yard field goal following a huge defensive stand from Green Bay’s defense. Officially, it was ruled a block, but a kick from that range should never be blocked. Instead of taking a 20-17 lead, the Packers lost 20-17.
Coach Matt LaFleur, who said he did not realize the kick was blocked, will move forward with Smack as the kicker.
In big games, points cannot be left on the field. One of the reasons the Packers drafted Smack is to stabilize the kicker position. They’ve missed a kick or had one blocked in every postseason game they’ve played in since 2021.
Smack left at least six points on the field today, and who knows how to account for the points that LaFleur may have left on the field due to lack of trust in his kicker. The broadcast showed a graphic that said Smack has two misses of 35 yards or less this season. The rest of the NFL has one.
That’s not going to cut it.
Sometimes all it takes is one bad play to end up on this list. That’s exactly what happened for these two players. The Lions were facing third-and-5 on the other side of the two minute warning.
A first down meant that the Lions could essentially run the clock down to kick a short field goal to end the game.
Jared Goff went to his hard count. Brooks and Van Ness both jumped offsides.
The game was essentially over from there. It was just another play in a long line of undisciplined plays from Green Bay’s team on Sunday.
When Green Bay got the ball back with 13:37 left in the fourth quarter, they had only been able to muster 57 yards of offense to that point. They’d scored a touchdown, but that was largely on the backs of a fumbled snap from Cade Mays that was kicked around before getting recovered by Isaiah McDuffie.
The offense, if they’re not hitting big shots down the field struggles to put games together. There were long stretches of the game where Tucker Kraft and Christian Watson became afterthoughts on offense.
They were only able to muster three points in the fourth quarter. They couldn’t pick up a first down after Keisean Nixon gave them the ball in scoring range.
They were a mess for most of the second half. Whether it was drops, penalties, or uninspired play. Ultimately the lack of offense cost them the game.
Green Bay’s first possession of the game stalled in the red zone when Jordan Love threw incomplete for Matthew Golden.
The Packers took a delay of game penalty to turn a 21-yard field goal into a 26-yard field goal. No big deal, right?
Wrong. Trey Smack made the initial kick at 21 yards, but missed the kick following the five-yard penalty.
That wasn’t the end of Green Bay’s red zone struggles. They failed on a fourth down in the first half where Golden was tackled short of the line to gain by DJ Reed.
Throwing the ball in the red zone is hard enough. It’s more difficult when a team is unable to run the football, which describes the Packers for the duration of this season.
That’s how the Packers continued to pile up yards in the first half, but only had seven points to show for it.
Maybe Josh Jacobs returning to the offense and becoming more acclimated will cure what ails them, but that wasn’t the case on Sunday as the Packers failed to score touchdowns against one of the worst defenses in the NFL.
Detroit’s best receiver is named Amon-Ra St. Brown. You may not have known that if you just watched the way the Packers covered him on Sunday.
There were a few plays during the course of the game where Javon Bullard proved to be a worthy adversary to St. Brown.
He was the only one. There were too many instances where St. Brown was running three into oceans of open zones in the middle of the field. He was Detroit’s go-to target all game.
He finished the day with nine catches for 153 yards. He accounted for more than half of Jared Goff’s passing yards on the day.
The Travis Glover experiment is over. Or at least it should be. Credit to Glover, he stepped in during an hour of desperation and proved to be a valuable piece of the offensive line while they were searching for answers on the interior.
Early numbers from PFF showed him giving up four pressures in the first half alone.
Kevin Zeitler, his presumed replacement, was a healthy scratch on Sunday. Zeitler said he was ready to play if  the team needed him earlier in the week. Do the coaches disagree? Do they think Zeitler is an old player who has lost a step? Is it just plain mismanagement?
Either way, the Packers need to figure out the answer. If they want to put their best five players on the field, it’s hard to believe the Glover is better than a decorated veteran like Zeitler.
On a day where Green Bay’s pass rush was mostly non-existent, former undrafted free agent Anthony Campbell made his presence known.
Campbell had a TFL in the second half on Jahmyr Gibbs, which was combined with a sack-fumble of Jared Goff in the first half.
With Devonte Wyatt hobbled and largely non-existent, the Packers need someone to step up on their defensive line. Sunday, Campbell was the answer to that question.
Games like Sundays often come down to the final few minutes of the game.
The Lions faced a fourth-and-1 from their own 22 yard line with 4:50 left in the game.
Dan Campbell kept his offense on the field to go for it. The FOX broadcast was in disbelief that Campbell was actually going to go for it, but he did.
Keisean Nixon and the Packers force a turnover on downs! GBvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XrT82gvFEh
They ran a slow developing run play to the left side, but Keisean Nixon did not have a receiver to account for on his side of the formation. Nixon triggered immediately into the backfield and threw Gibbs for a loss on the play, giving the Packers the ball with a chance to take the lead.
The Packers went three-and-out on the ensuing position, which led to a Trey Smack field goal attempt. The kick was missed, but Nixon put his team in a position to take the lead.

title: Packers Lose to Lions and Officials, Fall Into Last Place in NFC North
full_text:
DETROIT – The Green Bay Packers couldn’t beat the Detroit Lions. They couldn’t beat their own mistakes. And they couldn’t beat a few controversial calls by the officials.
It all added up to a 20-17 loss at Ford Field, a killer outcome with the Packers blowing opportunities to win a fourth consecutive game and instead falling into last place in the powerful NFC North.
With the score tied at 17, the Packers blew a chance to score a go-ahead touchdown – or at least a go-ahead field goal – after a crucial fourth-down stop. On the second play of the ensuing possession, Jared Goff completed a pass over the middle to tight end Sam LaPorta for 17 yards. Karl Brooks hit Goff instantly but was flagged for roughing the passer.
It was the eighth roughing penalty against the Packers this season; their opponents have been flagged for zero.
8-0 https://t.co/j8Pz6SlSgd
On the next play, Jahmyr Gibbs broke a tackle, turning a short gain into a run of 15 yards. The Packers had a chance to stay in the game. On third-and-5 at the 2-minute warning, Brooks jumped offside. So, the Lions bled the clock and kicked a walk-off field goal.
Jordan Love was 27-of-45 passing for 274 yards and two touchdowns. Goff threw for 303 yards, including 153 to Amon-Ra St. Brown, as the Lions overcame two bad fumbles.
With the game tied at 17, the Lions took the ball at their 22 with 4:50 to go. On second-and-1, Jahmyr Gibbs was stuffed. On third-and-1, Dani Dennis-Sutton made an unbelievable play in the flat on a pass to Gibbs On fourth-and-1, Keisean Nixon blitzed off the edge to bury Gibbs for a turnover on downs.
So, Green Bay took over at Detroit’s 22 with a chance to score a pivotal touchdown. Instead, on third-and-5, Josh Jacobs dropped a pass in the end zone. On fourth down, Trey Smack missed a 38-yard field goal; the ball was tipped by D.J. Wonnum.
So, now it was the Lions turn to go win the game, as they took over at their 25 with 3:21 to play.
The Packers trailed 17-14 entering the fourth quarter but were backed up after a key fourth-down stop. On first down from the 19, Jordan Love was flagged for intentional grounding. He obviously was throwing the ball away to avoid a sack, but Tucker Kraft was right in line with the ball. The call, in a word, was horrendous.
And important. The 11-yard penalty led to back-to-back deep balls by Love. Bo Melton failed to make a catch past midfield on the first. Then, on third-and-21, Brian Branch grabbed an arm-punt interception.
The Packers forced a three-and-out, though Evan Williams dropped what should have been an easy interception that probably would have set up the offense on the other side of midfield. Instead, the Packers took possession at their 14 with 13:44 to go.
The Packers marched to the tying field goal. Josh Jacobs had an 8-yard catch on third-and-6 and a 10-yard run; in between, linebacker Derrick Barnes was flagged for unnecessary roughness for clobbering MarShawn Lloyd after he dropped a pass.
Trey Smack, who missed an easy field goal to start the game, booted a 43-yarder to tie the game at 17 with 7:10 remaining.
The Lions were in position to perhaps deliver the knockout. Leading 17-14, they were in the red zone late in the third quarter thanks to two huge calls. First, on third-and-10 early in the drive, Jared Goff’s checkdown landed incomplete but the Lions were bailed out by a dubious roughing-the-passer penalty against Brenton Cox.
Moments later, Brandon Cisse intercepted Goff but was flagged for interference. That was probably a good call; Cisse was awfully physical with Amon-Ra St. Brown at the top of the route. That made it first down at the 11. First, Jahmyr Gibbs broke a tackle by Cox and gained 5. Anthony Campbell batted down a pass on second down and Cisse broke up a pass in the corner of the end zone on third down.
That made it fourth-and-5 at the 6, Goff had time and rifled one into the back of the end zone to Williams, who made the catch but couldn’t get both feet down because he was shoved out of bounds by Cisse.
The Lions led 10-7 at halftime and got the ball to start the second half. Instead of extending their lead, Jared Goff fumbled the snap, with Isaian McDuffie recovering at Detroit’s 42. The Packers scored moments later on a 25-yard touchdown pass to Josh Jacobs, who broke two tackles and somehow kept his balance and his foot off the sideline.
Detroit answered with an 80-yard scoring drive. On third-and-6, Goff hit Isaac TeSlaa for 10, and then Jameson Williams for 30.
Chaos ensued moments later on a short completion to Amon-Ra St. Brown. St. Brown, perhaps thinking he was not down, got up and was tackled. The official got knocked over and threw a flag from his back – on McDuffie. Coach Matt LaFleur blew a gasket on the sideline but it, of course, didn’t matter.
Moments later, Goff hit Williams for a 10-yard touchdown to put Detroit back in front 17-14.
The Packers went three-and-out on the ensuing possession. On second down, Matthew Golden couldn’t control a perfect deep ball from Love, with D.J. Reed jarring it loose. On third down, Golden wanted defensive pass interference against cornerback Khalil Dorsey but no flag was thrown.
The Lions led 10-7 at halftime. A score like that would suggest a defensive slugfest like in the good old days of the Black and Blue Division. Instead, the quarterbacks combined for 395 passing yards but the offenses just couldn’t seal the deal.
The Lions entered the game ranked 30th in the red zone and didn’t have a single goal-to-go stop. Instead, the Packers had first-and-goal at the 6 on their opening possession but not only failed to score a touchdown but failed to score at all.
Trey Smack kicked a 21-yard field goal but it was nullified by a delay-of-game penalty. It’s an inexcusable blunder but shouldn’t have mattered. After all, the re-do was a 26-yard kick. Instead, Smack missed it wide right.
A blink-of-an-eye later, the Lions led 7-0 on Goff’s touchdown pass to Jameson Williams.
The Packers answered on Jordan Love’s 14-yard touchdown pass to Tucker Kraft. Love hit Josh Jacobs for 10 on third-and-3 and Kraft for 22 on fourth-and-2 before the score to Kraft on third-and-9.
With the Lions up 10-7, the Packers once again wasted a red-zone opportunity. On third-and-4, Love almost threw a boneheaded interception. On fourth-and-4, Love’s completion to Matthew Golden didn’t have a prayer.
The Lions drove right down the field and into position to take a 17-7 halftime lead. Instead, Jahmyr Gibbs collided with lineman Cade Mays for an enormous turnover to keep it a one-score game at the break.
Love was 16-of-26 passing for 191 yards in the first half. The running game even with the addition of Jacobs was horrendous with 11 carries for 25 yards.
Goff was 13-of-17 for 204 yards, with St. Brown destroying the secondary with seven catches for 135 yards.
With the Bears beating the Patriots on Thursday and the Vikings rallying past the Colts on Sunday, here are the NFC North standings.

title: Studs and Duds for Packers (Including Red Zone) as They Trail Lions 10-7 at Halftime
full_text:
DETROIT – Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love and Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff combined for 395 passing yards in the first half but it’s only a 10-7 Lions lead at halftime at Ford Field.
In a seismic play, the Lions were in the red zone with a chance to take a 17-7 lead at the break when star running back Jahmyr Gibbs fumbled. Officially, Isaiah McDuffie forced the fumble; in reality, it was Lions lineman Cade Mays. Brenton Cox recovered for a pivotal turnover, considering the Lions will get the ball to start the second half.
It is all Love for Green Bay. He’s 16-of-26 for 191 yards. Josh Jacobs has five carries for 8 yards as the running game contributed 25 yards on 11 attempts.
Here are some first-half studs and duds.
The Packers got a first-and-goal at the 6 on the opening series. The Lions, with arguably the worst defense in the NFL, were one of only three teams without a goal-to-go stop. So much for that, Josh Jacobs gained 3 yards on first down and was stuffed on second down. On third-and-goal from the 3, backup center Jacob Monk missed his block and nobody blocked Levi Onwuzurike, who chased Jordan Love out of the pocket and forced an errant throw to set up what should have been a chip-shot field goal.
After the opening drive stalled, Trey Smack made a 21-yard field goal, but the kick was nullified by a delay-of-game penalty – inexcusable but meaningless, right?
After the penalty, Trey Smack was wide right from 26 yards.
Detroit took advantage of the missed field goal to race 80 yards for the opening touchdown. Jared Goff was 3-of-3 for 68 yards, including two completions for 40 yards to Jameson Williams. First, Williams was wide open on a crossing route against Green Bay’s zone defense for a gain of 24 to the 16. On the next play, Williams motioned to the wing on the right, sprinted across the formation, caught a pass at the 17 and raced past the defense. He left Javon Bullard in the dust and beat Xavier McKinney to the pylon to make it 7-0.
The Packers answered with a critical drive to tie the game at 7. On fourth-and-2, Jordan Love hit Tucker Kraft just beyond the first-down marker. He broke a tackle and gained 17 yards after the catch for a gain of 22. Then, on third-and-9 from the 14, Kraft broke free as Jordan Love escaped the pocket. Right when it looked like Love was going to scramble for a potential first down, he fired a pass into the end zone for his second touchdown of the season.
With a tenuous pocket and without starting center Sean Rhyan (ankle) and backup Jacob Monk (quad), Jordan Love was 10-of-14 passing for 122 yards and one touchdown in the first quarter. That included a 27-yard completion to Savion Williams on fourth down and the aforementioned passes to Kraft on fourth and third down.
On the first play of the second quarter, with the Lions approaching the red zone, Dani Dennis-Sutton beat all-world offensive tackle Penei Sewell. He missed the tackle on running back Jahmyr Gibbs but Karl Brooks was there to clean up the mess for a pivotal loss of 5 yards.
One penalty and one completion later, the Lions had a third-and-5 from the 20. A receiver screen to Jahmyr Gibbs was blown up by cornerback Brandon Cisse for a loss of 2. That held Detroit to a field goal and a 10-7 lead.
On the first play of the ensuing possession, Jordan Love tried a play-action fake to Savion Williams. With the penchant for giving the ball to Williams on those sorts of plays, it was a decent idea. However, Aidan Hutchinson ducked under left tackle Jordan Morgan. By the time Love was done with the fake, he was being tossed to the turf for a loss of 10.
A good pass defense is the combination of pressure and coverage. So far, the Packers have had neither. Jared Goff is lighting up Green Bay’s secondary because he’s mostly had time to eat lunch and answer some texts. Good things come when there is pressure, though, including Anthony Campbell being credited for a sack and strip to essentially kill a drive early in the second quarter.
The Lions’ defense entered the game ranked 31st in the league in the red zone, with opponents scoring touchdowns on about 81 percent of their opportunities. Green Bay’s offense was a woeful 23rd with a 50.0 percent touchdown rate. So far, the Lions have won by limiting Green Bay to one touchdown in three tries. On third-and-4 from the 7 late in the first half, Jordan Love had nowhere to go and was almost intercepted. On fourth-and-4, Love completed a pass into the flat to Matthew Golden, who didn’t have a prayer.
All the misdirection stuff doesn’t work for Savion Williams. What does work is using him as a receiver. He had two catches for 47 yards in the first half – a 27-yarder on a fourth-and-5 in the first quarter and a 20-yarder on third-and-9 in the second quarter.
Here are a few excellent notes from Stats Perform’s Opta data and other sources
The Packers have beaten the Lions 106 times. The only teams with more victories over an opponent are the Packers’ 109 wins over the Bears and the Giants’ 107 wins over the Commanders.
How close has the series been of late? It’s 207-207 over the last eight games. Jordan Love has a 110-plus passer rating in four of the last five meetings, including a 123.4 mark in his three starts at Ford Field.
The NFC North entered Week 7 with a combined record of 16-6. That’s the best mark in the league. Because everyone is good, the Packers could end the day in second place or last place.
The Packers entered the game having not allowed a play of 25-plus yards for its last 204 snaps. That’s the longest streak for any team this season and Green Bay’s longest streak in the last 30 years.
Matthew Golden is one of the NFL’s breakout stars. He entered the day averaging 83.5 receiving yards per game. That’s 57.7 more yards compared to last year. That’s the largest year-over-year improvement by an NFL player since the Browns’ Josh Gordon was plus-67.3 from 2012 to 2013.
The Packers have intercepted multiple passes in three consecutive games. That’s tied for their longest stretch since a four-game run in 2014. They have seven interceptions the last three games, as many as they had all of last season.
The Lions are 3-2 despite allowing 20 touchdowns. They are the first team in NFL history to allow 20-plus touchdowns in the first five games but have a winning record.

title: Packers-Lions Inactives: Eye-Opening Moves at Guard But Who’s Starting?
full_text:
DETROIT – Kevin Zeitler won’t be making his starting debut against his former team.
In fact, Zeitler won’t be playing at all.
The veteran right guard is inactive for the Green Bay Packers’ game at the Detroit Lions on Sunday. Instead, Travis Glover will make his fourth consecutive start.
On the other hand, Aaron Banks, who had been expected to be the starting left guard this season, is active for the first time since Week 2 against the Jets – his only game of the season. Is Banks back on the gameday roster or will he replace Laken Tomlinson in the starting lineup?
That question was answered once warmups begin, with Tomlinson staying in the starting lineup. He and Travis Glover will make their fourth consecutive start together.
Laken Tomlinson is starting. Aaron Banks a backup. pic.twitter.com/LkMU25Pm8G
The Packers’ inactives are:
RG Kevin Zeitler signed a one-year, $4.05 million contract after the offensive line imploded in the blowout Week 3 loss against Atlanta. It included a $1.22 million signing bonus. He played on special teams the last two weeks.
In his first 14 seasons, he started 213 of 214 appearances. From 2015 with Cincinnati through 2025 with Tennessee, Zeitler played in and started all but seven games.
“Hey, it’s just part of it,” Zeitler said this week . “It’s a big shoutout to Glove doing a great job out there as well as the group who’s been out there and kind of getting into a groove. Right now the only thing that matters is winning and right now they’re getting the job done. It’s a blessing. It obviously gives me time to keep learning the offense, keep getting back in the swing of things and I’ll be ready when I’m called upon, whenever that is. It is what it is.
G/C Donovan Jennings , who started for Banks in Week 1 and replaced Banks after halftime in Week 2, will be on the sideline for a third consecutive game.
C/G Jager Burton will miss his third consecutive game since his horrendous start against Atlanta in Week 3.
RB Kaleb Johnson is the odd man out with Josh Jacobs active.
CB Benjamin St-Juste will miss his second consecutive game with a hamstring injury, though he at least practiced this week.
LB Zaire Franklin , who was ruled out on Friday by coach Matt LaFleur after suffering an injured shin at practice on Thursday. With Edgerrin Cooper on injured reserve, the starting linebackers will be Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper.
As expected , after six weeks on the exempt list and following one week of practice, running back Josh Jacobs is active.
“My goal is to play,” Jacobs said on Wednesday. “I don’t know how much they’re going to allow me to play, honestly, especially with having a walkthrough today, I didn’t really get too many reps – real reps. I don’t know what their mindset is. If it’s up to me, I’m going to try to play.”
Also as expected, the odd man out in the backfield is Kaleb Johnson. Pierre Strong and MarShawn Lloyd carried the load the last two weeks with Johnson playing limited snaps. He got seven carries toward the end of the blowout win against Chicago two weeks ago and just one rush for minus-2 yards last week against Dallas.
The return of Jacobs should improve the Packers’ putrid rushing attack .

title: Josh Jacobs Will Play vs. Lions; How Should Packers Run Offense Going Forward?
full_text:
DETROIT – Running back Josh Jacobs will make his season debut on Sunday for the Green Bay Packers. He will be a critical addition for an offense that has been unable to run the ball at any point this season.
Heck, to say he’ll be a season-changing addition wouldn’t be hyperbole. The Packers are 4-2 with a three-game winning streak despite an offense as unbalanced as a teeter-totter with a ton of brick cheese on one end and a tablespoon of parmesan cheese on the other.
The Packers are last in the league in rushing with 59.8 yards per game and 2.97 yards per carry; Dallas is 31st with 76.0 rushing yards per game and Las Vegas is 31st with 3.03 yards per carry.
They are last in the league with 2.3 yards per carry on first down; Las Vegas is 31st with 2.8.
They are last in the league with 23 first downs gained on running plays; Las Vegas is 31st with 26.
They are 31st in average yards before contact and last in average yards after contact.
Jacobs will solve a lot of those problems with his vision, power and ability to fall forward to maximize every rushing attempt.
“He just has a different kind of juice to him,” center Sean Rhyan said. “Different vision, dawg. Can’t really ask for much more than for him to come back, and he’s coming back. So, we’re excited. Still going to block our plays as well as we can and go from there.”
However, coach Matt LaFleur has to be careful not to change the offense too drastically with the addition of a game-changing running back. In 2024, when Jacobs was a Pro Bowler in his debut season, they ran the ball on the third-highest percentage of plays. Last year, it was the fifth-highest percentage.
After being about a 50-50 split the last two years, the Packers are 30th with a run rate of 34.4 percent. To be sure, the Packers need to be more balanced.
But they don’t need to veer into the run-first attack of the past two seasons. Jordan Love has been too good to forget why the Packers have overcome the odds to be 4-2 despite a multitude of challenges ranging from dropped passes to players dropping out with injuries.
The trick will be for LaFleur to find his inner Goldilocks.
Love is a mediocre 15th in passer rating, though that number doesn’t paint an accurate portrait of his performance. According to Pro Football Focus, Love has had eight more passes dropped than any other quarterback. According to Next Gen Stats, he’s faced the third-most pressures.
However, he threw for 367 yards and two touchdowns in a blowout win over Chicago and would have blown past 300 yards and thrown at least three touchdown passes last week against Dallas without the drops.
Love is good enough to carry the offense if he gets enough help from his friends.
The addition of Jacobs would make life easier, though. Jacobs doesn’t need to run for 1,000 yards the next 11 games. He just needs to give the Packers a real rushing attack and keep them in favorable down-and-distance situations.
Last season, the Packers averaged 4.1 yards per first-down carry, or not far from double this year’s 2.3 average. What a difference it would make for Love to face second-and-5, second-and-6 or second-and-7 instead of second-and-8, second-and-10 or second-and-worse.
Second-and-shorter means third-and-shorter. The Packers’ average third-down conversion requires 7.6 yards, which ranks 22nd. They’ve faced the fifth-most snaps of third-and-10 or longer. No wonder they were last in the league on third down before last week’s victory over Dallas before surging to a lofty 24th now at 35.5 percent.
On third-and-10 or longer, they’ve converted 23.1 percent of the time. On third-and-6 or shorter, they’ve converted 47.5 percent of the time.
And then there’s the passing game. Even with no rushing attack, Love dropped a series of play-action bombs on the Bears two weeks ago. The Cowboys, however, weren’t taking the bait last week. Love had seven play-action dropbacks and was just 1-of-6 passing for 7 yards with one sack.
Teams will ignore the Packers’ running game with Jacobs in the lineup at their own peril. The Packers’ superpower on offense is Love going downfield to Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. More favorable down-and-distance situations and a real play-action attack will give them opportunities to make big plays.
The final area where Jacobs can help the Packers win is when it’s time to close out games. There will come a time when they’re going to have to run out the final few minutes. So far, the Packers are averaging 1.1 yards per carry in the fourth quarter. That’s a full yard worse than any other team.
Overall, though, after playing with training wheels with Aaron Jones in 2023 and Jacobs in 2024 and 2025, Love has earned the right to have the offense run through him. Jacobs should be the player in the supporting role and not the other way around.
“We’ve done some good things in the passing game, and it definitely helped us when our run game hasn’t been up to the standard that it has in the past,” Love said this week. “So, yeah, I think nothing will change. I think we’ll continue to lean on that.
QB1 pic.twitter.com/fLqs5VpYyF
“We’ll give Josh as many touches as he needs. Try to get him rolling. Obviously, first game back for him, he’s missed a lot of time, so it’s one of those things we’ll see. And I think Josh, he’s also a big factor in the pass game, as well, catching checkdowns, catching screens, things like that. So, yeah, he’ll have a huge impact on us, but I think still got to keep the game plan, the mindset of what we’ve been doing, just stay with it.”

title: Sacked: Three Reasons Why Packers Will Lose Shootout Against Powerful Lions
full_text:
DETROIT – The surging Green Bay Packers will face one of their biggest tests of the season on Sunday against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field.
The Lions have an elite quarterback with Jared Goff. An elite running back with Jahmyr Gibbs. An elite receiver corps led by Amon-Ra St. Brown. The offensive line is powerful.
To extend their winning streak to four games, the Packers are going to need to play their best game this season. Are they capable of eliminating their abundance of unforced errors to score enough points to beat the high-powered Lions?
No. Here are three reasons why the Packers will lose.
The Packers have played against one really good running back this season. That, of course, was the Week 3 game against Atlanta, when they were swamped by Bijan Robinson, who is either the best or second-best running back in the NFL.
On Sunday, they will face the Lions’ Jahmyr Gibbs, who is the other back in contention to be the best in the business.
Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon understands the challenge.
“He’s faster than everybody,” he said. “He has elite vision, I would say. He can make any cut that you want, he’s got really good contact balance, he’s stronger – for not like a huge back, I think he breaks a lot of tackles. And in the pass game, he’s a run-and-pass threat.
“He’s a really good player. Big-time challenge. We always say point of attack. There’s certain plays at the point of attack where the ball is. All 11 are at the point of attack when you defend this guy.”
There’s no place like home for Gibbs. On the road, he averages 4.77 yards per carry. At home, he averages 5.77 yards per carry. That’s the best in NFL history among running backs with 300-plus career carries in home games, according to Stathead.
The Packers have done well against him, though. In six career matchups, he’s never hit 70 rushing yards and he’s rushed for only one touchdown.
“We play him twice a year, so knowing who he is and knowing exactly what we got to do to contain him, because there’s going to be some plays where he’s going to get his,” nickel Javon Bullard said. “Sometimes it’s inevitable in this league – good players are going to make good plays. I think all of us have to do our job and be on the same page so we can contain them.”
Robinson leads the NFL with 785 rushing-receiving yards, a number gained over six games. Gibbs is third with 747 yards in five games.
He is one of five running backs in NFL history with at least 700 scrimmage yards and nine scrimmage touchdowns in his team’s first five games, and the first in almost a quarter-century. Three of the other backs are Pro Football Hall of Famers Jim Brown (1958 and 1963 with Cleveland), Eric Dickerson (1983 with the Rams) and Emmitt Smith (1995 with Dallas), and the other player was Priest Holmes (2002 with Kansas City).
Asked if there were lessons learned from the game against Robinson – the only game in which Green Bay’s run defense faltered – coach Matt LaFleur said:
“Sure. Lessons on what not to do. You’ve got to do a great job of maintaining your leverage. Everybody’s got certain leverage points on the play, and the other thing is you cannot relax for 1 second against this guy because he’s capable of reversing field and scoring touchdowns. He’s got elite change-of-direction skills, he can stick his foot in the ground, bounce one way, but he’s also got elite home-run speed, and then he’s also a factor out of the backfield.
“Shoot, he could go probably line up at slot receiver for most teams. I just think he’s a really dynamic player in this league.”
The Packers have to slow down Gibbs. Otherwise, the player listed below might be unstoppable.
Jared Goff has his flaws but it’s impossible to ignore his incredible efficiency. Since the start of the 2024 season, he is second in the NFL with a 108.9 passer rating. He is first in passing yards and passing touchdowns and third in yards per attempt and completion percentage.
It’s been more of the same this season. Goff has thrown 12 touchdowns and zero interceptions.
As is the case with most quarterbacks, Goff is lethal from a clean pocket. According to Pro Football Focus, he ranks fourth this season with a clean-pocket passer rating of 122.7. With time, he’s completed 74.1 percent of his passes. When pressured, he’s completed 50.0 percent. He also leads the league in play-action yards.
“I think it’s tough for any quarterback to throw when he’s on his back,” coach Matt LaFleur said. “You’ve got to try to move guys off the spot. I think he’s done such a tremendous job. He doesn’t need a lot of space to let the ball go. He’s pretty confident in what he sees, he will let it rip, and he trusts his playmakers to go make the plays. He’s always been a really decisive quarterback.
“He handles pressure really well, very poised, and I’ve always had a tremendous amount of respect, especially working with him for a year and just watching how he went about his business. Got a lot of love and respect for him.”
With Micah Parsons providing 2.5 sacks and serving as the closer, the Packers won 31-24 during last season’s game at Ford Field. Without Parsons, the Packers’ pass rush has been predictably sporadic. Mostly, it’s been up to Jonathan Gannon to create it.
The team’s four best pass rushers are arguably Parsons, Lukas Van Ness, Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin. Parsons and Cooper are on injured reserve and Franklin, an impact blitzer, won’t play after sustaining an injured shin at practice.
So, from Green Bay’s perspective, the best defense might be a productive offense. Maybe the only way to make life difficult for Goff will be forcing him to play from behind and getting him into third-and-long situations so Gannon can get creative.
“I think it’s going to be making sure that we put the ball in the end zone, scoring points, making them feel like they’ve got to push the ball down the field,” safety Xavier McKinney said. “And then I think another part of that is going to be the disguise game and what we do disguise-wise.”
A good pass defense, as any coordinator would quickly tell you, combines rush and coverage.
The Lions have a great pass rush. They play no coverage.
It defies belief that the Lions are No. 1 in the NFL in sacks and No. 32 in passing yards allowed.
Even while playing one fewer game than most teams, Detroit leads the league with 20 sacks. With so much attention paid to Pro Bowl defensive end Aidan Hutchinson (four sacks) and defensive tackle Alim McNeill (3.5 sacks), D.J. Wonnum enters the game tied for sixth in the league with five sacks.
Hutchinson, of course, is the game-wrecker. He had 11.5 sacks in 2023, 7.5 sacks in only five games in 2024 and 14.5 sacks in his comeback season in 2025. He rushes the passer from the left and the right side, meaning he’ll be probing for mismatches against left tackle Jordan Morgan and right tackle Anthony Belton, neither of whom have been consistently good.
Love has played much better this season when under pressure. He was at or near the bottom of the league last year in completion percentage, yards per attempt and passer rating when pressured. This year, according to PFF, of 34 quarterbacks who have been pressured at least 30 times, Love is 18th in completion percentage, fourth in yards per attempt and 13th in passer rating.
He destroyed the Cowboys last week, when he was under siege throughout but was 9-of-15 for 135 yards and one touchdown.
“Yeah, going against a good defense,” Love said on Wednesday when asked about facing a good pass rush with a sore back. “It’s one of those things where we see them twice a year so we’re familiar with these guys. First time playing them this year, but we know what that team’s about. Obviously, good defense, good offense, as well.
“It’s one of those things where you’ve got to have the right mindset coming into the week and just put all the preparation and focus into what we might see from them. And, obviously, we’ve got to go out there and play our best game and put…

title: Packers-Lions Prediction: Will Green Bay Beat Odds So It Can Beat Rivals?
full_text:
DETROIT – One of the biggest games of the season for the Green Bay Packers comes with one of the biggest scheduling mismatches imaginable.
The Packers are coming off a Sunday night home game. The Lions are coming off a Sunday at their homes with their bye week. So, Detroit – in a huge NFC North game, mind you, that could have playoff ramifications – has been given by the league a home game and a week of rest.
Will it matter? Here are our predictions.
Since the start of the 2020 season, teams with a home game after their bye are 63-41, according to Stathead. That’s an enormous advantage.
Will that alone decide the game? Probably not. But in a game between two quality teams – the Lions are 3.5-point favorites – it might not take much to be the tipping point. Eight consecutive games at Ford Field between the teams ended with a one-score differential; the last exception was in 2017, when Brett Hundley was the Packers’ quarterback.
Both teams are going to score points. A lot of points. The over/under of 55.5 points is the highest on the board at FanDuel.
The Lions on offense have been a well-oiled machine. It tallied 30 points in five of six games this season and is second in the league in scoring. Quarterback Jared Goff hasn’t thrown an interception all season. He is surrounded by probably the best quartet in the league with receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams, running back Jahmyr Gibbs and tight end Sam LaPorta.
Green Bay’s defense was great last week against the Dak Prescott-led Cowboys passing attack, but it didn’t have to contend with a back like Gibbs, who is arguably the best in the league – especially at home.
The Packers have been hit and miss on offense – which is about what you’d expect for a team with a big-time quarterback and two big-play receivers but with an inconsistent offensive line and an unimaginably bad running game.
The matchup is favorable, though, because the Lions’ defense has been terrible. It ranks 30th in points allowed and 32nd in total defense. At its current clip, it will threaten the 2011 Packers as the worst pass defense in NFL history.
For the Lions, the best defense has been a good offense. They are 3-2 despite allowing 20 touchdowns. According to Stats Perform’s Opta data, they are the first team in NFL history to allow 20 offensive touchdowns and have a winning record through five games.
Ultimately, three big issues stand the Packers’ way.
One, they have struggled to protect Love. Well, the Lions lead the NFL in sacks even while playing one fewer game than most teams. Can Green Bay’s tackles overcome the noise to keep Aidan Hutchinson away from Love?
Two, they have struggled to pressure the quarterback at times. Goff is an elite quarterback when given time. As coach Matt LaFleur said this week, “It’s hard for a quarterback to throw when he’s on his back.” Can the Packers put Goff on his back enough? Furthermore, the Green Bay defense will line up without Micah Parsons, Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin.
And, finally, there’s this festering problem: The Packers have fatal flaws they haven’t solved. Love has been stymied by 19 drops; no other quarterback has more than 11. They lead the league in penalties and penalty yards. Love has faced the third-most pressures.
“The simple stuff, whether from scheme-wise or the understanding of what we’re trying to get done, when you have some mistakes that can lead to negative plays, that’s the stuff we got to clean up and be better at,” Love said.
It’s those things that will put the Packers at a disadvantage in every big game – no matter the location or scheduling quirk – until they get them fixed.
Ultimately, the team that makes the fewest mistakes will win. Based on the first five games, it’s hard to believe that will be the Packers.
Bill Huber’s Prediction: Lions 31, Packers 27.
The Packers have lost too many games like these in recent years, which have caused them to travel the long road in the postseason.
In 2024, they lost all but one division game, which played a significant factor in them being the seventh seed in the NFC playoffs. Last year’s late-season debacle in Chicago essentially sealed their fate that the wild-card meeting rematch would be at Soldier Field instead of the friendly confines of Lambeau Field.
Simply put, the Packers need to knock off the Lions on the road on Sunday to keep pace with those in front of them and remain in position to be a legitimate NFC North contender.
In a game where points should be scored in bunches, one mistake could be the difference. Who do you trust more to play clean and disciplined?
Dan Campbell's Lions or Matt LaFleur's Packers?
That, combined with the Lions being at home off a bye, gives them the nod.
Jacob’s Prediction: Lions 34, Packers 31

title: Texans Dealing With Key Injury in WR Room After Loss vs. Giants
full_text:
The Houston Texans got hit with a reality check in their Week 7 loss vs. the New York Giants, as they would end up falling short in an overtime defeat, 21-27 that now sinks them to a 2-5 record on the year heading into the bye.
However, it seems the Texans were also hit with a key injury in their wide receiver room in the midst of their Week 7 loss, according to head coach DeMeco Ryans .
And that injury was to none other than second-year wide receiver Jaylin Noel, who ended up leaving in the middle of Sunday's contest against the Giants before inevitably being unable to return.
Per DeMeco Ryans' post-game press conference following Houston's loss vs. the Giants, the Texans' head coach revealed that Noel had suffered a turf toe injury against New York.
"Jaylin Noel had a turf toe injury. He's still being evaluated," Ryans said on Sunday.
Obviously, there's not a ton of information that we can gather from Ryans' post-game comments when it comes to Noel's status moving forward. However, a turf toe injury––depending on the exact severity––is one that can lead to some missed time for any player in the league.
Noel finished the game against the Giants with just two receptions for a loss of three yards. According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson, Noel was also reportedly in a walking boot following the Texans' loss.
The good news for the Texans is that they'll be heading right into their bye week following the events of their Week 7 loss. Which means, for Noel, he'll have an extra week of rest to bank on before he'll be tasked with suiting up for Houston's next game.
However, even with that extra time off, there's a chance that Noel could be due to miss some time for the Texans moving forward–– which would undoubtably be a big loss to Houston's offense knowing how strong of a start to the season the second-year wideout has had through seven weeks.
Through the start of the Texans' season, Noel has put together a total of 19 receptions for 331 yards and two receptions, really becoming one of the team's most noteworthy playmakers in the passing game, even with the immense depth that's come to surround him in the wide receiver room.
His ability as a downfield playmaker, someone who can excel after the catch, and even as a kick returner has shown up big in his second year pro. Yet, depending on just how bad his new turf toe injury might be, there's a chance the Texans will be forced to push ahead without him for a few games moving forward.
If Noel is due to miss any time for the Texans' offense, C.J. Stroud will be forced to lean on some other playmakers in this wide receiver room that does have the depth to support a solid offense, even without the second-year talent.
Keep an eye on the obvious candidates of Nico Collins and Marvin Harrison Jr. to likely see more responsibilities in the Texans' offense in the weeks ahead.
Yet, you can also expect guys like Kayshon Boutte, Xavier Hutchinson, and Tank Dell to step up and provide the playmaking this offense could desperately utilize without one of their more potent names at the position group altogether.
We'll likely know more on Noel's long-term status a bit better once we get to next week's practice leading up to the Texans' Week 9 battle vs. the Los Angeles Chargers. However, certainly brace for the possibility that this offense could be without Noel for some stretch of time, depending on how bad the toe injury is truly deemed to be.
