title: 3 Winners, 6 Losers From Texans' Deflating Week 7 Loss vs. Giants
full_text:
The Houston Texans have now dropped their fifth game in the first seven weeks of the 2026 NFL season a fter a brutal overtime loss against the New York Giants in Week 7 , 21-27.
There were a lot of blemishes of note for the Texans in this one. Players on both sides of the ball had their respective issues from start to finish in this game that ultimately led to Houston's fate looking as it did after extra time.
However, even throughout all of the chaos that the Texans faced on their home field in Reliant Stadium in Week 7, a select few names managed to shine through with a solid performance that provides a bit more optimism for their individual stock moving forward.
So as the dust is still settling from what's due to be considered one of the Texans' worst losses of this season, let's break down a set of three winners and six losers that set themselves apart from the crowd within Sunday's action.
Even in what was a pretty rough loss for the Texans' all around, you've got to give credit where it's due for the leader of Houston's run game in Woody Marks.
Marks was tasked to be the lead ball-carrier for the Texans throughout the day in a game where Houston had just two active running backs on the roster. And even after having to leave the game in the third quarter with an apparent leg injury, he managed to return and post a pretty solid stat line, all things considered.
19 rushes for 66 yards comes out to 3.5 yards per carry, and he also chipped in for a 15-yard reception in the process. He'll likely go back to splitting carries with his veteran counterpart in Montgomery after next week's bye, but for the time that he's been Houston's RB1, he's handled those expectations pretty well.
The Texans entered this game knowing that they were going to spread the ball around within their deep wide receiver room. And that's exactly what happened. All six active wide receivers on this roster managed to catch at least one ball over the course of this matchup vs. the Giants.
But in the process, the Texans found themselves essentially shutting out Collins of their game plan on that side of the ball entirely. Houston's star wideout finished the game with just two receptions for six yards; by far his lowest numbers of the season so far.
Of course, in a receiver room like the Texans have with many moving parts, there's going to be growing pains like there were in this game. Yet, coming out of the bye, Houston's can't afford repeat performances like this from Collins, knowing that he's the best talent on that side of the ball entirely.
Yes, Marvin Harrison Jr. did catch his first touchdown pass as a part of the Texans' receiver room. But that one play doesn't take away from just how limited he was over the course of the day in Houston's passing game.
That one six-yard touchdown reception was one of just four targets that Harrison Jr. was able to convert on throughout the day. After his hot start with the team just last week in London, you'd have expected those numbers to look a little bit better than they ultimately ended up being.
However, like Collins, the Texans now find themselves needing to figure out how to better include Harrison Jr. in their offensive plans after the bye. And if unsuccessful, it'll be hard for Houston's steep investment of a second-round pick to look like a wise move––especially if the losses keep on piling up.
One big bright spot for the Texans in an otherwise gloomy day in Houston: Tank Dell returned to the field for the first time in over 670 days. And in his first appearance back on the field, he turned in a pretty explosive 43-yard reception that turned out to be this offense's best play of the day––even if not exactly by design.
Dell didn't get involved much outside of that one play besides a two-yard rush in the second half. However, this day was bound to be a successful one for Dell knowing all the hard work it took to get back on the field once again since his devastating knee injury. Expect to only see more of him moving forward.
This game was another example of Texans Pro Bowl cornerback Kamari Lassiter not looking like his 2025 self, as he'd be a prime factor in what would be many explosive downfield plays from the Giants' offense over the course of the day.
Malik Nabers had his fourth-straight game with over 100 receiving yards. Malachi Fields chipped in for 88 yards on four catches. Perhaps those woes could be pinned on Houston's secondary as a whole, but there were multiple occasions in which Lassiter would simply get beat in his individual matchup, and thus let up a big chunk of play from J.J. McCarthy.
For this Texans' defense to be at its best, Lassiter's performance is a huge part of that. So far this season, he's been stuck in a bit of a third-year slump that Houston is now desperate for him to get out of.
The Texans' star edge rusher Will Anderson Jr. started off this season on about as high of a note as you could ask for. He had been a dominant force against opposing quarterbacks and offensive lines, having recorded a total of seven sacks through five games.
This showing from Anderson though would make for back-to-back games of failing to take down the opposing quarterback for a sack. His co-star on the Texans' defensive line, Danielle Hunter, took care of business for one himself, but Houston's Defensive Player of the Year candidate still left more to be desired.
In Henry To'oTo'o's second game back on the Texans' front seven from his shoulder injury that took him out for the first four weeks of the season, he made his impact felt in a multiple ways on the defensive side of the ball.
To'oTo'o became the Texans' second-leading tackler on the day (10) in a game where this defense really struggled in that department, while also recording two tackles for loss, one quarterback hit, and 0.5 sacks.
The Texans are going to need some of their key defenders around that side of the ball to step up over the next few weeks if they want to revert back closer to their 2025 selves. Thankfully, To'oTo'o held up his end of the bargain in Week 7.
No, we haven't forgotten about Texans second-round pick Marlin Klein. But it almost seems as if Houston's coaching staff has completely shut him out from their weekly plans entirely.
This would be Klein's fourth straight game of being deemed a healthy scratch on the Texans' active roster. His stat line has been stuck at his one catch for 21 yards ever since he made a nice play in the first game of Houston's season back in Week 1 against the Buffalo Bills, all because of what the team staff describes as a need to improve on special teams.
Well, the Texans' special teams can't look much worse than it does right now––at least outside of how Ka'imi Fairbairn has been performing as of late––so maybe it wouldn't hurt to give the day two pick a chance in the lineup moving forward.
While this blame for this loss could be put onto several names for the Texans, one aspect of the equation that can't go without some criticism is Houston's coaching staff––who didn't seem to have many redeeming qualities to bank on for this week in any of their three phases.
The offense looked without any dynamic ability and creativity compared to what was shown last weekend. The defense was an even worse blemish for Houston in this game, with their lack of tackling and lackluster coverage. Special teams still had their respective lapses. Penalties remained egregious, especially offensively.
And now at a 2-5 record on the year, it makes you wonder whether or not there's a change that needs to be made in some area of the Texans' personnel or coaching staff heading into the bye week.
At the very least, DeMeco Ryans needs to do some deep soul-searching of how to get this group back on track for the second half of the season. Right now, it's not looking too pretty.

title: 5 Key Quotes From Texans' DeMeco Ryans After OT Loss to Giants
full_text:
The Houston Texans dropped to 2-5 this weekend after logging a humbling overtime loss vs. the New York Giants on their home field , 21-27, that now leads this team into the bye week facing some big questions.
And after the Texans' latest loss, we were able to hear from head coach DeMeco Ryans at his post-game press conference, where he gave some candid thoughts on how he feels about his crew following the events of this contest.
Let's take a look at five key quotes from Ryans' post-game following up from Houston's overtime defeat:
The Texans' offense was far from as polished as they looked this time last week in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars. They had just 237 yards of total offense and went 3-12 on third-down.
As to why Ryans feels the offense struggled, he points to two factors: sustaining drives and converting on those third-down opportunities.
"We'll look at the film and see what happened offensively, but from my perspective, it comes down to third down," Ryans said of the Texans' offensive struggles. "You have to sustain drives and stay on the field on third down. We converted only three third downs, and that's definitely not good enough. That's not winning football."
"To beat a team like this, we knew we had to control the game. To control the game, you have to sustain drives. We didn't do that."
The Texans recorded eight penalties for 80 yards over the course of their matchup against the Giants. It's turned into a common trend for Houston to struggle when it comes to penalties this season, as they now average over eight flags per game through seven weeks.
Ryans went on to call the Texans' penalties ridiculous, and emphasized that the team has to get them fixed moving forward.
"The penalties are ridiculous. It keeps happening over and over again, so we have to find a way to fix it or get different people in so we don't make the same mistakes repeatedly."
The Texans looked extremely sloppy in pass coverage against a Giants offense that really didn't enter this game seen as the most daunting task to defend. In J.J. McCarthy's first start with New York, he finished with a solid 252 yards with over a 70% completion rate, while also not giving away a single turnover.
Between missed tackles, botched coverages, and explosive plays, the Texans' defense was far from the elite level we know they can be. DeMeco Ryans addressed those struggles in pass coverage after the game.
"When I look at the passing game, somebody has made an error somewhere in the coverage if a guy is wide open," Ryans said. "We don't design coverages for guys to be wide open. We have to be better with the details of what we're doing and make sure our eyes are focused on our assignments."
On a more positive note, the Texans were finally able to see Tank Dell back on the field for an NFL game for the first time in over 670 days. He finished the game with one big explosive catch-and-run for 43 yards.
Ryans called the return of Dell both "electric" and "fun to watch," while also hinting that the Texans will continue to increase his workload in the weeks to come.
"It was very electric seeing Tank come out of the tunnel. It was an awesome moment. You felt the energy from our crowd and the emotions running high as he ran out of the tunnel for the first time in two years.
Then he created an explosive pass play for us. It was fun to watch. I'm proud of Tank and all the work he's put in. I'm happy he was able to contribute and get some plays out there today. This is just a start for him. We expect to continue increasing his workload and see him do more for us and create more explosive plays."
The Texans, who now sit three games under .500, enter their Week 8 bye with a lot on their plate to fix. DeMeco Ryans knows that.
Ryan’s did note after the game that he's "not there yet" when it comes to making big personnel or staff changes. However, he did emphasize what the Texans do need to accomplish moving forward to turn the ship around in the right direction.
"We keep playing and practicing well. We keep putting in the work. At the end of the day, football comes down to blocking and tackling and running the football," Ryans said. "The fundamentals of the game don't change."
"We have to block better, stop holding and stop hurting ourselves with penalties. We have to protect better. We have to be able to beat man coverage and cover in man coverage. We have to tackle."
"There's no magical elixir that's going to drop out of the sky and fix everything. We fix it by putting in the work and getting better at the fundamentals of football. We have to own it as coaches and players, and we have to find a way to turn this thing around."

title: 3 Texans Takeaways From Egregious Overtime Loss vs. Giants
full_text:
The Houston Texans put together what could be their worst loss of the 2026 season yet in their Week 7 defeat at home against the New York Giants, with a final score of 27-21.
After the Texans pieced together a late fourth quarter comeback to force overtime behind a strong drive from Woody Marks and the offense , it wouldn't take long for Houston to drop the ball with extra time to now fall down to their fifth loss in seven weeks.
The Texans now sit at 2-5, look extremely disorganized in all three phases of the game, and have a real interesting bye week ahead to try and fix the plenty of woes that faced them throughout the day against New York.
But before even thinking of turning the page past this week, let's break down three of the biggest takeaways from the Texans' latest loss against the Giants:
Turn the clock back to the start of this season. Many who had seen how dominant this Texans defense was capable of being over the course of their 2025 campaign had expected them to be even better than they were previously, to the point that they were seen as among the best collective units in the NFL.
Now, seven weeks deep into the 2026 season, and this defense could have a real case of being among the bottom ten units in the league. Especially after this performance, we might've just been witnesses to some of their worst results of the year thus far.
Multiple blown coverages, explosive plays downfield, a ton of missed tackles, and a Giants run game that caught fire late in overtime all contributed to the calamity that resulted here on Houston's home field. In all, the Texans allowed over 400 yards throughout the day and came out to 6.5 yards per play from New York's attack.
Do the Texans decide to shift their personnel around? Maybe pivot back to Matt Burke as their defensive play-caller ? Whatever the answer might be, Houston is almost forced to make a big change on this side of the ball moving forward, knowing how talented this unit can be, but also factoring in the brutal results that have led to five losses in seven weeks of action.
Stop me if you've heard this before: the Texans struggled immensely with penalties throughout the day.
The Texans finished their overtime outing against New York racking up a total of 10 penalties for 80 yards. Five of those flags came from the offensive side of the ball for offensive holding, and really held back this scoring attack––whether it be because they set back the drive, or simply by negating a big play to gain some yards.
The Texans are now up to a total of 58 penalties for 508 yards called against them through seven weeks. That's an average of over eight calls against them for 72 yards per game.
It's pretty easy to tell that such a formula is far from a winning recipe. Those flags and undisciplined play have been a consistent issue for this Texans roster all season long, and turned out to be a major difference in this game en route to an embarrassing loss at home.
The Texans are now 2-5 heading into their Week 8 bye. The past two weeks of wins against divisional opponents had offered some optimism that things were turning around in the right direction for the second half of the season.
But now, it's extremely tough to have that same confidence in this team after the events of this loss.
The offensive side of the ball looked stagnant and lacked any true identity. The defense lost any identity that they had previously built up through all of last season, losing their ability to cover, tackle, and generate any immense number of turnovers. This team still has failed to win a game at home.
The Texans couldn't have asked for their bye week to hit at a better time. Of course, the Texans have proven from the events of last season that a mid-season turnaround could be well within the cards. It was when Houston was at a 3-5 record when they went on to win nine straight games to end the year out.
Yet at the same time, these first seven games of the season have seemed to prove that this Texans team is anything but the same group as last year. DeMeco Ryans needs to stay busy in the lab throughout the next week off to figure out how to fix this group to forge together a similar run, but it remains to be seen if that same fate even possible at this point.

And for both sides, there's some key absences that are worth noting.

The Texans will be dealing with a few injury concerns in the form of a few starters being inactive for this Sunday; three to be specific.
The most notable of the Texans' absences will be none other than their versatile nickel defender Jalen Pitre , who's due to miss a second-straight week with the shoulder injury he suffered back in Week 5.
Given that Pitre's status was deemed week-to-week upon the announcement of his injury, there's some optimism that he'll be ready to get thrown back into the lineup in time for Week 9 after next week's bye. However, Houston will have to make some key changes to their defense without him in the meantime.
The Texans will also be without another starter in their secondary as Reed Blankenship sits in concussion protocol. Blankenship was also listed to have a hand injury throughout this week in practice, so he'll be getting the day off for this game against New York.
Then, the Texans will also be down their starting running back, David Montgomery, who, like Pitre, will be missing a second straight week after first going down in Week 5 with a groin injury . You can expect Woody Marks to take a large share of the workload in the backfield this Sunday, especially knowing that Houston only has two running backs on their active roster.
Of the names that will be active who are due for some attention, two players on the Texans' end stick out.
Of course, wide receiver Tank Dell is the big story here as he'll officially be taking the field for an NFL gamr for the first time in over 670 days . But also, offensive tackle Braden Smith will finally be making his debut for Houston after missing his first four games of the season on injured reserve, and has been out of the mix for the past two weeks.
Now, with Blake Fisher ruled out for his first game of the season, it allows for Smith to get his first opportunity of the year, likely in a similar role as Fisher, being a jumbo tight end/sixth offensive lineman in certain personnel.

For the Texans' offense that's just been finding some consistency through the air by the command of quarterback C.J. Stroud, that could set up for a much easier day on that side of the ball.

title: Why Derek Stingley Will Be Texans' Most Important Player vs. Giants
full_text:
The Houston Texans' Week 7 date vs. the New York Giants is right around the corner.
And for the Texans, it's a massive matchup for them to take advantage of. They enter the game as favorites of more than a touchdown , are looking to win their third straight game, while also heading into their Week 8 bye on a bit of a high note.
However, even while the Texans enter this one with the upper hand in terms of talent on paper, that doesn't mean this game is going to be easy–– especially against a talent like Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers . A standout game on his behalf could quickly make this game a bit more interesting to watch unfold.
And that's why, for the Texans, All-Pro cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. might be their most important player on the field this Sunday.
Throughout most of this season, Stingley hasn't exactly looked like the All-Pro talent he was over the course of last season. And really, that disappointing start could be said about a vast majorty of the Texans' output in the secondary.
For Stingley, he's allowed his highest passer rating when targeted throughout his career (87.3), while also failing to haul in a single interception through his first six games.
A large part of those lapses can be attributed to Houston's increased use of zone coverage. Stingley has played zone on 76.6% of his coverage snaps, up from 63.3% in 2025, and he's allowed 146 yards in those coverages–– already 41 more than he allowed throughout the course of 2025 (107).
This week though, the Texans could be preparing to decrease that usage of zone that's taken a hit to their secondary's production.
Their starting safety, Reed Blankenship––known to be a better fit in zone coverages–– has been ruled out with a concussion/hand injury . Houston will likely start M.J. Stewart next to Calen Bullock and hope to spark some similar success within this pass defense as was seen through 2025.
And that adjustment comes at a perfect time, because the Texans will be up against one of their more challenging matchups at wide receiver in Malik Nabers; someone who's seen 35 total targets over the past two games he's played in en route to hauling in over 23 receptions, 286 yards, and a touchdown.
The Texans can't afford to let Nabers have another explosive day against their defense. Nabers will be the centerpiece of the New York offense–– especially for a scoring attack led by J.J. McCarthy in his first start–– and any strong performance on his behalf will likely allow the Giants to stay within striking distance of an upset on the road.
So that's why Stingley Jr. needs to have a statement game here. Odds are, he's going to see a lot of Nabers over the course of this Sunday. We've seen just how badly an elite receiver can have their way against this Texans defense this season ( look back at CeeDee Lamb's stat line from Week 4 ), and a repeat performance here certainly wouldn't be ideal.
Not only would shutting down Nabers boost his individual stock after an up-and-down start to the season, but the Giants' ability to put points on the board takes a significant hit if their No. 1 target is completely shut out by one of the league's best cornerbacks.
Without Nabers making a huge impact, the playmaking for the Giants' offense comes down to the likes of Isaiah Likely, Malachi Fields, Darnell Mooney, and their currently dysfunctional running game committee.
That's a much easier assignment for the Texans to handle, and only becomes possible if Stingley holds up his end of the bargain for a standout day covering one of the league's best receivers on the other end.

title: 3 Reasons the Texans Should Beat the Giants in Week 7
full_text:
The Houston Texans' home date against the New York Giants for Week 7 is right around the corner.
And it's a game for the Texans that, when looking on paper, could be one that this Houston team has the upper hand in for multiple reasons.
Outside of the fact that the Texans are riding the high of two straight wins against a couple of divisional opponents, there are a select few aspects of this matchup that benefit Houston's chances of landing a big win pretty noticeably.
Whether it be matchup-based, the recent play of some key names on Houston's side, or a combination of both, there's good reason to believe that the Texans will be able to walk out of this weekend and into the bye week having logged a third straight win against this John Harbaugh-led Giants squad.
Let's break down three of the biggest reasons as to why the Texans should be able to beat the Giants in their Week 7 matchup at Reliant Stadium:
Turn the clock back to the start of the Texans' 2025 season. When sorting through each of Houston's matchups in terms of opposing quarterbacks, there's been a pretty steady trend of this defense getting the best of subpar play under center.
Last season, the Texans ravaged any lackluster quarterback that was sitting on the other side. Snoop Huntley, Mac Jones, Jacoby Brissett, Geno Smith, Riley Leonard, and Cam Ward (twice) were all prime examples of just that in 2025.
This season, Houston's been faced with some tough assignments in terms of those opposing quarterbacks through six weeks. However, they did take care of business against Ward and the Tennessee Titans once more in dominant 26-3 fashion.
Really, the only blip on the radar comes from this season's Week 3 loss vs. Daniel Jones and the Indianapolis Colts. Even then, the Texans' defense forced him to just 211 passing yards and three total turnovers.
Other than that loss, Houston has consistently dominated against signal-callers that aren't at least above-average talents at the position.
Now, take a look at the task Houston has on their hands this weekend: J .J. McCarthy is making his first official start for the Giants after a solid end to last week's game against the New Orleans Saints.
Unless McCarthy has some real magic up his sleeve, the Texans' recent track record tends to hint towards a favorable matchup from their perspective. And if Houston's defense can take advantage of McCarthy for a tough day and force a few mistakes, the road to victory becomes a whole lot easier.
One clear weakness of the Giants' defense is just how poor their efforts to stop the run have been through the first six weeks of the season.
New York currently sits in the bottom-five of the NFL for rushing yards allowed per game (135.5, and are only one of six teams in the league allowing a positive EPA per rush. The Giants also tie for second-lowest in the league for rushing yards over expected (+139).
Those numbers certainly make for a defense that the Texans can take advantage of in their game plan, even without the help of their starting veteran running back, David Montgomery, who's due to be sidelined for a second straight game due to a groin injury.
Now, let's state the obvious here: the Texans aren't a very good rushing offense. They're currently in the bottom 10 in the NFL for rushing yards per game (84.8) and are in the bottom four in the NFL for rushing success rate (34.5%).
However, the past two weeks of the Texans' production on the ground has been the best we've seen all season behind the lead of Woody Marks. He's averaging nearly four yards per carry while taking a hold of at least 15 carries a game, and has added a sense of playmaking and explosiveness that wasn't quite as noticeable when he was splitting touches with his veteran counterpart.
So knowing that Marks is set to take the lead role again in the Texans backfield against what could be their softest matchup of the year so far in terms of rushing defenses, there's little reason to believe he can't keep his recent momentum going for one more strong performance before the bye.
And if the Texans' run game is flowing, in addition to their rising passing offense and star-studded defense, the Giants quickly have a lot of challenges on their hands to take on if they want to defy the odds for a statement win on the road.
On top of the Texans' advantageous matchups in terms of opposing quarterback play and the Giants' run game, C.J. Stroud and this Houston passing offense have proven that they're catching their stride after a few weeks of bumps and bruises to start the season off.
He's limiting mistakes in a major way having recorded just one interception through six games, he hitting his highest completion percentage (65.3) and yards per game (285.7) of his career, and he's shown no signs of slowing down after last week's outing in London where he recorded over 300 passing yards with three touchdowns.
It's gotten to the point that Stroud is starting to sneak into some MVP-level play. And in this game, Stroud will have his arsenal of pass-catchers looking the deepest and healthiest it's been all season . That tends to make his chances of another big day look even better.
Now, the Giants' passing defense isn't anything to be overlooked, and they could make Stroud's job of extending his high-end play a bit easier said than done. New York is currently one of six teams in the NFL to allow less than 200 passing yards per game.
However, New York has consistently struggled to get pressure on the quarterback as well, currently tied for the second-lowest sack total (8) in the NFL through six weeks.
Stroud is going to have a lot of time in the pocket, and he's got the playmakers around him to move the chains. And when those two aspects of Stroud's supporting cast are in check, he tends to look a whole lot better individually as a result.

title: Texans' Latest Roster Decision Sets Woody Marks Up for Huge Week 7
full_text:
Without David Montgomery in the Houston Texans' lineup for Week 6 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, this offense heavily relied on second-year running back Woody Marks to lead the way on the ground with a majority of the work for the day.
Marks found his way to 17 touches both on the ground and in the passing game, combined for over 80 all-purpose yards, and turned in a second-straight week of solid performances en route to a big win in London.
Now, the Texans are heading into Week 7 against the New York Giants. Montgomery is out once again with the same groin injury , and Marks seems prepared to take a bulk of Houston's workload at the running back position.
And against a Giants rushing defense that hasn't been too stellar for six weeks of the season, there could a road for Marks to have another strong day as he's had for the past couple of games.
However, based on the Texans' latest roster decision for their running back room for Week 7, there tends to be even more optimism surrounding just how solid of a day Marks could have, strictly based on the vast opportunity he'll have on his hands.
According to KPRC2 's Aaron Wilson , sources say that the Texans will not be signing or elevating any running backs from the practice squad for Week 7 against the Giants––thus leaving Houston with just two running backs on the roster for this weekend: Woody Marks and Dare Ogunbowale.
The Texans do have a third running back on their practice squad in Deuce Vaughn that some speculated could be elevated on gameday in order to provide a bit more depth at the running back position.
Instead, the Texans will steer clear of using one of their practice squad elevations on Vaughn, and face this Giants team with as slim a running back room as they've utilized so far this season.
Now, of course, such a setup in the Texans' backfield isn't expected to be one that'll be used long-term. Odds are, Houston will see Montgomery return to the lineup as soon as they get out of their bye in Week 9 against the LA Chargers.
However, for this game against the Giants in particular, the Texans will have just two running backs to bank one; and one of those names in the backfield in Ogunbowale has yet to record a carry through six weeks of the season so far.
So when taking a step back to look at the Texans' running back situation for Week 7, all signs seem to be pointing towards a big day for Marks.
Through both Weeks 5 and 6, that Marks has been the lead ball carrier in the Texans' offense, he's seen a snap share of 85% and 78%, respectively . It seems almost certain that his snap share will look largely similar to those two showings in this weekend’s game vs. the Giants, and lead to what might be his most impressive statistical game yet.
So far this season, the Giants have found themselves ranked 29th in the NFL for total rushing yards allowed, and 31st in yards per carry allowed.
If the Texans can gain any consistency on the ground similar to the past two weeks, Marks will likely be the biggest beneficiary of that plan of attack. That already seemed to be the case leading into this weekend , but becomes even more certain now that Houston's depth at the running back position will probably be as barren as it will be all season long.

title: Texans' Biggest Keys to Victory vs. Giants to Extend Win Streak
full_text:
The Houston Texans have won back-to-back games heading into their Week 7 game against the New York Giants .
And with just one game to go before the Texans take on their bye, claiming a win here against New York to extend their win streak and head into the break on a high note would be a huge confidence booster after having previously started this season off at 0-4.
However, in order to add another win on the books here against the Giants, the Texans will have to ensure they take care of business with a select few keys to victory. And if they miss the mark on those, it'll make claiming a Week 7 win at home just a little bit tougher.
Let’s take a look at the Texans' three biggest keys to victory for their Week 7 battle against the Giants:
Through the first six weeks of the Texans' season–– even through the ups and downs of the first four weeks–– quarterback C.J. Stroud has done a really solid job of taking care of the football.
Since his Week 1 game vs. the Buffalo Bills , where he recorded a pair of fumbles, he's only had one interception, coming this past weekend against the Jacksonville Jaguars. And as Stroud has been able to be at some of his best when it comes to ball security and decision-making, it tends to have a domino effect on the rest of this offense.
The Texans get a road to more scoring opportunities themselves, and have a much easier time winning the turnover battle if Houston's defense steps up for their own takeaways.
Against a Giants team that's recorded a total of 11 offensive turnovers through six weeks, there's a perfect opportunity for the Texans to win that turnover battle once more on Sunday. That is, so long as Stroud and Co. can continue to limit their own mistakes. So far this season, they've done quite well.
The Texans' run game looked a whole lot better than usual this past weekend against the Jaguars in London, which came as a bit of a surprise given not only the challenge that Jacksonville's run defense presents, but also because of the fact that David Montgomery was sidelined due to a groin injury.
Woody Marks then stepped up to the plate as the Texans' RB1 for the week. And in a short amount of time, Houston's run game seemed to take a big step forward thanks to the explosiveness and dynamic playmaking ability that Marks provides.
Through the past two weeks, Marks has averaged 15 attempts per game, is averaging nearly four yards per rush, and has also chipped in for six receptions and 47 yards in that same stretch.
Now for Week 7, the Texans are in a pretty similar situation that they were against Jacksonville. Montgomery is out for another game, Marks is going to be the starter in the backfield, but this time, their matchup against the Giants rushing defense looks like a bit of an easier task to take on.
The Giants are allowing over 135 rushing yards a game through six weeks of the season, making them one of six teams in the NFL through six weeks to allow an average of 130 or more rushing yards per game. That tends to set up as a pretty advantageous matchup for Marks and the Texans.
If Marks can continue to be efficient in his opportunities on the ground in combination with what should be a potent passing attack, it’s going to become really tough for this Giants defense to contain the Texans from start to finish.
While the quarterback situation in New York has seen its fair share of changes this season–– even for this weekend as J.J. McCarthy is deemed the Giants' new signal-caller –– what has become very clear over the past two weeks is that this offense wants to get Malik Nabers involved however they can.
Nabers has seen a whopping 35 targets over the past two weeks he's been on the field for the Giants. He's turned those opporutnities into 23 receptions, 286 yards and a touchdown, and thus sets up for a real challenge for the Texans' defense to face up against this weekend.
The good news is that the Texans have the right personnel on paper to limit Nabers a bit more than he's seen through the past couple of weeks. With two star corners in Derek Stingley and Kamari Lassiter, Houston could have exactly what it takes to prevent a repeat performance from the Giants' star receiver.
The bad news is that this Texans secondary has been nothing like the form we knew it to be throughout 2025. Currently, Houston is allowing the sixth-most passing yards per game in the NFL and has been prone to getting exposed on several explosive plays over the course of the first six weeks this season.
If the Texans allow Nabers to have another impressive day as he has for the past two weeks, it could allow for the Giants to stay within striking distance of Houston down the stretch, and would thus lead to even further questions for this Texans secondary moving forward.

title: Shane Steichen Doubles Down on Daniel Jones Despite Poor Results
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have lost three straight games, fallen to 2-5, and watched their season spiral out of control. Yet head coach Shane Steichen apparently has no interest in reconsidering his quarterback situation.
Following Sunday's 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, Steichen reaffirmed his confidence in Daniel Jones, saying he has a “ton of faith” in the veteran quarterback.
At this point, that faith is unjustifiable . Jones has struggled all year and is a shell of the player the Colts had for 10 games a season ago.
Jones has thrown just four touchdowns to seven interceptions through seven games this season. Sunday's performance was another low point: he finished with 108 passing yards, no touchdowns, and an interception on the Colts' final drive.
The contrast with last season is stark. In 13 starts in 2025, Jones threw for 3,101 yards and 19 touchdowns against eight interceptions while completing 68% of his passes, giving the Colts a reason to believe he could be their answer at quarterback.
The current version of Jones has done little to warrant Steichen’s dogged commitment.
Despite those struggles, Steichen is digging his heels in, determined to do anything but entertain the possibility of benching Jones. When asked after Sunday's loss whether he had considered a quarterback change, Steichen said he had not, reiterating his confidence in the veteran.
Here’s the problem. Everyone can see that Jones isn’t producing the results necessary. That is, everyone but Steichen.
Steichen’s response is difficult to defend. Coaches should stand behind their players, but that support cannot come at the expense of making necessary decisions. Jones has had seven games to affirm last year wasn't a fluke, but he's done next to nothing to inspire confidence.
At 2-5, the Colts have reached a point where continuing to roll Jones out there with the starters week in and week out borders on malpractice.
The bigger question is what Steichen's refusal to consider a change says about Anthony Richardson. If Jones' struggles haven't been enough to prompt a serious evaluation of the alternatives, it raises questions about how the coaching staff views the former fourth overall pick and whether he has any realistic path back into the starting lineup.
Richardson hasn't exactly made his own case easier .
In addition to swinging and missing at his first chance as the starter, Richardson’s recent marijuana-related charge and subsequent comments expressing no regret have added another complication to an already uncertain situation.
Still, those issues shouldn't eliminate the possibility of giving him another chance. If Steichen no longer believes Richardson can be a viable option, the organization needs to confront that reality. If he does, it's difficult to understand why the Colts wouldn't at least explore a change with their season slipping away.
Richardson doesn't need to be the long-term answer to justify giving him another opportunity. With the season slipping away, there is little to no downside to finding out whether he can offer something Jones hasn't.
Even if Richardson fails to capitalize, Indianapolis would have a clearer picture of its quarterback situation heading into the offseason.
Ultimately, Steichen's unwavering support for Jones says as much about the coach as it does the quarterback. At 2-5, Steichen has every reason to reevaluate his approach. Instead, he appears determined to stick with his guy regardless of the results.
If Steichen is going down with the ship, he's making it clear that he'll do so on his own terms.

title: Biggest Winners and Losers From Colts' Loss to Vikings: Who Stood Out Most?
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts fell to 2-5 in the 2026 regular season after losing 16-10 to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings on the road.
While this season is all but over, there are still some positives to pull from, at least from an individual performance standpoint.
The current-look Colts are dead in the water , but not all is lost with their future outlook, regardless of how bleak it may seem.
With that being said, I'm taking the opportunity to break down who stood out most in the Colts' most recent showing.
Follow along as I break down the Colts' biggest winners and losers from their Week 7 loss to the Minnesota Vikings.
We've been watching Adetomiwa Adebawore's career with great interest, and it's slowly but surely paid off.
The Colts drafted Adebawore in the fourth round of the 2023 NFL Draft (110th overall), betting on his absurd athletic profile and intriguing pass-rush tools.
The fourth-year interior defensive lineman was always envisioned to become the ideal complement piece to veteran DT DeForest Buckner, and that vision is quickly coming into shape.
Adebawore improved upon his career-best performance from earlier this season, a 1.5-sack showing against the Houston Texans, with a legitimate arrival against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 7.
Against the Vikings, Adebawore was all over the place:
5 tackles, 2.0 sacks, 2 tackles for loss, 1 pass broken up, and 2 QB Hits.
Adebawore notched career-highs in sacks and tackles for loss, and now sits with a career-best four sacks after just seven games.
Even though Adetomiwa Adebawore is breaking out right at the worst time for the Colts, aka doing so on an expiring deal when the franchise is staring down a full-blown rebuild, the belief the organization has shown in him throughout the years may grant them a solid building block for the future once free agency comes around.
Shocker: Jonathan Taylor is still a superstar running back.
Taylor had one of his best performances of the 2026 regular season against the Minnesota Vikings, totaling 95 rushing yards and one score on 18 carries.
Taylor's 5.3 yards-per-carry is his best single-game performance of the season so far, and although he failed to reach 100 yards rushing for the first time this season, it's still impressive considering the Colts' opponents have been regularly stacking the box and/or blitzing to disrupt Daniel Jones and Co.
More than anything else, Taylor's performance improved his personal stock.
As the NFL trade deadline nears (11/10 at 4 PM EST), teams will be calling the Colts as they embark upon a cleaned house, and Jonathan Taylor is the top trade candidate to call about.
Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as "a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," according to ESPN Insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter .
This makes sense given his fresh extension and consistent production, but the Colts can't value loyalty over the future if the right price comes calling.
Any legitimate Super Bowl contender will be interested in Jonathan Taylor's services, especially those without a bona fide RB1, so while it'd be ideal to keep him around for the looming rebuild, the Colts can't turn down worthwhile trade compensation.
The Colts' second pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, safety A.J. Haulcy, is finding his footing as an NFL starter.
Haulcy has had some up-and-down showings to kick off his NFL career, but against the Minnesota Vikings, he appeared to have an "I get it now" moment.
The Colts' third-round pick (78th overall) led the team in total tackles (9) and solo tackles (5) in their Week 7 matchup against the Vikings.
Haulcy did have a miscommunication in coverage that led to the Vikings' lone touchdown of the day, but I'm willing to chalk it up to rookie growing pains.
Outside of his lone blip in coverage, Haulcy was lights out.
The rookie defensive back was flying around the ball and looked to be the ideal Nick Cross replacement at strong safety that the Colts envisioned he could become.
Although the future is bleak, at least some of the Colts' recent draft picks are looking like solid foundational pieces to build on.
The Indianapolis Colts know what the quarterback carousel looks like after a near-decade of Chris Ballard roster construction, and Daniel Jones's recent installment looks no different.
Jones had arguably his worst showing of the season in Week 7 , which is saying something, considering he's had a handful of stinkers to choose from, and was fresh off his poorest performance of the year against the then-winless Tennessee Titans.
Against the Minnesota Vikings, Jones had similarly poor showing:
13-22 (59% completion) for 108 passing yards (4.9 yards per completion), one interception, and was sacked four times for a 52.8 passer rating
According to Next Gen Stats, Flores' Vikings defense blitzed Jones and Co. on 85.2% of dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four of its sacks coming when blitzing.
The Vikings knew exactly how to stop Jones and Co., and the Colts did nothing to stop it.
Jones is just one of two starting quarterbacks in the NFL who have thrown more interceptions (7) than touchdowns (4) through seven weeks of play, joining Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert.
The Colts may have financially tied themselves to Daniel Jones for the foreseeable future, but there's an out in his contract that would allow Indianapolis to save ~$38 million if they make him a post-June 1st cut designation.
Regardless of what the Colts decide when it comes to Jones's future in Indianapolis, we've been given no reason to believe that he'll magically become the brief version of himself that helped the Colts jump out to an unforeseen start in 2025.
There's simply no justification as to why Daniel Jones should remain the Colts' starting quarterback moving forward , despite whatever belief head coach Shane Steichen says he has in him.
Aside from his first kick attempt of the new season, a missed extra point attempt, Spencer Shrader was perfect entering Week 7's matchup against the Minnesota Vikings.
Shrader was a perfect 19-for-19 on field goal attempts entering Week 7, including an impressive 6-for-6 on 50+ yard attempts.
However, when the Colts' anemic offense needed him most, Shrader vanished.
Shrader went 1-for-3 on field goal attempts against the Vikings, his second miss being a 48-yard attempt that would've tied the game 13-13 with a little over four minutes remaining in the fourth quarter.
To be fair, Shrader had been the team's MVP through six weeks of play, but as Ross Tucker said during the broadcast, "it's like every week, somebody for the Colts takes turns not doing their job."
I wouldn't be too concerned with Spencer Shrader moving forward, as the worst thing we learned about him from his uncharacteristically poor performance is that he's indeed human after all.
Shane Steichen's Colts offense looked to have found a groove against the Minnesota Vikings, as they went 8-15 on third-down conversions and successfully converted their lone fourth-down attempt; it wasn't enough to suggest that they'll perform any better down the stretch.
The Colts entered Week 7 with the worst turnover margin (-8) in the NFL, having gone 11 consecutive games without winning the turnover margin — the longest active streak in the league and the longest for Indianapolis since a 13-game stretch in 1998-99, according to Next Gen Stats — and that streak continued as the Colts lost the turnover battle (-1) against the Minnesota Vikings in Week 7.
Neither Steichen nor defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo is doing enough to get the job done.
Although longtime general manager Chris Ballard's midseason firing and the ongoing pressure from ownership suggest they would be coaching elsewhere come next season, the coaching staff's collective seat is getting hotter by the week.

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly From the Colts’ Loss in Minnesota
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts suffered another frustrating defeat on Sunday, falling 16-10 to the Minnesota Vikings on the road. What began as a promising afternoon ended in another missed opportunity for a team desperately searching for something to build on.
Indianapolis has now lost three consecutive games and dropped to 2-5 on the season. With the losing streak growing and the season slipping further off course, the pressure is mounting on a franchise that needs to find a way to turn things around.
Here's a look at the good, the bad, and the ugly from Sunday's loss.
Indianapolis leaned heavily into their run game against a Vikings defense that caused chaos for Daniel Jones through the air.
The Colts recorded 154 rushing yards as a team, with Jonathan Taylor accounting for 95 by himself. Taylor also had the lone Colts’ touchdown, a 38-yard scamper in the first quarter.
Seth McGowan was the most impressive, however. He saw the most run of his young career up to this point, knowing the Colts needed to keep Taylor fresh if they were to continue leaning into the run game.
McGowan had 46 yards on 11 carries, both career-highs. If Indianapolis does have a true fire sale ahead of the trade deadline and move on from Taylor, McGowan will have a chance to audition for a larger role in the seasons to come.
It’s safe to say Adetomiwa Adebawore has finally arrived.
The fourth-year defensive tackle was easily the best player for a Colts defense which played with the most energy and effort we’ve seen from them this season. Adebawore logged two sacks, his second multi-sack game of the season, tying his career-high for sacks in a season (4).
Adebawore is a pending free agent at the end of the season. If Colts interim general manager Ed Dodds signs him to a contract extension, I don’t think there would be many complaints.
With the DeForest Buckner era all but over, Indianapolis may already be looking at their 3-tech of the future.
The Vikings defense entered Week 7 leading the league in third-down defense, allowing a conversion just 22% of the time. Yet, the Colts found a way to have success.
Indianapolis finished 8-for-15 on third down (53%), with several conversions coming on the ground. For a unit that came into the game moving the chains just 37.3% of the time, that’s a noteworthy improvement.
Unfortunately, that didn't translate to more points.
The Colts offensive line knew they’d be blitzed, and blitzed, and blitzed again by Brian Flores’ defense. But even knowing what was coming, they couldn’t handle the pass rush.
Minnesota got to Daniel Jones for a sack four times, picking on the Colts running backs in pass protection most of the time. It’s the second week in a row the Colts have surrendered at least that many and the fifth time this season they’ve given up multiple in a game.
While Jones isn’t blameless himself, the Colts offensive line, which was supposedly one of Indy’s biggest strengths, has been all over the place through seven games. A lot to clean up moving forward.
Shane Steichen is far from devoid of blame for this loss.
Steichen's offense continues to look increasingly dysfunctional. Indianapolis managed just 10 points despite winning the time of possession battle. While the Vikings have one of the league's best defenses, Steichen couldn't find a way to consistently generate offense when the passing game stalled.
The Colts leaned heavily, maybe too heavily, on Jonathan Taylor and the running game, but that wasn't enough to compensate for the lack of a passing attack.
Steichen deserves criticism for failing to find answers against Brian Flores' aggressive defensive scheme as well as continuing to stick with Daniel Jones at quarterback, especially with the season slipping away.
Daniel Jones didn't make enough plays in the passing game, but it’s not all on him.
Indianapolis' receivers did little to help Jones against Minnesota's aggressive defense. Josh Downs managed just two catches for 18 yards, while no Colts receiver finished with more than 31 receiving yards.
The offensive line and Jones deserve plenty of blame, but the pass catchers didn't do their job, either.
Shane Steichen has continued to vehemently defend Daniel Jones to the media despite continued poor play. Sunday, Jones did nothing to back his head coach’s claims up.
Jones managed just 108 passing yards and threw an interception on the game’s final drive, ending any chance the Colts had at a late comeback.
Steichen can continue to stand behind his quarterback publicly, but at some point, the results have to justify that confidence. Jones has done little to warrant the unwavering support, and Sunday's performance only strengthened the case that Indianapolis needs to reconsider its options under center.
With the season already a wash at this point, the Colts truly have nothing to lose by giving Anthony Richardson Sr. a shot. Your move, Shane.
Indianapolis' pass rush was once again a major disappointment.
Adetomiwa Adebawore came to play, but the rest of the defensive front did not, struggling to consistently pressure Kyler Murray or disrupt Minnesota's passing game. The rest of the defense covered for their pass rush and found ways to get off the field, but that can only take a defense so far.
For a team that entered the season with questions about its ability to rush the passer, Sunday was yet another reminder that the problem remains unresolved.
DeForest Buckner can only do so much (and may be on the way out), and Indianapolis needs more players capable of making an impact up front. With the Colts now 2-5, addressing that weakness should be a priority as the organization evaluates its roster moving forward .
Spencer Shrader has been one of the most consistent players on the Colts this season, but Sunday was his worst performance of the season so far.
Shrader picked a bad day to have a bad day, missing two field goals, from 56 and 48 yards each. Given the Colts lost by six, those misses ultimately made the difference.
Definitely a day to forget for the 27-year-old, who can only hope a day like Sunday is just a fluke.

title: It's Time For Colts to Accept Their Fate: Loss to Vikings Confirms Rebuild is Imminent
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts fall to 2-5 in the 2026 season after losing 16-10 on the road to the undefeated Minnesota Vikings.
The new look (same old?) Colts lose their first game since firing longtime general manager Chris Ballard, proving that the roster he built is simply not good enough.
The Colts actually looked like a competitive team for most of the game, as most post-firing squads appear, but at the end of the day, this is the same roster that got Ballard fired after six weeks.
Indianapolis' season is over, and now the Colts need to put all of their focus and resources into kicking off their rebuild.
Colts' head coach Shane Steichen has put his undying faith in quarterback Daniel Jones , and this loyalty has resulted in an unsustainable offense through seven games of the 2026 regular season.
The Colts' offense looks nothing like it did in the early stages of the 2025 season, the very version Steichen has clung to for far too long.
A worse offensive roster and lingering side effects from Jones's infamous torn Achilles have given us peak Daniel Jones (derogatory), and Steichen's continued belief in his starting quarterback has become unwarranted.
Entering the Colts' Week 7 road matchup against the Vikings, Daniel Jones was just one of three starting quarterbacks with more interceptions (6) than touchdowns (4), and that trend only continued in Minnesota.
This was always set to be a brutal matchup for Daniel Jones and Co., but man, did it bring out the worst in the Colts' starting quarterback.
Jones has struggled immensely against pressure this season, specifically against the blitz.
Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is known for his blitz-heavy scheme, and he took advantage of the matchup in question.
According to Next Gen Stats, Flores' Vikings defense blitzed Jones and Co. on 85.2% of dropbacks, the highest blitz rate by a defense in a game in the Next Gen Stats era (since 2016). Minnesota generated pressure on 60.9% of those blitzes, with all four of its sacks coming when blitzing.
As a result, Jones put up the following numbers against Flores and Co.:
13-22 (59% completion) for 108 passing yards (4.9 yards per completion), one interception, and was sacked four times for a 52.8 passer rating.
Following the loss, head coach Shane Steichen said that he has not considered a change at quarterback because he has "a ton of faith in Daniel [Jones]."
But through seven weeks of play, there's no reason to think this offense led by Daniel Jones is so much better than one led by Anthony Richardson or Riley Leonard that Indianapolis needs to ride this train until the wheels fall off.
Steichen is wrong to be so confident in this version of Daniel Jones , and such loyalty may be his ultimate undoing as the Indianapolis Colts' head coach.
The Indianapolis Colts wanted to give Shane Steichen one last fair shake after longtime general manager Chris Ballard was let go, but that's already looking like a mistake.
The Colts aimed to treat their next two games against the undefeated Minnesota Vikings and the division-leading Jacksonville Jaguars as final tests for how this roster will look once the regular season ends, seeing if there's enough to warrant keeping top trade pieces around for a playoff push.
The season was already over entering this two-game stretch, as evidenced by the roster, but this showing against the Vikings proved that this version of the Colts is not good enough.
After longtime assistant manager Ed Dodds took over as the Colts' interim general manager earlier this week , it was revealed that head coach Shane Steichen and all non-personnel staff will report directly to ownership for the remainder of the season.
The Colts are at a point where trading off as many assets as possible for the future is most important, but they can still muster a miracle out of their current roster, but Steichen has refused to give them that hypothetical look.
There have already been numerous instances this season where Steichen could turn to Anthony Richardson, whether that be as a pure rushing threat in the red zone or as a last-resort Hail Mary thrower.
Steichen has been out on Anthony Richardson since the young quarterback's sophomore season showcased a brutal example of the 'terrible twos,' but with his seat hotter than ever, you'd expect him to make any move that could save his job.
Richardson's recent charge for marijuana possession provided Steichen with more reason not to turn to him , but there's simply no reason not to turn to any quarterback not named Daniel Jones at this point.
Steichen's unwarranted belief in starting quarterback Daniel Jones is at the forefront of such coaching malpractice, and this decision to roll with Jones may just be his own final nail in his coffin.
The Indianapolis Colts have become the hot topic of the NFL trade deadline for the second consecutive season - but not because they're unforeseen buyers, but because they've become sellers.
No player is expected to be off-limits if the Colts indeed decide to begin wholesale changes to their roster, but there are a couple of players they'd prefer to keep around for the new era.
Star running back Jonathan Taylor is still viewed as a cornerstone player.
Colts Owner/CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon views Taylor as "a key part of the organization and a likely mainstay in their rebuild," according to ESPN Insiders Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter .
This makes sense given his fresh extension and consistent production, but the Colts can't value loyalty over the future if the right price comes calling.
A high second-round pick remains the starting point in negotiations, but if a contender wants to trade away a late first-round selection for Taylor's services, you simply cannot say no.
Taylor is no doubt a superstar that you can lean on, but with the Colts' immediate future looking bleak without a first-round pick at their disposal, you have to take that opportunity.
Taylor will help the 2027 Colts stay afloat, but he'll be 29 years old entering his first season alongside Indianapolis' quarterback of the future, if they choose to do so in the 2028 NFL Draft.
Furthermore, the Colts would likely also like to re-sign future Hall of Fame guard Quenton Nelson to kick off the rebuild, but his expiring contract makes convincing almost impossible.
Nelson has stuck around for multiple rebuilds, and given that he's reached his thirties, a fresh start elsewhere feels most likely.
Finally, the Colts are in such a brutal position when it comes to draft capital due to their blockbuster trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner at the 2025 trade deadline, which included two first-round picks in compensation.
Indianapolis would likely jump at any opportunity to recoup any lost capital from said trade, but given that Gardner has played in just 10 games since joining the Colts, it's likely they won't receive even a fraction of what it cost to obtain him.
Ideally, the Colts start their rebuild with a franchise pillar on each side of the ball (Nelson, Gardner), but if enough compensation comes calling, tearing down the franchise to its studs could be on the table.
Outside of those three players, as well as wide receiver Alec Pierce and any players still on their rookie contracts, the Colts are shopping their entire roster.
The only thing that would hold them back from making such a drastic move is the state of the AFC South. The Colts remain second in the division despite their 2-5 record, but the Jaguars aren't too far behind at 4-2.
However, the lowly AFC South shouldn't determine how the Colts operate moving forward. The season is over, and the future is now.
Noah Compton is the Publisher of Indianapolis Colts On SI. Noah is from the Indy area and has been covering the Colts since 2022, including stops at FanSided, The Blue Stable, and SBNation.

title: Colts Could Make Entire Roster Available Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts could be approaching a significant turning point in their season. After firing general manager Chris Ballard, the franchise now faces a decision that could reshape its roster heading into 2027.
With Indianapolis sitting at 2-4 and the NFL trade deadline approaching on Nov. 10, the next few weeks will determine whether the organization remains committed to trying to win with its current roster or begins getting ahead of the rebuild that's on the horizon.
According to NFL insider Tom Pelissero, the Colts have received strong trade interest in offensive guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. Pelissero also reported that no player is expected to be off-limits if Indianapolis decides to sell before the deadline.
Despite the team's recent struggles, Indianapolis wants to see whether head coach Shane Steichen can get the season back on track before making any major decisions about the roster.
NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport explained the team's approach during an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show , saying, "They want to give Shane Steichen the opportunity to see if he can win games."
Rapoport added that the next couple of games may determine whether the Colts commit to contending for a playoff spot or begin to get the ball rolling on their inevitable roster retooling.
"If they win two, it's like okay, we're in the mix, it's still out there, we'll see what happens," Rapoport said. "If they lose two then it's like, alright, we probably know which way the season is going, let's capitalize on some of these really good assets."
The bad news for the Colts is that the schedule offers little room for error. Indianapolis faces the undefeated Minnesota Vikings before traveling to Jacksonville to take on the 4-2 Jaguars, a place they haven't won since 2014. So the path forward is far from encouraging.
If the team fails to respond, the organization will shift its attention toward preparing for the future. With Ballard already gone, the next few weeks could determine the direction taken by the next permanent general manager.
Nelson and Buckner are the most prominent potential trade candidates after Pelissero reported that both have drawn strong interest. The veteran offensive guard and defensive tackle are in the final year of their current contracts, making them attractive options for contenders seeking immediate help.
Nelson has been a cornerstone of Indianapolis' offensive line since being selected sixth overall in the 2018 NFL Draft. Trading him would leave a significant hole up front, but it could also allow the Colts to acquire valuable draft capital before he's a free agent. That way, they get something in return.
Buckner could provide a contender with an immediate boost to its defensive front. Green Bay has reportedly explored the possibility of acquiring the veteran, with Packer Report's Easton Butler identifying a second or third-round pick as Indianapolis' reported asking price.
The Packers have called the Colts about DTs Grover Stewart and DeForest Buckner, per source. The asking price for Bucker is a 2nd/3rd, while Stewart is a 4th. pic.twitter.com/dYGXGIWwWR
Butler also reported that the Packers had inquired about defensive tackle Grover Stewart, with a fourth-round pick representing the reported asking price. Those figures are only potential starting asking prices and any deal would also need to account for the financial implications of acquiring either player.
The most consequential possibility could involve running back Jonathan Taylor. Multiple teams have reportedly expressed interest in the star, and Butler's reported asking price is a first-round pick plus additional compensation, though that feels steep for a running back, even a star.
The Colts are opening to trading some key players, following the firing of GM Chris Ballard. One of the players is RB Jonathan Taylor, but the price wont be cheap. Per sources, the Colts are looking for a 1st + more for the star RB. pic.twitter.com/KmdAGOHXWM
Taylor signed an extension in August and remains under contract beyond this season, making a potential trade a much larger commitment to a rebuild than moving veterans approaching free agency. Still, if a team is willing to meet Indy's high asking price, then Taylor may be onto a new chapter.
Although Indianapolis could make much of its roster available, it would be foolish for the organization to blindly accept whatever offers come its way.
The reported asking prices suggest the Colts want meaningful compensation for their established players. Taylor's reported price is particularly notable, while the potential returns for Buckner and Stewart could give Indianapolis additional selections to work with in future drafts.
The team's draft situation adds another layer of complexity to those decisions. Indianapolis lost its own 2027 first-round pick in  the trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, making the possibility of recouping premium capital especially relevant if the franchise ultimately decides to rebuild.
Of course, asking prices are mere speculations of what the Colts may receive. The market for each player will depend on competing offers, contract considerations and how aggressively other teams pursue reinforcements before the deadline.
For now, Indianapolis appears willing to give Steichen and the current roster another opportunity to respond. But if the next few games go poorly, the organization could quickly shift its priorities toward the future.
And no player will be off-limits in that scenario.

title: Colts 5 Best Bets to Cash in Week 7 Against Undefeated Vikings
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are 2-4, their general manager is gone, and trade rumors are swirling around some of the biggest names on the roster.
Some think this team is ready to roll over. I think there are plenty of players with a fire lit under them, and despite Minnesota entering undefeated and favored by 6.5 points, I believe Indianapolis can stay inside the number.
Through six weeks, we're 13-3 on Colts-specific props and 15-13 overall. Even if this team keeps making Sundays painful, hopefully we can keep making them profitable.
Here are my best bets for Week 7.
Brian Flores is intimidating and his defense's unprecedented pressure rate is exactly why I like this play.
Minnesota has blitzed on 77.8% of its defensive snaps this season, meaning Jones will likely be forced to move around against one of the league's most aggressive defenses.
Jones rushed for 30 yards against Tennessee last week, his highest total of the season, and cleared this line in his last regular-season matchup against Minnesota.
As he continues working back from his Achilles injury, it's about time Jones starts getting after it with his legs again.
At this point, Taylor is one of the few things keeping this Colts offense afloat.
He has seven rushing touchdowns through six games and has found the end zone nine times over his last nine games.
With Indianapolis' passing attack struggling, Minnesota will undoubtedly focus on slowing Taylor down. But sometimes it's simply good-on-good, and I'm trusting the Colts' best offensive player to find the end zone again.
We have ridden this bet all year, it has cashed in five straight games, and Shrader is a perfect 18-for-18 on field goals this season.
Flores' defense has been immaculate, and I can easily see Indianapolis moving the ball enough to create scoring opportunities without consistently finishing drives.
Shrader has cleared this line in eight of his last 10 games and 11 of his 14 healthy career starts with Indianapolis.
Until this bet stops printing money, I'm going to continue to put it on the card.
Addison is developing chemistry with Kyler Murray, hauling in five receptions against Tampa Bay and four against Miami in his last two games played.
He also caught five passes the last time he faced Indianapolis, and with Sauce Gardner ruled out, this secondary could have its hands full.
I expect Murray to look Addison's way plenty on Sunday.
Murray has completed 27 and 24 passes in his last two starts, and this line has hit in seven of his last 10 games. Indianapolis' coverage unit ranks 29th in the league via PFF, and with all the turmoil surrounding this franchise, the defense has plenty to prove.
Unfortunately, I expect Murray to do what just about every quarterback has done against this Colts secondary: carve it up.
The Colts might surprise people with their effort Sunday, but that doesn't mean their defensive problems will suddenly disappear.
The approach is straightforward this week. Trust Taylor, keep riding Shrader, and take advantage of the matchups Minnesota presents. Good luck and bet responsibly.
