title: Colts Stars Respond to Trade Rumors as Deadline Approaches
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts have already made one massive change this week, and with the Nov. 10 trade deadline getting closer, the speculation is not slowing down.
Since firing general manager Chris Ballard on Monday, Indianapolis has become one of the NFL's most intriguing teams to watch as the trade deadline approaches. At 2-4, names like DeForest Buckner, Jonathan Taylor and Quenton Nelson have naturally been pulled into trade conversations.
I still don't believe the Colts should tear this roster down. There are too many cornerstone players worth keeping around for whoever takes over this front office next.
But the players themselves are hearing the noise, and this week, several of the biggest names in Indianapolis addressed their futures.
Buckner is probably the easiest name to connect to trade speculation because he is 32 years old and playing on an expiring contract.
When asked directly whether he wants to remain with the Colts, though, Buckner wouldn't entertain the conversation.
“Yeah, right now I'm just focused on the Vikings,” Buckner said.
He acknowledged that he knows how the business works, but called the speculation a distraction. His focus remains preparing to help Indianapolis beat Minnesota on Sunday.
Buckner also spoke highly of Ballard, saying the two had a “great relationship” and that he has “nothing but love for him and his family.”
Like the rest of the locker room, Buckner's approach to a chaotic week has been simple: move forward and focus on the task at hand.
Taylor was much more emotional when discussing Ballard, the general manager who drafted him in 2020.
“Just lost for words,” Taylor said. “Definitely upset because at some point, it's on the team as a collective, coaches and players, in order to prove the GM right.”
Taylor said Ballard meant “a ton” to his career, pointing to their Wisconsin connection and the belief the organization showed in him coming out of the draft.
As for the possibility of being traded, Taylor wants no part of that conversation right now.
“I haven't given it any thought,” Taylor said. “That'd be crazy right now.”
He called looking ahead to what could happen a disservice to his teammates and the organization with an undefeated Minnesota team waiting Sunday.
Taylor also made it clear why he wanted to remain in Indianapolis when he signed his recent extension. He praised the way the organization treats its players and staff, calling the Colts “a special place.”
Nelson took a similar approach when asked whether Ballard's departure created questions about his own future.
“No, I have no questions,” Nelson said. “I leave that up to God.”
His focus is on getting better and being at his best this week, and Nelson called facing an undefeated Vikings team a “great opportunity” for Indianapolis to start turning things around.
But when asked if Indianapolis is somewhere he would like to continue playing long term, Nelson left little doubt.
“I love it here,” Nelson said. “Met my wife here. Really appreciate and love this organization.”
Nelson also expressed appreciation for Ballard, recalling the accountability his former general manager showed him as early as his rookie season.
For now, Buckner, Taylor and Nelson are all saying essentially the same thing: ignore the noise and prepare for Minnesota.
The trade rumors aren't going away before Nov. 10, especially after a front-office shakeup. But at least publicly, three of the Colts' biggest names are more concerned with saving this season than worrying about where they might be playing next.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Anthony Richardson May Have Just Put Final Nail in Colts Coffin
full_text:
Just when it looked like Anthony Richardson might have one last path back onto the field for the Indianapolis Colts, another problem has entered the picture.
Richardson is facing a misdemeanor charge for marijuana possession stemming from an Oct. 12 traffic stop in Carmel, Indiana.
According to court records, Richardson was pulled over after police noticed an expired registration that did not match his vehicle. An officer reported smelling marijuana, and Richardson admitted he had smoked inside the car so he would not do so around his children.
Police found a small amount of marijuana and THC-infused gummies inside the vehicle. Richardson was briefly handcuffed during the search, but he was not taken into custody and was instead issued a summons.
The charge was formally filed Oct. 19, and a bench trial is scheduled for Jan. 4, 2027.
“We are aware of the situation involving Anthony Richardson and are currently gathering additional information. We will have no further comment at this time,” the Colts said.
The timing could not be much worse.
Indianapolis is 2-4, Chris Ballard was fired Monday, and Daniel Jones has struggled through six starts with 1,290 passing yards, four touchdowns and six interceptions.
That had at least reopened the conversation about Richardson getting another opportunity if Jones continued to struggle. Noah Compton recently argued for Colts On SI that putting Richardson back on the field should at least be on the table as Indianapolis evaluates what is left of this season.
Richardson remained QB2 behind Jones for Sunday’s loss to Tennessee and has continued practicing with the team since the Oct. 12 stop.
Also, forty states have legalized cannabis for recreational or medical use, while Indiana remains without either a recreational or comprehensive medical marijuana program. Richardson just happens to play in one of the states where possession can still result in a criminal charge.
So no, this shouldn't suddenly change everything. But Richardson could still face consequences from the NFL.
Under the league's substance abuse policy, a first-time violation of laws involving drug possession can result in a suspension of up to four games, depending on the circumstances.
That is far from a guaranteed suspension, but it adds another layer of uncertainty to Richardson's future in Indianapolis. For a quarterback already struggling to find his way back onto the field, potentially losing more time is the last thing he needs.
The stop happened one day after Indianapolis lost 34-22 in Pittsburgh. One week later, the Colts lost at home to a previously winless Titans team, Ballard was fired the next morning, and now this becomes public four days later.
Everything surrounding this team is moving downhill fast.
If this ends up serving as the final nail in Richardson’s Colts coffin, it would be an unfortunately poetic ending to one of the most dysfunctional quarterback experiments this franchise has had.
A former No. 4 overall pick with rare physical talent, repeated injuries, a 2024 benching and a lost starting job may now have his Indianapolis tenure further complicated by something that, in most NFL markets, probably would not have become much of a story at all.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Grading Every Colts Position Group Through Six Weeks
full_text:
The Indianapolis Colts are six games into the 2026 season, and at 2-4, there is plenty of blame to go around.
Most of it belongs on the defensive side of the ball, but there are still a few bright spots keeping this team competitive. Here is my position-by-position report card through six weeks.
Daniel Jones has been underwhelming, throwing for 1,290 yards, four touchdowns and six interceptions while completing just 59.6% of his passes.
His legs have also been a complete non-factor with only 55 rushing yards, but there are two important caveats: he is still working back from a torn Achilles, and this receiving corps has given him very little help.
Jonathan Taylor is once again proving he is one of the best running backs in football.
He has 492 rushing yards and seven rushing touchdowns, tied for the most among NFL running backs through six weeks. But Seth McGowan and the rest of the room have provided very little offensive impact behind him.
Injuries have crushed this room, but the production has still been nowhere near good enough.
No one has consistently created separation or provided the explosive element this offense desperately needs, allowing defenses to key in even more on Taylor.
Tyler Warren is carrying this room.
The tight end room has accounted for three of Indianapolis' four passing touchdowns, but five different tight ends have combined for only around 275 receiving yards.
This is one group I am not putting much blame on.
Indianapolis owns PFF's third-best run-blocking grade at 74.0 and seventh-best pass-blocking grade at 71.1, and the offensive line has given this offense enough to be much better than it has been.
The Colts rank 31st in run-defense grade via PFF, and the pass rush has not been much better.
This group simply has not gotten to the quarterback consistently, which has made life even harder on an already shaky secondary.
This has been one of the worst position rooms on the roster.
Akeem Davis-Gaither has had some strong moments against the run, but the coverage has been poor, the run defense has been inconsistent and the rookie linebackers have done very little to inspire confidence moving forward.
Indianapolis owns PFF's 28th-ranked coverage unit at 43.6, and the corners have struggled against both the pass and the run.
Sauce Gardner has been decent overall, but quarterbacks have had far too much time in clean pockets, exposing this secondary repeatedly.
Cam Bynum and A.J. Haulcy have both fallen short of expectations.
Bynum finally recorded his first interception against Tennessee, but both safeties have been inconsistent in coverage and against the run.
Special teams has easily been the most reliable unit on this team.
Spencer Shrader continues to deliver, and Rigoberto Sanchez remains one of the league's best punters. The blocked punt against Tennessee was a disaster, but this unit has still been one of the few consistent positives through six weeks
Six weeks in, the Colts have far more questions than answers, and the grades reflect exactly that.
Jonathan Taylor, the offensive line and special teams have done their part, but the rest of this roster needs to step up in a hurry. If Indianapolis has any hope of turning this season around, the defense has to start pulling its weight.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: What Shane Steichen Must Do to Save His Job With the Colts
full_text:
Chris Ballard is gone. And if this season keeps trending the way it has, I have a hard time believing Shane Steichen will be far behind.
Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon made her expectations clear when she fired Ballard on Monday. The standard is to compete for championships, and at 2-4, Indianapolis is nowhere close right now.
Steichen still has 11 games to change that. Here is what I think he needs to do to remain the Colts' head coach in 2027.
First and foremost, Steichen has to start winning football games.
This roster is too talented to finish under .500 again. Indianapolis went 8-9 in each of the last two seasons, and after Irsay-Gordon preached urgency all offseason, another losing record should not be enough.
At 27-30 through his first 57 games, Steichen has yet to make the playoffs. He needs to show signs this team is moving forward.
A winning season might not be enough by itself. The Colts need to find a way into the postseason.
Jacksonville sits two games ahead at 4-2, so winning the AFC South will require a serious turnaround. But whether it comes through the division or a wild-card spot, Indianapolis needs to be playing meaningful football in January.
This is where I need to see Steichen take more ownership.
The Colts allowed 24.2 points per game in Lou Anarumo's first season and are allowing 27.3 through six games this year. Those results are not good enough for a team that has invested heavily on defense.
Steichen has always been known for offense, but being a head coach means owning all three phases. If this unit continues to struggle, he has to be willing to make changes.
Jones looked completely different in 2025, completing 68% of his passes with 19 touchdowns, eight interceptions and a 100.2 passer rating. Through six games this season, those numbers have fallen to 59.6%, four touchdowns, six interceptions and a 71.1 rating.
Steichen was hired in large part because of what he helped build around Jalen Hurts in Philadelphia. That 2022 Eagles offense leaned on an elite offensive line and dominant rushing attack to make life easier on its quarterback.
The Colts have Jonathan Taylor, a strong offensive line and enough weapons to do something similar. Steichen has to find that version of his offense again.
Lastly, this team has to stop beating itself.
The Colts just blew a 13-0 halftime lead to an 0-5 Titans team, with a blocked punt helping swing the game. Irsay-Gordon specifically talked about finishing games when she brought Steichen back after last season.
Bottom line: Steichen needs to win, make the playoffs, fix the defense and prove the offensive creativity that got him this job is still there.
If he cannot do that over the next 11 games, I would expect the Colts' next general manager to be hiring a new head coach.
Michael Greene is a graduate of Indiana University and the Scouting Academy. He's in his first year covering the Indianapolis Colts and NFL, with a unique focus on fantasy football.

title: Jaguars Get the Perfect Week 7 Outcome Thanks to AFC South Rivals
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- As far as bye week Sundays go, this one could not have gone much better for the Jacksonville Jaguars.
The Jaguars had some clear games they needed to see go their way in Week 7 as they enjoyed their bye week after a 4-2 start, and that is exactly what they got. Of course, they got some welcomed help from their AFC South rivals in the process.
The AFC South went 0-3 during the early afternoon slate of games on Sunday, with the Houston Texans losing at home in overtime to the New York Giants, the Tennessee Titans losing on a walk-off field goal against the Cleveland Browns, and the Indianpolis Colts losing yet another game, this time against the Minnesota Vikings.
The Jaguars were always going to remain in firm control of first-place in the AFC South regardless of Sunday's results, but their position was made even stronger by the fact that every single other team dropping their Week 7 game. As a result, the Jaguars gained a bit of a cushion against the rest of their rivals, with the space between them and the Texans as the highlight.
The AFC South through 7 weeks: pic.twitter.com/ltUY5NJ9BT
The Jaguars will get another chance to take a big step in the AFC South over the next few weeks, starting with Week 8's game against the Indianapolis Colts. With the Colts now at 2-5 and offseveral brutal losses, it certainly stands to reason the Colts could shop some of their key veterans and look very different a week from now as their season continues to slip out of control.
The Colts are already a cursed team when it comes to playing games in Jacksonville, but they could reasonably trade any of Jonathan Taylor, Quenton Nelson, or DeForest Buckner over the next week as they prepare for next year's rebuild. If the Colts are without any of those players, a scenario that was made more possible by Sunday's loss, then they are an even easier target for the Jaguars to hit next week.
As for the Texans, they are on a bye next week. This means a Jaguars win over the Colts in Week 8 would bring the Jaguars back to being three games ahead of Houston in the AFC South, which was the exact spot the Jaguars were in before they lost to Houston in Week 6. Few teams start 2-5 and win their divison. Even if the Texans are still far from done, they took a big hit this week.
The Jaguars play three AFC South games in their next five weeks, with next week's game against the Colts and then two games against the lowly Titans in the next four games after that. In part due to today's results, the Jaguars can make things look very, very good for their playoff chances by December.
Outside of this week's news about left tackle Anton Harrison being ruled out for the rest of the season , the bye week went about as good as the Jaguars could have hoped. Consider this a winning weekend for Duval and Liam Coen's squad.

title: 4 Players the Jaguars Desperately Need to Step Up After the Bye Week
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars' bye week is almost over, and it is nearly time for the Jaguars to turn their focus to the rest of the 2026 season.
The Jaguars are in a good place as they enter the final day of their bye week, but things can always get better, can't they? The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 right now and in first-place of the AFC South, but they will need a team effort to continue their winning ways over the next few months.
For the Jaguars to keep taking strides after the bye week, though, they will need to see a few players take some big steps to pave the way. Here are those players they will need to seize the moment the most:
Walker Little is set to be the Jaguars' starting left tackle after Anton Harrison's season-ending injury , and the Jaguars will need him in a big way. Little played very well against the Houston Texans in the Week 6 loss in Houston against the NFL's best pass-rush duo, and he has a long history of being a productive blindside protector. When comparing their careers, it doesn't look like the numbers indicate there is much of a drop-off from Harrison to Little, if one at all.
Still, the Jaguars will need Little to step up and be at his best down the stretch. They still have to play the Texans and some other fierce pass-rushes this season, and Little will be an important piece of Liam Coen's offense as they look to continue set up Trevor Lawrence for an MVP-caliber season like the one he has had to this point.
The Jaguars' secondary has plenty of questions entering Week 8, and one of the biggest questions might be Jourdan Lewis -- especially when the Jaguars get Montaric Brown back from his hamstring injury. Lewis has done some good things for the Jaguars in the run game and he has recorded two interceptions as their primary nickel cornerback this season, but he has also given up some big plays in the process in the Jaguars' only two losses.
With the amount of attention teams clearly have on Travis Hunter, who they have been avoiding in coverage for the most part, more and more passes are going to come Lewis' way. The Jaguars will need Lewis to become more consistent and cut-down the explosive plays allowed in coverage if they are to fix their secondary issues.
If the Jaguars' pass-rush is going to get home more often over the second-half of the season, it will likely hinge on the interior pass-rush. Defensive ends Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen are consistent pass-rushers who bring plenty of pressure off the edge, but it is easier for quarterbacks and offenses to negate their impact when the Jaguars are not getting much of a pass-rush from the interior group.
Armstead has had some games where he has absolutely taken over, and other games where he has been just marginally productive. If the Jaguars are going to start ramping up their pass-rush production as the stakes increase each week, they will need Armstead to help lead that charge in a big way.
If the Jaguars trade Brian Thomas Jr. , it is clear that they will need Josh Cameron to step up in a big way. Even if the Jaguars do not trade him, they still likely need to see Cameron be ready to step into a larger role than the limited, but impressive, role he played for the Jaguars during the first six weeks of the season. Cameron has stepped up each time the Jaguars have gone his way, and he needs to continue this trend moving forward.
Cameron very easily could be the Jaguars' WR3 after the bye week, depending on how they view Thomas and his place in the offense. That would mean more on his plate than his duties over the first six weeks of the season, and the Jaguars will have to ensure that their sixth-round rookie wide receiver is ready for the moment if it comes to that.

title: What the Jaguars Can Realistically Afford at the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The 2026 NFL Trade deadline is just a few weeks away, and the Jacksonville Jaguars could certainly be a big factor.
Most of the trade talk around the Jaguars understandably centers around third-year wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. , but what if the Jaguars are buyers at the deadline?
The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 and in first-place in the AFC South during their bye week , and they could reasonably look to add a potential difference-maker or depth piece at a number of positions before the trade deadline hits.
But what can the Jaguars afford when it comes to the deadline , both in terms of cap space and draft picks?
As things stand today, the Jaguars are set to have nine picks in the 2027 NFL Draft: six of their own original selections and three picks via the compensatory draft pick system after they saw Devin Lloyd, Travis Etienne, and Greg Newsome depart in free agency. The Jaguars have used the draft compensatory formula to give themselves more at bats in the draft, as well as give themselves more chances to trade for depth pieces such as Tim Patrick last season and Daniel Faalele this season.
"I think that's something in the spring we highlighted quite a bit about the idea of going down the compensatory picks approach and not signing immediately some of the street free agents. Really where we were going to turn our attention to was during training camp and the regular season, knowing that we had a larger stock of future draft picks to utilize to answer any questions that we might need to in those moments," Jaguars general manager James Gladstone said at the conclusion of training camp this summer.
"Yeah, that gives us more flexibility to pursue those paths and those options. I think that that's an ever-evolving strategy as to whether or not you're going to deploy that one year after the next. It was where we found ourselves this past cycle, and I think that's why you probably saw some willingness there, not to say that we weren't unwilling a year ago, because we were. I think the equivalent of that was probably [WR] Tim Patrick and using a sixth-round pick to get him from Detroit. We still have avenues for pursuing those into the regular season."
Compensatory Pick (Devin Lloyd)
Compensatory Pick (Travis Etienne)
Compensatory Pick (Greg Newsome)
When it comes to cap space, things are a bit tighter. The Jaguars can always work to create more room, but a lack of cap space now means that players on hefty deals, such as Daron Payne, may be tougher to trade for than players on their rookie deals still like Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Moro Ojomo.
The Jaguars did some work to create cap space with restructures ahead of Week 1, and Spotrac has the Jaguars currently at $4,659,858 in available cap space, which ranks No. 25 in the NFL.
"I think that's a move to make so that we're not forced to do anything should we pursue an avenue. We want to make sure we have the flexibility we need to keep things on the table as the season progresses," Gladstone said before the season began.
"In the same breath, we're always going to do our part to consider all options, and through that lens not all those are going to come to the table or to the public's understanding. I think the understanding that we are always going to turn over every stone is certainly going to be the case."
In short, the Jaguars have plenty of flexibility before the deadline to be aggressive from a draft pick standpoint. From a cap space standpoint, a player either on their rookie deal or a cheaper contract makes the most sense.

title: Jaguars' Travis Hunter Becomes Latest to Be Hit Big By NFL's Fine Policy
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The NFL has been quite fine-heavy this season, and Jacksonville Jaguars star Travis Hunter is the latest to be hit with one.
Hunter was fined $14,926 by the NFL this week for removing his helmet on the field against the Houston Texans in last week's 34-31 loss, which happened after Hunter picked off C.J. Stroud in the end-zone in the fourth-quarter for arguably the biggest moment in the game from the Jacksonville side.
Travis Hunter just making impact plays on both sides of the ball. HOUvsJAX on NFL Network Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/2iCxZBs80j
While this seems like quite the expensive fine for Hunter merely celebrating an exceptional play at a pivotal moment of the game, it does follow the letter of the NFL's rules, and the Jaguars are lucky that they were not hit with an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty for 15 yards, which Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1 of the NFL's rules state is the penalty for "Removal of his helmet by a player in the field of play or the end zone during a celebration or demonstration, or during a confrontation with a game official or any other player."
A bit silly? Yes, but it is the NFL's rules, and Hunter will now see the amount taken out of his next game check unless he appeals the decision and wins it, which seems unlikely since Hunter did clearly and plainly take his helmet off.
With that said, the Jaguars would likely welcome any future fines (but no penalties in close games) if Hunter keeps looking like one of the best players on the field and, arguably, the most versatile player in the game if he continues to produce on both sides of the ball. It seems like the Jaguars have found the right balance for Hunter, letting him play every snap on defense as their full-time CB1 and then stepping in on offense in certain packages.
Hunter clearly doesn't need a large snap count on offense to make an impact, either. He played just nine offensive snaps against the Texans last week but still produced four catches for 59 yards and a touchdown, racking up two explosive plays to set up two different scoring drives for the Jaguars. He did all of this while shadowing Nico Collins and more than held his own in that regard as well.
"That was part of the plan, getting him a little bit more involved early, made some critical plays for us on both sides of the football, obviously. Had the interception late, that gave us a chance to win the game. Proud of the way he completed, made some plays for us on offense and got to keep building off it," Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said about Hunter after Week 6.
Hunter has looked like an elite cornerback over the past month, and now the production is starting to see an uptick on offense. As long as Hunter keeps making plays, and remembers to keep his helmet on, the Jaguars are going to continue to see their 2025 draft gamble pay off in a big way.

title: Ranking the 8 Best Fits for Jaguars, Brian Thomas Jr. Ahead of Trade Deadline
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- With the NFL Trade deadline quickly approaching, it is clear where the majority of the focus is set to be for the Jacksonville Jaguars: Brian Thomas Jr.
Perhaps the Jaguars continue to be reluctant to deal the talented former first-round pick and 1,000-yard receiver before the deadline in a few weeks, but all signs (and reports) indicate that there is a better chance than not of him being moved sometime soon.
So if the Jaguars do trade Thomas, which teams make the most sense as trade partners? We identified eight below, ranking them from best to worst.
The Washington Commanders have always made sense for Thomas due to his connection and relationship with Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels, who was his college quarterback. We have already seen that kind of connection play a factor in a receiver trade earlier this season with Marvin Harrison Jr. and the Houston Texans and CJ Stroud, and this would be a similar fit. Even with Dan Quinn on the hot seat, this move would make sense in the short- and long-term for Commanders general manager Adam Peters.
The Commanders badly need receiver help now due to the season-ending injury to Terry McLaurin. Even before McLaurin was injured, the Commanders were seen as a team that badly needed to retool its receiver room entering the season. They signed Stefon Diggs, who has been fine, but they need a new future No. 1, and Thomas could be that,
If the Jaguars were to trade Thomas to a fellow AFC team, the one that makes the most sense is clearly the Las Vegas Raiders. The Raiders make a ton of sense as a long-term landing spot for Thomas since they have a hopeful franchise quarterback waiting in the wings in Fernando Mendoza, and their need for a receiver moving forward is clear. Even with the Raiders slipping over the last few weeks, they could also see it as a short-term move.
The Raiders are getting nothing from the receiver room right now outside of Tre Tucker, who is talented but not a WR1. Brock Bowers is elite and Michael Mayer is a nice secondary option, so adding a player with actual WR1 potential (and past WR1 production) like Thomas would make sense. The Raiders are also the type of franchise that could be willing to pay a premium price, too.
Davante Adams and Puka Nacua combine to make up over 40% of the Rams' targets, and each is dealing with injuries: Nacua has a calf injury and his skill-set and play-style makes him a bit of an injury prone player, while Adams will miss most of the rest of the season with a 6-to-10 week injury he sustained earlier this season. The Rams receivers after them are Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, and Jordan Whittington, which, yeah...
The Rams are in serious trouble of missing the playoffs, and Sean McVay and Les Snead need to find some playmakers quickly. The Jaguars and Rams are very close as franchises due to Liam Coen's and James Gladstone's connections with the franchise, which could potentially make a deal even smoother if the Rams are willing to live with Thomas' flaws as a pass-catcher,.
The Falcons have one of the best skill player trios in the NFL with Bijan Robinson, Drake London, and Kyle Pitts, but they are really lacking in pass-catchers after them. The Falcons' No. 2 receiver right now is Jahan Dotson, and their backup receivers Olamide Zaccheaus and Zachariah Branch have a combined 21 targets through six games. Thomas could be the perfect foil for London and his ability to win across the middle.
The Falcons are in one of the NFL's most winnable divisions and Thomas' skillset could fit well with Michael Penix's trebuchet downfield throwing style. This would also put Thomas far away from having to face off against the Jaguars anytime soon, which would be another welcomed aspect of a deal with the Falcons.
The Steelers were mentoned by ESPN's Jeremy Fowler as one team that could be looking for receiver help, and I think they make more sense for the Jaguars to do a deal with than most other AFC teams that currently look like a potential playoff team. The Steelers swinging a deal for an explosive field-stretcher with their current offensive ecosystem would be a bit odd but, hey, the Steelers do odd things.
The Steelers' leading target-eaters at wide receiver are a middling DK Metcalf and rookie receiver Germie Bernard. Michael Pittman Jr. has been injured and Roman Wilson is getting fewer looks than Jaylen Warren and Pat Freiermuth, which means a big-play option like Thomas could make a lot of sense for the pass-happy team/
The San Francisco 49ers seem to lose a wide receiver to injury every week or so, and right now it looks like they could be eagerly awaiting the return of Christian Kirk from injury to provide a boost. The 49ers look like one of the best teams in football and have Brock Purdy playing at an MVP-level, so they should not hesistate to add an explosive outside option like Thomas if given the chance to be aggressive with an open window.
The fact that Thomas has struggled with drops and in-breaking routes could prove to be problematic in the 49ers' scheme, but Kyle Shanahan is an elite offensive mind and would likely find a way to fit Thomas in somehow. With that said, Liam Coen is also an elite offensive mind, and he hasn't been able to help the Jaguars find a way to make things work with Thomas.
We have noted the Seahawks as a team to watch in the past, even if the fit feels a bit more unlikely than the others. The Seahawks are 3-3 at the time of the writing and could be south of .500 by the trade deadline and could need to add an explosive piece to put their struggling offense over the top to gear up for a playoff run. They also lack a strong No. 2 option next to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, with Rashid Shaheed and Cooper Kupp not exactly scaring anyone. Teams keep rotating all their coverage to JSN, and Thomas could benefit from it in a big way with a big-armed quarterback like Sam Darnold.
If we were ranking the teams that needed Thomas the most, the Chiefs would probably be at the very top of the list. The same logic applies for if we were ranking the teams where Thomas would fit the best skill-set wise. But if you are the Jaguars, are you exactly rushing to give the Chiefs a talented weapon like Thomas? They are the only team on this list who is a true AFC contender, and the Jaguars should be rooting against the Chiefs most weeks , not trying to give them a potential game-changing weapon who they might have to defend in the playoffs.
Kansas City makes a ton of sense as a team who could be interested in Thomas, thus it is impossible to leave them off this list. With that said, the Jaguars would be better off not doing business with the Chiefs right now, for the same reason the Jaguars shouldn't want to send a talented player to a team like the Buffalo Bills.

title: Jaguars Week 7 Rooting Guide: How the Bye Week Can Help Liam Coen's Squad
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars might not be suiting up in Week 7, but that doesn't mean they can't still get a boost from the week's results.
The Jaguars are sitting at 4-2 entering their Week 7 bye and they are still in first-place in the AFC South despite a recent surge from the Houston Texans. With the right results in Week 7, the Jaguars' spot in the AFC South's very early playoff race could be made even better.
So, what results should the Jaguars root for in Week 7 as they take Sunday off for their bye week ? We break it down below.
This one does not need much explanation at all. The Texans are the only real theat in the AFC South when it comes to the Jaguars' top spot, and the Jaguars can benefit from any potential hurdle that gets thrown up in the Texans' way along the rest of the season. A Texans win would put them close to the Jaguars in the AFC South standings, so the Jaguars have the almost unwinnable position of rooting for J.J. McCarthy. Good luck, but it is what it is.
AFC seeding is the focus here. The Jaguars and Broncos each sit at 4-2 but the Broncos have the tiebreaker over the Jaguars after the Week 2 result in Denver. As a result, the Jaguars should hope the Broncos find a few more losses to ensure the Jaguars can have a higher playoff seeding and prevent any chance of having to go into Mile High in January. The Jaguars need to do their part, of course, but they could use sme help starting this week with the Cardinals.
Rooting Interest: Cardinals
This one is clear. The Chiefs and Buffalo Bills are the only two AFC teams with a better record right now than the Jaguars, but the Bills are on a bye week. The Chiefs are the team to chase in the AFC right now due to their undefeated record, and the Jaguars should be rooting for them to slip weekly. A matchup in primetime against the Seattle Seahawks would give them the chance to make that slip, even if the Chiefs look like the most likely winners.
Rooting Interest: Seahawks
Like the other games mentioned above, this one is about future AFC seeding. The Browns are nowhere near as impressive as their 4-2 record says, but the Jaguars need to root against every team that is competing for a playoff spot in the AFC. Somehow, someway, that is the Browns this season. It feels unlikely that this will be the Titans' second win of the season, but it would go a long way for the Jaguars down the road.
The Jaguars are set to play a wounded Colts team in Week 8, which is a critical battle for Jacksonville after their loss to the Texans. The Colts are already quiet quitting on the season, as evidenced by their decision to fire Chris Ballard after six games, so I do not think the Jaguars need the Vikings to win for an AFC South reason. I do think that a bad loss to the Vikings could push the Colts to start getting serious about trading some of their few difference-makers, starting with DeForest Buckner and Jonathan Taylor. Imagine this Colts team coming into Jacksonville without one of those players? Imagine them without both?

title: Is the Tide Finally Turning on the Jaguars' Reluctance to Shop Brian Thomas Jr?
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- Could the tide finally be turning for the Jacksonville Jaguars and Brian Thomas Jr., at least when it relates to a potential parting of ways?
It feels like the chances of Thomas turning things around with the Jaguars are minimal, and things have simply not worked out for him with the new regime and coaching staff. In 20 games of the Liam Coen era, Thomas has caught 57 of 111 targets (51.35% catch rate) for 813 yards and three touchdowns. In 17 games as a rookie, he caught 87 of 133 targets (65.4%) for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns.
That really leaves the Jaguars and Thomas with one clear option: a trade ahead of next month's NFL trade deadline. And according to ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler, it appears the rest of the league believes the Jaguars may finally start to be open to the idea after a year of pushing back against the idea of trading the former first-rounder.
Multiple league execs believe Jacksonville will seriously consider trading Brian Thomas Jr. at the deadline now that his role has decreased https://t.co/9ri1RjpGtA
"Brian Thomas Jr., immensely talented but I have talked to several teams who believe he could be dealt over the next few weeks," Fowler said.
"Jacksonville has relented in the past. They have kept him because he is such a big talent, they hoped that his deep threat would balance things out, but there are other receivers. Last two weeks, no catches. Had just 15 snaps, so was essentially benched in that London game against Houston, so something has to give. There are going to be some interested parties. Kansas City has been looking around at potentially adding a receiver, Pittsburgh to some extent."
So, could it be a real possibility that the Jaguars' focus when it comes to Thomas is shifting after his benching against the Texans?
Simply put, the Jaguars would be committing team-building malpractice if their stance on Thomas hasn't shifted by now. It made sense last season for the Jaguars to want to work through things with Thomas. It even made sense this offseason, when Thomas had the best offseason program and training camps of his career and seemed to improve on his connection with Trevor Lawrence.
But things have changed since then. Thomas wasn't getting benched a year ago; he was still on the field and providing value. And even this offseason with Jakobi Meyers and Parker Washington ahead of him in the pecking order, he was still a starting receiver in three-receiver sets and the Jaguars' only true X receiver on the roster.
Since then, though, the Jaguars have seen Thomas' role get reduced for two reasons: drops, which led to his benching in the second-half of Sunday's game against the Texans, and Josh Cameron. Cameron, a sixth-round pick in April, flashed a ton during the offseason program and training camp but there was no true sample size that indicated he should see snaps over Thomas, thus making Thomas expendable.
That has changed. Cameron has been uber-efficient in a limited role and has simply been much more consistent with the ball coming his way than Thomas has been this season. The Jaguars may not have known what they had in Cameron, but they do now. As a result, the math has changed.
With Cameron emerging, Thomas continuing to struggle, Travis Hunter proving he can provide value at receiver while being the No. 1 cornerback, and the Jaguars' increase in multiple tight end sets, the oppurtunity for Thomas is simply not there like it was a year ago, or even like it was in May or July. The situation has changed, and the Jaguars' minds should as a result.
If Fowler's senses are correct, the rest of the NFL is following the same math. The only outcome that really makes sense here is for the Jaguars to get some value out of Thomas, who likely would still be a very attractive player on the trade market.

title: The Jaguars' Top 2027 Roster Need Just Became Crystal Clear
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars still have a lot of football left in 2026, but that doesn't mean they can't always keep an eye on the future.
The future became a bit more clear for the Jaguars this week, at least as it pertains to what the Jaguars' top need might be in the 2027 offseason. With Jaguars' left tackle Anton Harrison now out for the year with an ACL injury, the Jaguars' biggest draft need a year from now has become crystal clear: the Jaguars need a young tackle to develop and bring into their system, and they need one badly.
The Jaguars have the ability to sustain Harrison's injury without much disruption to the offense thanks to Walker Little, who will now slot in at left tackle. Losing Harrison is obviously not ideal, especially because it takes the Jaguars from a great offensive tackle depth chart to one that has second-year guard Wyatt Milum an injury away from stepping in. But the Jaguars should be OK.
With that said, it is the long-term ramifications of Harrison's injury, both for himself and the Jaguars, that now make offensive tackle the team's biggest need before the 2027 offseason is even close to kicking off. The Jaguars' present at tackle looks fine, but Harrison's injury has made the future a lot murkier at a key spot.
Harrison was thought to be the best candidate to be the Jaguars' long-term answer at the left tackle spot, though he needed to prove himself this season to truly land the kind of big-money deal that would have made him a franchise pillar. Harrison started just six games at left tackle in his first four seasons, all of which came this season, which means the Jaguars' sample size of him on the blindside isn't exactly enough to feel confident in picking up extension talks.
Had Harrison stayed healthy and played well to end 2026, he likely would have been a prime extension candidate, either at the end of the season or at some point while playing on his fifth-year option. If he stayed healthy and was inconsistent, as he had been in six games this year, he likely would have entered next year as the starting left tackle for at least one more season as he attempted to prove himself again. That would have at least given the Jaguars some time to figure out left tackle.
But, that didn't happen. Harrison's season is over after only six games, and the Jaguars have no better idea now of whether he is their future at tackle than they did when the season began. That won't change with Harrison sidelined for the rest of the season, and the Jaguars will likely look to simply get by at left tackle until then, at least in terms of the long-term view.
That then brings 2027 into focus. The Jaguars' tackle situation will be Harrison coming off an ACL injury and still being a relative long-term unknown; Little entering a contract year; Cole Van Lanen in his age-29 season. The Jaguars would likely feel fine with rolling into the season with those as their top-3 options because it would be very similar to what they entered 2026 with.
But they also entered 2026 with the hope, perhaps even the expectation, of Harrison entrenching himself as the left tackle of the future. They likely can not enter 2027 with the same expectations, which means finding that tackle is critical. And for all of the positions the Jaguars have added to over the last two drafts, a young tackle is one thing they haven't found.
The only two offensive/defensive positions the Jaguars haven't drafted since James Gladstone took over as general manager are quarterback (duh) and offensive tackle, since Wyatt Milum was drafted as a guard. They have taken a center, running backs, receivers, tight ends, linebackers, safeties, a cornerback, defensive ends, and a defensive tackle ... but no offensive tackle.
The Jaguars need one they can develop, and Harrison's injury has made it clear that finding that tackle should be a top priority. An even bigger one than finding defensive line depth or secondary pieces. Instead, the Jaguars need to find a talented tackle who they can develop for at least a year before turning over the left tackle spot to him in the future.
Jacksonville might have needed the tackle even if Harrison stayed healthy. But now, there is no question. The Jaguars need to find some insurance at tackle, and it should happen within the first two rounds of the 2027 NFL Draft.

title: One Trade Deadline Move the Jaguars Must Prioritize ASAP
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars are a good team. A really good team, even. But, like any team, they could still use some help.
Help normally comes in the form of a trade around this time of the year, with the trade deadline just a few weeks away and rumors and interest starting to heat up. For the Jaguars, there is no reason this year's deadline can't be a productive one.
But what type of moves should the Jaguars prioritize with the deadline around the corner? Should they look for swing tackle help after Anton Harrison's season-ending injury? Should they add more pass-rushers or defensive backs? All of these moves would make some sense, but there is one player who stands out above all the other options: Los Angeles Chargers pass-rusher Khalil Mack.
The Jaguars have bigger needs than the edge position; at least from my view. The Jaguars' secondary has been banged up all season and there is a real and true need for cornerback depth. The secondary is why the Jaguars lost in the Wild Card last season, and it is facing some of the same issues today despite Travis Hunter being a true lockdown No. 1 cornerback.
But there is a reason that Mack is the top target the Jaguars should focus on landing, and one they should work to do so as quickly as possible. The Jaguars have a talented pair of edge defenders in Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen, but they have not gotten much production from the rest of the pass-rush unit on a down-to-down basis.
The Jaguars rank No. 9 in pressure rate this season at 39.1%, about a 4% increase from their 2025 number. But the Jaguars have had to blitz at a high clip to make that happen. When the Jaguars blitz, they have a pressure rate of 49.3%, which would rank No. 1 in the NFL this year in terms of standard pressure rate. But when the Jaguars do not blitz, their pressure rate drops to 33.6%. That is still 10th-best of all teams when they are just rushing four, but it is clear the Jaguars are getting more pressure when they send the house.
The reason for that is simple: the Jaguars are not getting any pass-rush from anyone not named Hines-Allen or Walker. Arik Armstead has had some big games inside, but also some quiet ones. And out of 130 qualifying rushers, Dennis Gardeck, Bryan Thomas Jr., and Danny Striggow rank No. 90, No. 123, and No. 129 in pass-rush win-rate.
This means that the Jaguars have two players on their roster providing pressure, and they have to scheme the rest of it up. To fix this, the Jaguars should offer the Chargers a fifth-round pick for Mack. Mack's win rate ranks just No. 70, but that is as the Chargers' No. 2 guy. He would be the No. 3 guy in Jacksonville, a better fit for where he is at in his career and a better fit for what the Jaguars truly need in their edge rotation.
Mack, who would be a cheap rental, would also allow Dennis Gardeck to be more rotational of a pass-rusher than he is now, a better role for his skill-set. It would also allow Walker to slide inside on more passing downs which is, you guessed it, a better role for his skill-set as well. It would make several members of the defense better, improve the pass-rush depth, and give the Jaguars a chance to not have to rely solely on two players to provide that spark.
The Jaguars could also recoup whatever they send over for Mack depending on where he signs in free agency next season. Getting a few months of production from Mack and then getting some kind of future compensatory pick for his services would be a big win in terms of team-building. With that said, the Jaguars would have to move with some quickness.
Mack will likely be a sought-after target on the trade market due to his position, years of production, and the fact that it is clear he will only take a Day 3 pick for the winless Chargers. A lot of teams are bound to be interested in a player like that, with the Chicago Bears already being tied to a potential move.
The Jaguars should move quickly to prevent anyone else from getting in on renting out Mack and then getting a future pick for him, because it is a smart move to move.

title: The Jaguars Only Have 3 Post-Bye Week Options For Brian Thomas Jr's Future
full_text:
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. -- The Jacksonville Jaguars have some big decisions to make after the bye week, and more than a few center around wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr.
The former first-round pick is the most embattled member of the roster through the first six weeks of the season, and the question now is what the Jaguars will do with their former No. 1 wide receiver.
So, what are t he Jaguars' options with Thomas as they near the end of their bye week? We break down each potential path below, starting with ...
The Jaguars trading Thomas , of course, is the most logical (and to me, probable) scenario for a few reasons. Jacksonville made it clear by benching him against the Texans that they are more or less done with trying to help him out of his slump, and the Jaguars have the depth that would make it possible to unload him in a deal. They didn't have that proven depth this offseason when his value was at its highest, but things have changed since then.
The fact that Marvin Harrison Jr. went for a second and a Day 3 pick swap suggests Thomas could net the Jaguars similar value, and there are several teams that would make sense as landing spots for the former LSU product. Washington Commanders with his college quarterback? A banged-up Los Angeles Rams team that is running short on wide receivers? A Las Vegas Raiders team that has a young quarterback and a middling receiver room?
The possibilities are all there for the Jaguars, and we should know sooner than later whether the Jaguars will be ready to part with the uber-talented Thomas.
Liam Coen set a bit of a precedent with the way he handled Thomas a week ago against the Houston Texans, which brings his post-bye week plans into focus. The Jaguars did not have Thomas play a single snap in the second-half last week against the Texans despite the Jaguars trailing for much of the game. Even with the Jaguars chasing points with a pass-first attack while facing a deficit, the Jaguars prefered to have Travis Hunter, Josh Cameron, or multiple tight ends on the field over Thomas in a key game.
The Jaguars could enter Week 8 against the Indianapolis Colts with the same idea; either making him a healthy scratch or just simply not playing him or playing him in a marginal role. The fact he has no special teams value suggests there is a real scenario he might simply be inactive, but this path would have a few issues for the Jaguars. Namely, it would tank any kind of value Thomas has on the trade market or, at the least, tank any leverage the Jaguars have in trade talks.
If Thomas isn't seeing any playing time, there is no real reason for teams to offer premium picks for his services. His traits and pedigree suggests the Jaguars could still land a second-round pick for him, but that idea likely goes out the window if he doesn't see the field anymore. Still, the Jaguars will have to weigh what is in their best interests to win on each Sunday, which means sitting him might end up being the only real answer.
This is what the Jaguars have been doing for a while , and it just hasn't worked. Thomas became the clear third-fiddle for the Jaguars in the passing game last season after the Jaguars added Jakobi Meyers: in the six regular-season games Thomas played last year for the Jaguars alongside Meyers, he had one game with a target rate above 20%, compared to four games before Meyers was traded for. He was still playing, but he wasn't seeing the ball thrown his way. After being the undisputed No. 1 entering 2025, he clearly fell down the pecking order.
As a result, it was clear entering the season that Thomas would be a part of the passing game's equation, but far from its clear focus. But after a ho-hum Week 1 where he caught three passes for 40 yards, Thomas has caught three passes for 25 yards and a touchdown on eight targets over the last month. That is less than what Travis Hunter and Josh Cameron have produced in single games this season, and Thomas' playing time didn't really start dipping until this past week against the Texans, sans a reduced role in Week 3.
The Jaguars could still have Thomas on the field and keep trying and hoping that something suddenly clicks. But this path, which is the one of least resistance, has cost the Jaguars some real points and first-down conversions in critical moments this season. Maybe the Jaguars let Thomas try to get his groove back, but this feels unlikely.

title: Andy Reid Defends Chiefs Kicker Harrison Butker After Rough Night: ‘He’s Off a Bit’
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs' 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks during Sunday Night Football can hardly be attributed to one player's mistakes. It was a putrid showing in all facets of the game for KC, and Mike Macdonald's squad came out dominant from the get-go.
With that said, kicker Harrison Butker's shortcomings continued to loom large on special teams. It's become a consistent theme for the 31-year-old, who has slipped significantly from his prime and endured several rough seasons in a row. Butker's first field-goal attempt of the evening came from 58 yards out. He wasn't able to connect. There's nothing dishonorable about missing a near-60 yarder, but the kick would have split the uprights had it traveled the distance.
That raises real questions about Butker and what has been causing this prolonged slump. He's only two months removed from drilling a record-shattering 69-yard kick in the NFL Preseason that had fans believing he was back to his elite self. Is there a lapse in focus with his kicks, a mechanical issue, or even an underlying injury?
He partially redeemed himself in the third quarter, hitting his second field goal from 50+ yards this season. However, he squandered that momentum by missing a 45-yard attempt wide right with more than eight minutes remaining in the final quarter. The kick would've cut the Chiefs' deficit to seven points and given them a chance to get back into the contest, but Butker couldn't capitalize on the opportunity.
In his postgame press conference, head coach Andy Reid acknowledged that Butker hasn't been himself lately but maintained that he remains confident in his longtime placekicker. "Listen, he's been one of the most consistent kickers in football," Reid said. "He's off a bit. So, we've got to fix that."
The numbers don't necessarily back Butker's reputation as one of football's most "consistent kickers," though. As noted by Associated Press writer Josh Dubow , his 15 missed kicks since the start of the 2025 campaign lead the NFL. That many failed attempts in that span is a far cry from the consistency Reid described.
Harrison Butker's 2026 field goal percentage and ranks via @TruMediaSports : Overall: 71.4 (29th) FG40%: 100% (T-1st) FG50%: 20% (28th) XP%: 93.3% (T-24th) @KCSportsNetwork pic.twitter.com/U9Gbiy1YNg
Dating back to the 2024 season, Butker has converted exactly 50% (9-of-18) of his field-goal attempts from 50 yards or deeper. While raw leg strength has long been his trademark, the fact that he's falling multiple yards short on long-distance tries now indicates that his value is no longer what it once was.
Reid has consistently defended Butker through his recent struggles, and there was a point when it was reasonable to believe the veteran could return to form. However, he's getting closer to the point of no return, having statistically performed like a bottom-tier kicker in recent years despite his penchant for coming through in clutch moments. Kansas City isn't exactly in a position to simply cut ties with the Georgia Tech graduate, who is signed through 2028 and ranks as the NFL's fourth-highest-paid kicker. Regardless, his current production is no better than what the Chiefs could get from the average practice squad kicker. If he continues costing the team games, a serious conversation about his future will have to be had.

title: Andy Reid Clears Air on Reported Spat With Josh Simmons in Team Meeting
full_text:
In the aftermath of their most embarrassing performance of the 2026 season by an insanely wide margin, the Kansas City Chiefs have bigger fish to fry than engaging in hypotheticals regarding those who aren't even on the active 53-man roster.
Given the lack of consistency or clarity with one particular player, however, it was only a matter of time before head coach Andy Reid was asked about left tackle Josh Simmons once again.
Just days removed from Kansas City placing the 2025 first-round pick on IR , a national report from ESPN revealed that Simmons had a back-and-forth with Reid on Wednesday and was asked by him to leave a team meeting. Did that incident have anything to do with the transaction the following day?
Speaking to the media after a 20-3 loss on Sunday Night Football to the Seattle Seahawks, Reid shot down any correlation between the two.
"Listen, Sam (McDowell), I've said so much on him," Reid said of Simmons. "Rick (Burkholder) has talked about him, this and that. Things happen. That's no reason that he was put on IR. He's got a bad back. He's got to get that worked out, and that's the main thing. I'll leave it at that, and that's where we're at with it."
According to the aforementioned report, Simmons was called out for having his feet up while sitting during the meeting and told Reid it was because of an aching back and hips. Upon being directed to seek treatment if he was indeed in pain, the former Ohio State star allegedly "disrupted the meeting" and even led to quarterback Patrick Mahomes to urge Simmons to step out as well.
Burkholder, vice president of sports medicine and performance, provided a statement to lead off Thursday's media availability and described Simmons' Wednesday absence from practice as something that allowed him to "get with his people" and decide next injury-related steps. After all, the second-year man is attempting to recover from a bulging disc in his back that's bothered him since mid-August.
With the Seattle game in the books, Simmons will miss at least the club's next three contests against the Denver Broncos, New York Jets and Atlanta Falcons. Mike Garafolo of NFL Network reports that the team holds out hope for Simmons eventually hitting the ground running again with the "right attitude and healthy, ready to go" for the stretch run of the season.
Reid appears to share that same end goal. Even if it's been an awkward week on the Simmons front, the leader of the team reiterates that the focus remains solely on the back injury and subsequent recovery.

title: 10 Instant Observations From Chiefs' Ugly Week 7 Loss to Seahawks
full_text:
Before the Kansas City Chiefs even took the field in Seattle to battle the Seahawks, most figured it would be a trying night for one of football's last undefeated teams. That certainly proved to be the case in Week 7, as head coach Andy Reid's crew got throttled in prime time.
The hosts came out firing on the Sunday Night Football stage, taking advantage of the visitors' shorthanded offense and also making the most of favorable matchups on the other side of the ball. Kansas City did attempt to snap out of its funk in the second half of play, yet it never got close and wound up dropping a brutal game by a final score of 20-3.
Here are 10 instant observations and Chiefs takeaways from Week 7.
It feels like forever ago that fifth-round rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen was dazzling during the summer and becoming a fan-favorite player, but in reality, it's only been a few months. Given the injuries to wideouts Tyquan Thornton ( ankle ) and Rashee Rice ( hamstring ), the door was opened for the Cincinnati product to make an impact. After logging a pair of catches for 27 yards in Week 6, he stood out from the jump on Sunday.
On just the second play from scrimmage for Kansas City, Allen hauled in a pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes down the left sideline and gained 18 yards. It was a dead silent half for him the rest of the way, however, which raises questions about his true involvement in the offense. Is Allen a scripted player or a difference-maker?
Look, it was glaringly obvious that finding a way to slow down someone who came into Week 7 with 49 catches for 717 yards and seven touchdowns would be super difficult. Flat-out stopping the reigning Offensive Player of the Year? Forget about it... which the Chiefs seemed to do at first whistle.
Receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba wasn't fair in the opening half of play, routinely burning cornerback L'Jarius Sneed in the slot and even providing first-round rookie Mansoor Delane with two "welcome to the league" moments. He finished the first two quarters with six snags for 129 yards and a touchdown, serving as a walking nightmare for Steve Spagnuolo's defense.
That defense was downright terrible on late downs in this one; JSN was a top force in that unfolding.
It's always difficult having a nuanced dialogue about Mahomes' play. On one hand, he's held to such a high standard by many that it seems fair to point out when he doesn't meet the bar. On the other hand, he rolled into Week 7 without the aforementioned receivers and both of his starting offensive tackles.
There's room to meet in the middle. According to RBSDM , he owned an ugly mark of -0.39 EPA per play in quarters one and two. No. 15 missed plenty of throws on SNF , leaving many of them short and also putting too much mustard on one pass that got picked off. That said, constant duress made his life much more difficult.
It's impossible to consider Mahomes' shortcomings and not directly jump into the offensive line situation. In our Week 7 preview, we briefly touched on how Kansas City has typically operated a quick-game passing offense and relied on explosive rushes and play-action to help open up the occasional deep shot. With no Jaylon Moore ( and with Josh Simmons still out ), operating a functional offense seemed far more difficult than it needed to be on Sunday.
Undrafted rookie free agent Kahlil Benson whiffed on multiple occasions, and right tackle Joshua Ezeudu also had his fair share of rough moments. Sure, Reid didn't do a ton to protect his linemen and Mahomes was far from perfect, but this can't be sustained for much longer.
After he missed an extra point last week, I opened the floor for there being an active Harrison Butker problem on the Chiefs' hands. He's years removed from producing a season that lives up to his prime, and his variance from long range makes him far from the slam-dunk kicker he used to be. That trend continued into the Seahawks game.
In a vacuum, there's no shame in missing a 58-yard field goal. When Butker left his short to end the first half, though, that sent KC into the break scoreless. He redeemed himself temporarily with a 50-yard connection in the third frame, only to push a 45-yarder midway through the fourth quarter. The more the sample size grows, the worse this looks.
Speaking of the Butker miss, that opportunity was only presented due to a brilliant play on the ball by cornerback Nohl Williams on defense. He picked off quarterback Sam Darnold's pass in the end zone and returned it for 64 yards, followed by a run and timeout by the offense. Had Seattle put up seven points on that drive, it would've been far more demoralizing than facing a 10-point deficit.
With the Chiefs driving in the fourth quarter, a drop by receiver Xavier Worthy and a holding penalty on left guard Kingsley Suamataia put the offense in a second-and-20 situation. The following two plays may fade into the void over time, but rookie running back Emmett Johnson 's 12-yard catch made third down manageable. He then threw a critical block on a scramble by Mahomes for the first.
Butker wound up missing the 45-yard boot at the end of the drive, but Johnson deserves props for being a gamer when needed.
The unfortunate thing for Worthy is he just recorded seven targets and 70-plus receiving yards in back-to-back games. On the surface, he looked like he was building some significant momentum, and he even acknowledged such this week. Gifted a massive chance to be the X-factor in Week 7, however, he flopped.
It wasn't just the fourth-quarter drop, either. The former first-round pick displayed minimal or no awareness on multiple plays, including one where he ran out of bounds and another in which he failed to throw a block on a reception by running back Kenneth Walker. The latter play could've been the most explosive of the night. Unless he's getting the ball in space and given some runway, Worthy just isn't a huge impact piece.
Anyone hoping for the third-year man to blossom into a WR1 can officially call it. They can likely sell stock on him being a high-end WR2, too, even in KC.
Through five games, Walker had fully justified the Chiefs' investment in him and then some. He's been the team's best player to this point and almost singlehandedly transformed the offense from a player standpoint, leading the sport in a variety of statistics on the ground. Citing a lackluster showing in the box score is in no way an indictment on him — it's more of a praise of the home team.
Walker finished Sunday Night Football with 14 carries for a measly 36 yards, throwing him off pace and also ignoring just how hard he had to work for that output. Week 7 wasn't a talent problem for the star halfback, as just about anyone would've failed to thrive in these conditions.
At the end of the day, the Chiefs were never going to run the table, even if fully healthy. Considering the circumstances of a lack of health on offense and facing a Super Bowl-caliber team, it shouldn't be a complete and utter shock that the Seahawks looked good. It is a surprise that the Kansas City offense looked so inept.
It's this writer's view that only a handful of teams truly matter at the moment. The Chiefs are still one of them and had to face off against a member of that group on the road in prime time. The sky isn't falling in the slightest, although this is a wake-up call for many.

title: Complete Chiefs Inactives for Week 7 vs. Seahawks: Jaylon Moore & Others Sitting Out SNF
full_text:
The Kansas City Chiefs return to prime time in Week 7, this time for an interconference tilt on the road against the reigning Super Bowl champions. The Seattle Seahawks await on Sunday Night Football , with Mike Macdonald's 3-3 club looking to gain some ground in the NFC West standings and defend home turf.
Neither team rolls into this one fully healthy, which is to be expected at this point in a grueling season. The hosts had multiple players carrying questionable designations entering the weekend, whereas the visitors ruled out a pair of key offensive starters while also shuffling the roster quite a bit.
With that in mind, here's who's inactive for Kansas City and Seattle in Sunday's matchup.
Here are the Chiefs’ inactives for tonight’s game against the Seahawks: WR Rashee Rice OT Jaylon Moore QB Garrett Nussmeier DB Jadon Canady FB Ben VanSumeren DE Jack Pyburn
Earlier this week, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid revealed that wide receiver Rashee Rice and right tackle Jaylon Moore wouldn't be suiting up on Sunday. Rice still hasn't returned to practice since sustaining a hamstring injury in Week 4's win over the Las Vegas Raiders, and Moore got knocked out of Week 6's win over the Los Angeles Chargers and has been in concussion protocol ever since. Joshua Ezeudu steps in for Moore at right tackle.
Cornerback L'Jarius Sneed, who didn't originally travel with the team on Saturday due to a personal issue before joining everyone on Sunday, is active. Sneed (knee) was previously questionable to play in Week 7 after being limited in practice all week.
On Saturday, the club placed second-year running back Brashard Smith on injured reserve with a hamstring issue. Undrafted rookie free agent Jadyn Ott was signed to the 53-man roster to take his spot.
At the same time, wide receiver Justin Watson was elevated from the practice squad and linebacker Cooper McDonald came off IR and is set to play for the first time since Week 1 .
Left tackle Josh Simmons doesn't appear on Sunday's inactives because he's now on IR. Earlier on Sunday, a report shed light on the day leading up to him eventually being placed on the list, including being told to leave a team meeting by Reid and quarterback Patrick Mahomes.
Tonight’s @Seahawks inactives; QB Drew Lock will serve as the emergency 3rd quarterback. pic.twitter.com/OzEKzer0eH
After being non-participants in practice on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday, the Seahawks ruled linebackers Chazz Surratt (calf) and Drake Thomas (ankle) out.
