title: Patriots' Rhamondre Stevenson Details 'Momentum' Last-Second TD Scamper
full_text:
CHICAGO — The Chicago Bears had just scored, with Luther Burden weaving his way into the end zone. They were up 20-7 over the New England Patriots and looked like they might run away with the game at halftime.
And yet, in a blink of an eye, the Patriots stormed into the locker room trailing by just one possession.
After hitting A.J. Brown on an 18-yard in cut, the Patriots quickly called a timeout with three seconds left. Then, lining up in a Hail Mary-like formation (three receivers spread out wide to one side), Drake Maye checked it down to Rhamondre Stevenson out of the backfield.
Brown came across the field to help clear out room for Stevenson, who'd use a big block from DeMario Douglas to pick up what turned into a 48-yard touchdown run to close the first half.
RHAMONDRE STEVENSON‼️ 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/heXDiTFnzW
It was a play that's been in the Patriots' back pocket for the last few seasons.
"I was just trying to make a play, put my team in a position to swing the game a little bit as much as we can," Stevenson said after the Patriots' 30-24 loss to the Bears on Thursday Night Football .
"We've been working on that play for a long time and came in handy today. Executed on that play, so felt good to do that."
What was Stevenson's mindset during the play?
"Score. Score," he said. "I felt like it brought us some momentum. Felt like it brought us some momentum, but obviously, not enough, you know? We didn't come out with the win."
That play was part of Stevenson's career-high 93 yards through the air, the most on the team. The running game wasn't really working for the Patriots all night, but Stevenson was able to impact the game through the air.
"Just trying to give us a chance to go down and run. And I think it’s hard when those things, I kind of had a feeling they were going to come after me and blitz," Maye said on the play. "So when it leaves, we get five out in the pattern and they bring five. We got really five, four blockers, and Mondre with the ball, and they got six defenders, and it all takes one cut. So that was pretty cool. How you draw it up. That’s how we drew it up all. We’ve been practicing that play since OTAs. So, it definitely brought us some life at halftime, and then just didn’t really swing for us in the fourth quarter."
As a runner, Stevenson carried the ball six times for 22 yards. It wasn't much better for the other running backs on the roster either. TreVeyon Henderson was rarely used (three carried, nine yards), while Corey Kiner (four carries, 13 yards) appeared to be second-in-command for most of the first half .
"We didn't run the ball well enough, but moved it however we needed to move it, which sometimes you're going to have days like that," head coach Mike Vrabel said. "I though we'd be able to run it a little better. We didn't. ... We'd like to run the ball a little better, but it didn't happen tonight."
Stevenson has been on some really good Patriots teams and some really bad Patriots team. That play, although it didn't spark a comeback on Thursday, could be a sign that there's something below the surface for this year's group that's ready to come out.
"We know this team's gonna fight," he said. "We got some relentless people in this locker room. That's great, that's great. We just gotta come out and win games though, that's the main thing. We just gotta watch the film and see what we did well. We had shots to win the game. Bunch of credit to them, that's a great team. But we had shots to win the game, I think."

title: Patriots Stock Report: Which Position Groups Rose, Fell vs. Bears?
full_text:
The New England Patriots' battle with the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on Thursday night had the visiting team flash plenty of inconsistencies.
Many of New England's positions shined, or struggled, as a collective. Here are the stock reports on the groups which had the biggest impacts in either regard.
New England's wide receiver room may have been the biggest contributor to the team's loss on Thursday night. A.J. Brown, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism and Kyle Williams combined for just seven receptions on 12 targets. Those catches went for 87 yards and no touchdowns.
As the primary target at wide receiver, Brown struggled once again. He has caught just three passes in each of his trio of games as a Patriot.
"I think (the Bears' defense) did a really good job," Brown said after the game. "Early on, (offensive coordinator) Josh (McDaniels) tried to do a really good job of getting me involved and Drake just was taking what they were giving. They were trying to take me away early on, and that's just kind of how the game played."
What the Patriots lacked in production from its wide receivers, it made up for with its tight ends. Veteran Hunter Henry tallied seven receptions for 71 yards, including multiple crucial first down conversions. Also, rookie Eli Raridon got on the board for three receptions, 56 yards and a touchdown.
The main highlight from those two? Raridon's 30-yard score late in the third quarter.
Drake Maye DIME to Eli Raridon 🪙 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/ajUvbcD8Oo
"(He's) great, man," Henry said on Thursday about Raridon. "Just continuing to get better and growing that confidence. A lot of fun to play with."
To address the elephant in the room, yes, Drake Maye's interception was borderline unacceptable. After being turnover-free in his last two games, the third-year signal caller reverted back to his early-season struggles by tossing a pick in the red zone.
Other than that, however, Maye was near-perfect on the evening. He finished 24/31 passing for 321 yards and two touchdowns, alongside the interception. On the ground, he added an extra 26 yards and a score.
In a game where he was constantly pressured, and his receivers were struggling to get open, Maye was one of the lone reasons why New England had any chance of beating Chicago.
"He gave us a chance," Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said about Maye after the loss. "He competed. And I know he'd like to have that throw back to Eli, but I thought that he really competed. Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football, he gave us a chance."
The Patriots' pass defense was borderline non-existent on Thursday. Their completion percentage allowed (66.7%) was largely aided by a few bad drops by Bears receivers. Plus, Caleb Williams tossed for over 300 yards and two touchdowns.
While the defense as a whole improved in the second half, the secondary struggled immensely in the first 30 minutes against dynamic wide receiver Luther Burden III. The second-year pass catcher hauled in four receptions for 130 yards and a touchdown — all coming in the first half of play.
New England's running back room struggled immensely in the ground game, but helped make up for the wide receivers' struggles in the pass game. Rhamondre Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner combined for only 13 carries and 44 yards, and played a significant role in the Patriots' slow start to the night.
However, Stevenson also ended the night with five receptions for a team-high 93 yards and a touchdown. The score came on a 48-yard catch-and-run with no time remaining in the first half to cut the Bears' lead to one possession.
Crazy things happening 🤯 @budlight | 📺 Prime Video pic.twitter.com/QdmQ1DOPPX
Between penalties, pressures allowed on Maye and an inability to find momentum in the run game, the Patriots offensive line combined for a perfectly imperfect performance on Thursday.
Offensive tackle Morgan Moses was called for a hold to back New England up from 2nd-and-2 to 2nd-and-12. Plus, he allowed three pressures and a sack on the evening, per PFF. Every other starter on the line allowed one pressure and was called for a penalty, except for center Jared Wilson who had a clean sheet in both regards.

title: Patriots, Bears QB Duel Lived Up To The Hype
full_text:
CHICAGO — It lived up to the hype, that's for sure.
The second-ever meeting between Drake Maye and Caleb Williams was far better than their first one two seasons ago. The young quarterbacks for the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears had excellent days for their respective sides on Thursday Night Football, with Williams' Bears grabbing the 30-24 win in the final moments .
"Shoulda, woulda, coulda," Maye told reporters postgame. "I'm proud of the guys for the effort. I think we did some good things, we've got a lot of stuff to clean up."
But that loss wasn't on Maye's shoulders, at least not entirely. The 24-year-old went 24-for-31 for 347 total yards and three total touchdowns (two passing, one rushing). It was a fantastic effort by Maye, who kept the Patriots offense in the game all night.
And yet, it was Williams' scrambling and elite arm talent that led the Bears. He finished the night going 22-for-33 for 308 yards and two passing touchdowns, and hit Rome Odunze on a pair of first downs that started to break the Patriots' proverbial defensive back.
It was two juggernauts dueling it out.
"Drake's a competitor, man," tight end Hunter Henry said in the locker room. "That's what he does. We always got a chance when 10's back there, that's for sure."
"He did a great job extending plays," A.J. Brown, who caught three passes in the loss, said. "He did great."
Maye's one blip on his radar was a bad interception in the first half. Looking to hit rookie Eli Raridon in the end zone, he didn't put enough air on his pass and Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson picked it off. It was Maye's third INT thrown in the end zone this season, the most in the entire NFL.
On the other side of the field, Williams completed eight passes of 20+ yards, tied for the most by any quarterback in 2026. He didn't turn the ball over and used his legs to buy some time for his receivers, which hurt the Patriots secondary's ability to defend "the second play."
"We talked about it all week," Christian Gonzalez said. "He's very gifted with how he can run and how he can extend plays. ... You gotta defend the second play. There's a play and then there's a second play with a quarterback like Caleb."
"Anytime a quarterback that's as mobile as him gets out of the pocket, they definitely put stress on the DBs," Charles Woods told Patriots On SI. "It's definitely difficult, but that's what we signed up."
Williams ran for just 18 yards, but his legs helped set up some of the game's biggest plays. He rolled out to find Colston Loveland on a 12-yard touchdown in the third quarter. He escaped the pocket to help pick up big conversions late in the fourth. He was the victor in Week 7, and deservingly so.
If this was the type of matchup these two young quarterbacks can provide , watch out NFL. Instead of rookie gunslingers on bad teams in 2024, these were two grown quarterbacks that offer plenty of skills under center. It was a fun one to watch at Soldier Field.
"I just appreciate we have him back there and (to) be able to block for him," Walter Rouse, who started his first game of the season at left guard, told Patriots On SI. "Drake's an awesome, great guy."
The loss wasn't the outcome the Patriots had hoped for, but it was a gutsy effort by their quarterback. It's just the latest in a string of them, and it's proving why he's the face of this franchise.
"He gave us a chance," Mike Vrabel said. "He competed. ... He'll learn from it like he always does. I'm glad he's ours."

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' 16-10 Loss to Steelers in Paris
full_text:
Hoping to build momentum ahead of their upcoming bye week after a major victory last week, the New Orleans Saints instead fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday in Paris, exposing several recurring issues under coach Kellen Moore .
New Orleans' offensive struggles continued as missed scoring opportunities proved costly as the Saints fell to 2-5.
From an emerging young playmaker to a disastrous rushing performance, here is a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from the Saints' disappointing loss to Pittsburgh .
One of the few bright spots in New Orleans' disappointing loss was rookie wide receiver Barion Brown's emergence.
The sixth-round pick got a chance to show his explosiveness, finishing with three receptions for 57 yards and adding another 97 yards on four kickoff returns.
His biggest offensive play came in the first half when he caught a 49-yard pass from Tyler Shough , setting up Daniel Carlson 's 38-yard field goal.
Brown also returned a kickoff 42 yards in the second quarter, setting up a possession that ended with Shough's 1-yard touchdown pass to Devaughn Vele .
Despite those contributions, Brown received just three targets.
That limited involvement raises questions about whether coach Kellen Moore is maximizing one of the offense's most explosive young playmakers.
With rookie Jordyn Tyson still sidelined by a hamstring injury, Brown has a chance to become a more consistent contributor alongside Chris Olave and Vele.
New Orleans gets a vital jolt on offense from Brown's explosive speed and big-play dynamism.
Following a sluggish 281-yard performance against Pittsburgh, integrating him must become a top priority for the Saints. To fully leverage the rookie's skill set, Moore ought to scheme designed touches, vertical routes and run-after-catch opportunities for him. Given how much he has delivered on minimal opportunities, Brown has earned a larger role.
In a narrow 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, kicker Daniel Carlson missed a crucial 52-yard field goal in the fourth quarter — his fourth failure in 11 attempts this season. This ongoing volatility in special teams poses a critical problem for the 2-5 Saints.
The fourth-quarter miss was particularly damaging because New Orleans had already wasted a promising red-zone opportunity earlier in the second half. Rather than positioning themselves to tie or take the lead with a field goal late in the game, the Saints remained trapped in a six-point deficit.
Carlson's 63.6% conversion rate stands in sharp contrast to Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who accounted for nine points by flawlessly making all three of his field goals (from 28, 47 and 39 yards).
With three one-score defeats recorded this year, New Orleans simply lacks the margin for error to withstand repeated scoring blunders in tight contests. Carlson's continuous field goal woes add to head coach Kellen Moore's list of bye-week priorities, as unreliable special teams only exacerbate the team's offensive stalls, defensive breakdowns and turnovers.
While much of the focus has centered on Tyler Shough's growth, an inept rushing attack still severely limits the Saints' offensive ceiling.
Sunday's outing represented a new low point for the ground game.
New Orleans generated a paltry 18 rushing yards across 17 carries, resulting in an abysmal 1.1 yards per carry.
The stat line is even more damning because Shough — a quarterback whose primary role isn't to lead the run game — was the team's top rusher with just 7 yards on three carries.
It is downright appalling that primary backs Alvin Kamara (six carries, five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries, six yards) both logged more rush attempts than total yards gained.
This embarrassing output highlights a backfield without a true lead option, further compounded by an offensive line that failed to establish leverage up front.
Such complete non-production is intolerable at any level of football—especially when relying on a developing quarterback to sustain drive after drive.
By stifling the run, Pittsburgh's defense put the burden entirely on Shough's shoulders.
Even with Shough connecting on nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans repeatedly stalled because it lacked offensive balance.
Unfortunately, this isn't merely a single bad afternoon.
The Saints' season-long inability to establish the run has made the offense predictable and easy for physical front sevens to counter.

title: 3 Takeaways From Saints' Loss to Steelers: Same Problems, Different Country
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints traveled across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to build momentum heading into their bye week and salvage their season. Instead, they returned home with its fourth loss in five games and it just seems like another repeating nightmare for Who Dat Nation.
New Orleans fell 16-10 to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in Paris, dropping to 2-5 through seven games under second-year coach Kellen Moore . It was the NFL's first regular-season game in France.
Despite another efficient passing performance from quarterback Tyler Shough , the Saints struggled to establish their rushing attack, failed to capitalize on scoring opportunities and couldn't get off the field defensively when it mattered most.
The loss marked New Orleans' third one-possession defeat this season, reinforcing concerns about the team's ability to execute in critical situations.
Here are three takeaways from another disappointing performance from the Saints performance.
For all the attention surrounding Shough's development, New Orleans' inability to run the football continues to undermine its offense.
Sunday's performance might have been its most concerning yet.
The Saints finished with just 18 rushing yards on 17 attempts, averaging a dismal 1.1 yards per carry.
Even more alarming, Shough led the team with 7 rushing yards on three attempts. However, he is a quarterback and that is not his job.
But for Alvin Kamara (six carries for five yards) and Kendre Miller (eight carries for six yards) to have more carries than rushing yards is disgusting.
It shows the lack of life in a running back room without a primary option, compounded by an offensive line struggling to create leverage.
That level of production is unacceptable for any offense regardless of the level of play, especially one relying on a young quarterback to consistently move the ball.
Pittsburgh's defense shut down the run, forcing Shough to carry nearly the entire offensive load.
Although Shough completed nearly 79% of his passes, New Orleans could not consistently finish drives because it lacked balance.
The problems extend beyond one disappointing performance.
New Orleans has struggled to generate consistent production on the ground throughout the season, making the offense increasingly predictable against physical defensive fronts.
Because of the rushing problems, the Saints had to rely on Shough again.
Shough did everything you could ask of him, completing 30 of 38 passes for 278 yards and a touchdown. However, one costly mistake ultimately changed the game's complexion.
Trailing 13-10 at the start of the second half, New Orleans put together a 13-play drive that moved the offense inside Pittsburgh's 10-yard line as the Saints appeared positioned to take their first lead of the afternoon.
Instead, Shough threw a pass intended for Chris Olave , which Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson intercepted at the Pittsburgh 11-yard line.
The turnover erased a scoring opportunity and let Pittsburgh respond with a field goal, extending its lead to 16-10.
The interception proved costly, but it also highlighted the impossible position Shough has found himself in because of New Orleans' offensive struggles.
Despite completing nearly 79% of his passes, the quarterback could not afford even one mistake because the Saints had virtually no rushing attack to complement him.
That is an unrealistic expectation for any quarterback, much less one still developing at the NFL level.
Shough showed he could move the football against a Pittsburgh defense, distributing the ball effectively and keeping New Orleans competitive despite a one-dimensional offensive approach.
However, his play reinforced a troubling reality: when Shough plays well, the Saints can win; when he makes one mistake, the operation unravels.
Until Moore builds a credible run game and finishes drives, Shough bears an unreasonable load and New Orleans must create an offense where its quarterback does not need to be perfect to win.
Unless the Saints give Shough a credible rushing attack and adequate protection, they risk repeating a familiar chapter in franchise history: asking a talented young quarterback to overcome problems far beyond his control, much like Archie Manning decades ago.
Daniel Carlson 's fourth missed field goal in 11 attempts this season — a 52-yarder in the fourth quarter — kept New Orleans trailing in a 16-10 loss to Pittsburgh, highlighting a critical special teams weakness for the 2-5 Saints.
The missed 52-yard attempt came while the Saints trailed 16-10 in the fourth quarter, keeping Pittsburgh's lead at six points. Carlson's 63.6% success rate contrasts with Steelers kicker Chris Boswell , who converted all three attempts (28, 47 and 39 yards) for nine points.
The fourth-quarter miss was especially costly as New Orleans had already squandered a promising red-zone drive earlier in the second half. Instead of entering the final minutes needing only a field goal to tie or lead, the Saints remained six points behind.
Carlson's kicking struggles add to head coach Kellen Moore's bye-week concerns. For a team hampered by offensive inefficiency, defensive lapses and turnovers, unreliable special teams further shrink a narrow margin for error.
With three one-score losses this season, New Orleans cannot afford missed points. Sunday's loss highlights that the Saints lack the margin for error to overcome recurring scoring mistakes in tight games.

title: Saints Fans Should Know These 3 Things About the Steelers Before Sunday
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints (2-4) enter Sunday's historic matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) at Stade de France, looking to build momentum after their 34-27 win over the New York Giants .
However, Pittsburgh presents a considerably different challenge.
Under first-year coach Mike McCarthy , the Steelers have established themselves as a competitive AFC North contender, winning four of their first six games despite an offense that has struggled to consistently produce explosive plays.
Pittsburgh enters Sunday's contest averaging 22.8 points and 320.5 yards per game, ranking 18th and 21st in the NFL, respectively. However, its defense has been considerably more effective, allowing 307.5 yards per game, the ninth-fewest in the league.
For Saints coach Kellen Moore , Sunday's matchup offers a chance to secure consecutive wins for the first time this season before the team's Week 8 bye.
Here are three things Saints fans should know about the Steelers.
While 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers continues to anchor Pittsburgh's offense with his elite ability to read defenses and capitalize on errors, the Steelers' aerial game has produced fairly modest results.
Across six games, Rodgers has completed 61.4% of his pass attempts for 1,487 yards, throwing 12 touchdowns against five interceptions.
Despite these respectable individual metrics, Pittsburgh ranks just 18th in the league through the air, averaging 221.3 passing yards per contest.
Physical wide receiver DK Metcalf gives Rodgers a dependable downfield threat capable of winning contested balls and creating opportunities on intermediate routes.
However, Rodgers' statistical split against specific zone schemes presents a critical storyline for this matchup.
NFL Next Gen Stats reveals that Rodgers has struggled against Cover 3, registering a 32.9% success rate—the third-lowest figure among qualified quarterbacks—compared to a 52.9% success rate against all other zone schemes.
This dynamic is especially relevant given that New Orleans deploys Cover 3 on 55.9% of defensive dropbacks, leading the entire NFL.
Consequently, defensive coordinator Brandon Staley must balance disciplined zone coverage with an effective pass rush to contain Pittsburgh's passing attack.
While Rodgers draws significant focus, the Steelers' ground attack could pose a greater threat to New Orleans.
Running back Jaylen Warren has rushed for 460 yards on 84 carries, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt.
His ability to gain yards after contact, identify lanes and contribute in the passing game gives Pittsburgh multiple offensive options.
That creates a difficult matchup for New Orleans.
The Saints allow 138 rushing yards per game, ranking 30th in the NFL, while Pittsburgh averages 99.2 rushing yards per game, ranking 20th.
Despite Pittsburgh's modest team average, Warren's efficiency indicates the Steelers can exploit the Saints' run defense.
While returning veteran linebacker Kaden Elliss should bolster the Saints' run defense, containing Warren remains a critical priority. Allowing Pittsburgh to establish its ground game early will open up play-action opportunities for Rodgers.
While Pittsburgh's offense has experienced inconsistencies, its defense remains the team's most reliable strength.
The Steelers enter Sunday's matchup allowing 21.3 points and 307.5 yards per game, ranking 12th and ninth in the NFL, respectively.
A key part of its defense has been its ability to defend the pass as the Steelers have surrendered just 204.3 yards per game, the eighth-fewest in the league.
Pittsburgh has also recorded 16 sacks and six interceptions through six games, contributing to a plus-three turnover differential.
Outside linebacker T.J. Watt , who has a team-high 4.5 sacks, remains one of the league's most disruptive defensive players.
Alex Highsmith provides another formidable presence on the edge, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward anchors the interior.
The Steelers also one of the league’s top cornerbacks, eight-time Pro Bowler Jalen Ramsey , giving their secondary an experienced playmaker who can create turnovers.
For Saints quarterback Tyler Shough , protecting the football will be especially important.
Shough has thrown for 1,443 yards, 12 touchdowns and five interceptions this season, but his performance against zone coverage presents a potential concern.
According to Next Gen Stats , Shough has thrown five interceptions against zone coverage this season, tied for the second-most among qualified quarterbacks.
Pittsburgh has utilized zone coverage on 82.8% of opposing dropbacks, with five of its six interceptions occurring against zone concepts.
This creates a compelling schematic test between Moore's offense and Pittsburgh's defense.
If Pittsburgh generates pressure without compromising coverage, Shough may struggle against an opportunistic unit. To build on last week's win, New Orleans will need to establish the run, avoid clear passing downs, and minimize turnovers.

title: Saints vs. Steelers: Injury Concerns Mount Ahead of Historic Paris Showdown
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints face several injury concerns as they prepare for Sunday's historic international matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Stade de France in Paris.
Running back Alvin Kamara and starting offensive guard Cesar Ruiz headline New Orleans' injury report, while Pittsburgh is monitoring several key defensive players, including T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith and Jalen Ramsey.
According to the Saints' official Thursday injury report , 11 New Orleans players were listed Thursday, with three missing practice and three participating on a limited basis.
The Saints (2-4) are looking to build momentum following Sunday's 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, which snapped a three-game losing streak. Meanwhile, Pittsburgh (4-2) enters the matchup seeking its second consecutive victory.
Both teams have several injury situations worth monitoring before Friday's final practice report.
The Saints' biggest offensive concerns involve Kamara and Ruiz, who have been dealing with back and knee injuries, respectively.
Kamara was limited for the second consecutive practice Thursday, leaving his availability worth monitoring heading into Sunday's game.
The veteran running back remains an important part of Kellen Moore's offense, particularly as New Orleans attempts to establish a more consistent rushing attack.
Ruiz's situation is potentially more concerning. The veteran offensive lineman missed practice Wednesday and Thursday because of a knee injury, raising questions about his availability against Pittsburgh's defensive front.
However, Jeremiah Wright played well in his absence during New Orleans’ win over the Giants last week.
Meanwhile, linebacker Kaden Elliss (calf) and edge rusher Anfernee Jennings (knee) were limited for the second consecutive day. During today's player roundtable , Elliss was asked if he would be available to play Sunday, and he said, "Yes."
There was some encouraging news for New Orleans.
Shough, who appeared on the report with a left-hand injury, participated fully in both practices. Cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry (head) and defensive lineman Nathan Shepherd (illness) also practiced without limitations.
Running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) improved from limited participation Wednesday to a full practice Thursday.
Kicker Daniel Carlson missed his second consecutive practice because of a personal matter unrelated to injury (he and his wife are having a baby), while defensive lineman Davon Godchaux received a rest day Thursday.
Backup quarterback Spencer Rattler was added to Thursday's report with a knee injury but participated fully.
Pittsburgh is also dealing with significant injury concerns, particularly on defense.
The most notable development Thursday was star edge rusher T.J. Watt, who was limited with a calf injury after sitting out Wednesday's practice for rest.
Watt's status matters, given the Saints' offensive line concerns. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year has 4.5 sacks through six games.
Fellow pass rusher Alex Highsmith remained limited with a groin injury, while veteran defensive tackle Cameron Heyward missed his second straight practice for rest.
The Steelers also received encouraging news about star cornerback Jalen Ramsey, who returned to practice on Thursday, albeit in a limited capacity. He missed Wednesday's session with a wrist injury.

title: Saints Stock Up: 3 Heroes From New Orleans' Win Over Giants
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints earned a much-needed victory over the New York Giants as they broke a three-game losing streak.
Now, the Saints are in Paris as they turn their attention to the Pittsburgh Steelers to win consecutive games for the first time this season. However, it will be a tough task: Pittsburgh still has a solid quarterback in Aaron Rodgers at 42, and the offense has plenty of weapons; on defense, they have a solid pass rush.
After fully reviewing the Saints’ win over New York and looking at which players have been trending upward, here are three players whose stock is rising.
The Saints historically produce standout special teams performers, including Morten Andersen , Michael Lewis , and Steve Gleason .
Linebacker Isaiah Stalbird has continued that tradition this year, keying special teams unit success and executing the decisive sequence of the game.
Down 10-3 late in the second quarter, New Orleans seemed poised for a halftime deficit before Stalbird made a game-altering play on coverage.
The second-year backer stripped the ball from Charlie Jones on a kickoff return, which tight end Oscar Delp recovered to set up New Orleans inside the red zone.
Shough converted the takeaway into points, finding rookie Bryce Lance for a game-tying touchdown right before the break.
That turnover shifted game momentum entirely and helped spark a 31-point unanswered run that gave New Orleans a 34-10 lead before the Giants mounted a furious fourth-quarter comeback.
Cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. posted his top outing of the year in the 34-27 victory, accumulating seven tackles, two interceptions, and four pass breakups.
His effort earned an 88.4 defensive rating and a 90.2 coverage rating from Pro Football Focus, leading all team defenders in Week 6. Emerson was named NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his efforts.
Emerson held opponents to four catches on 10 targeted passes while picking off throws from Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy . The performance provided valuable depth after Kool-Aid McKinstry exited due to a migraine.
Rookie guard Jeremiah Wright capitalized on unexpected playing time against New York, filling in when starter Cesar Ruiz left with a knee injury in the second quarter.
If one thing is certain, the run game started to click when Wright went into the game as he added toughness to the interior line, anchoring a run game that piled up a season-best 175 yards. If you want to know how much of an impact Wright had? When the Saints ran to the right, they averaged just over 5 yards per carry. When they ran to the left? 3.1-yards a clip.
The fourth-round selection surrendered just a single QB pressure in his most extensive action of the season.

title: Harbaugh’s Giants Show What They’re Made Of
full_text:
In past years, a season-ending injury to the starting quarterback or key pass rusher, or a gut-punch loss to a team they were supposed to beat, might have reduced the New York Giants to a pile of rubble.
But not John Harbaugh’s Giants. They’re operating with one of the league’s worst injury situations , one that has robbed them of several key players, including starting quarterback Jaxson Dart, outside linebacker Brian Burns, and inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, among others.
And while the team is far from a juggernaut, Harbaugh’s scrappy Giants have fought and clawed their way to last year’s win total while also padding their lead in the NFC East after a hard-fought 27-21 overtime win against the Houston Texans.
“Man, that was a players’ win in every way — blocking, tackling, special teams, covering kicks, pass game, operating, getting stops when we needed stops, fighting back from adversity,” Harbaugh said after the game.
“But just play one play at a time, as well as you can, regardless of the last play, with no thought for the next play, as hard as you can. As [OLB] Abdul Carter told the guys at halftime, ‘No matter what, empty the tank. No matter what, come back in here with nothing left,’ and that’s what they did.”
The Giants, who have now played two overtime games in three weeks, have shown resiliency, maturity, and determination. When they get punched in the mouth — and they have a couple of times this season — they don’t wave the white flag.
They take their lumps and come back ready to serve a helping of their own.
“It tells you who they are. You might have thought before the game, we’re going to find out about our guys. We’re going to find out about who they are, and we did, and you saw it. They did, they took the bull by the horns, and they got the job done,” Harbaugh said.
A look around the Giants locker room offers so many individual stories of resiliency, starting with running back Cam Skattebo. Dealt a “quasi-benching” a week ago for carelessness with the ball and his assignments, Skattebo zipped his lip, went to work, and produced a career-high 124 yards on 17 carries and one of the four rushing touchdowns the Giants had that day.
Then there is Devin “Motor” Singletary, who finished with 41 rushing yards on five carries and the game-winning touchdown, a 30-yard dash. Singletary, who took a pay cut to stay with the Giants, found himself squeezed out of the running back rotation for three straight weeks.
He didn’t complain and kept working to earn his chance. And when it came, he made the most of it.
“I can’t say enough about ‘Motor’ [RB Devin Singletary], and that’s on me. That’s on me. We were looking for the formula, and he was the odd man out for several weeks. Not because of anything he did or didn’t do; he just was the odd man out, and that’s exactly what I told him,” Harbaugh said.
“He asked me, ‘What can I do?’ I said, ‘There’s nothing you can do; you’re doing everything you can do, and your time will come.’ It was going to come. And look where it came, right there, and he came through.”
Inside linebacker Micah McFadden is another who rose to the occasion. A starter until a season-ending foot injury last year, McFadden never got the chance to reclaim his starting job once the team signed veteran Tremaine Edmunds and drafted Arvell Reese.
But McFadden, whom Harbaugh always called a starter, was right there to step into Edmunds’ role as the defense’s “quarterback” when Edmunds was lost for the rest of the season with a shoulder injury.
McFadden’s first start resulted in a 10-tackle day (all solo efforts), plus two tackles for loss and a quarterback hit, the most productive stat line of any Giants defender.
“He had a bunch of tackles. Then he made the first-down tackle when they ran that sweep play; he shows up out of nowhere and tackles it for a one-yard loss, and that set the tone. That’s really what got them off the field and gave us a chance,” Harbaugh said.
There are so many more stories of resiliency.
Quarterback J.J. McCarthy, whose career was on life support in Minnesota before he was traded to the Giants for a fifth-round draft pick a few weeks ago, has looked right at home in this offense, finishing 20 of 28 for 252 yards with no touchdowns and no interceptions.
Cornerback Deonte Banks, who many thought was on his way out the door at the end of last season, has played lights out since winning the starting cornerback job. This week, with Greg Newsome II sidelined with a concussion, Banks drew the Texans’ top receiver, Nico Collins, and limited him to one catch on four targets for just four yards.
“I probably should have given him a game ball,” Harbaugh quipped. “Maybe he’ll get defensive player of the game. But he was on it, man. He had so many tight coverages. You have to cover these guys tight, especially in breaking routes, man and zone, because his quarterback is really accurate, especially when he moves in the pocket.”
Other contributions helped make the win possible, but the common trait they all share is resiliency. And that starts with Harbaugh and his staff, who have worked to implement a support system that builds players up rather than tears them down.
“I would say just a lot of moments stacked on top of each other because they just didn’t bat an eye and they continued to work hard and fight. Every type of situation, they met the same way,” he said when asked if there was a moment when he realized the team had the mental makeup to withstand adversity the way it has.
Moving forward, Harbaugh said players who underwent season-ending surgery will be allowed to travel with the team.
“I just think it’s an ongoing type of a thing,” he said. “That’s how you build — it’s shared experiences. It’s fighting through all these things together that draws people close together, and that’s how a team is built.”
For now, Harbaugh’s scrappy, first-place Giants will go into their bye week with their effort and resiliency rewarded, and with a chance to heal up for what should be a tough second half of the schedule.
“Now, you’ve got to make something of it,” Harbaugh said. “It doesn’t mean anything if you don’t build on it, right? But it doesn’t mean we’re going to win a championship yet. It means we have an opportunity, though. We have an opportunity to get ready for the next two games starting with Philadelphia, and then a quick turnaround, so we’ll be thinking about two games as a coaching staff over the bye week.
“The two most important games of the season will be coming up after we come back from the bye, which will set the direction for the rest of the season, really. But we’re going to be in this thing until the end.”

title: J.J. McCarthy Delivers a Winning Debut as Giants Starter, Beating Texans in Overtime
full_text:
New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy is clearly enjoying his change of scenery.
Making his first start for New York since being acquired via trade with the Minnesota Vikings on Sept. 28, McCarthy, the 10th overall selection in the 2024 NFL Draft, led the Giants on four scoring drives en route to a 27-21 Week 7 victory in overtime against the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium.
McCarthy completed 20 of 28 passes (71.4% completion) for 252 yards, earning a passer rating of 99.1. Across four quarters and overtime, the 23-year-old showcased his multifaceted skill set while maintaining a calm, cool, and collected demeanor.
McCarthy gave the Giants (4-2-1) exactly what they needed to topple the Texans. Despite throwing neither a touchdown pass nor an interception, the Giants’ new starter had only one number on his mind.
“Truly the only stat I care about is going 1-0,” McCarthy said from his postgame podium. “I couldn’t care less how we get it done. At the end of the day, you want to perform well. You want to execute well.”
“I’m as happy as I can be,” he added. “Whether I’m throwing the touchdowns, I’m as happy as I can be. At the end of the day, all that matters is getting that victory.”
Though he may be best suited to an offense built on zone reads, designed runs, and RPO packages, McCarthy showed his prowess in the deep passing game during the first half. The former Michigan Wolverine connected with star receiver Malik Nabers for 42 yards, wideout Malachi Fields for 47, and tight end Thomas Fidone II for a 29-yard near-touchdown.
When the Giants’ running game came to life in the second half, McCarthy adjusted his approach, using the underneath area to let the running backs find productive yardage.
All the while, McCarthy exuded the look and feel of a team leader while staying focused on his job.
“It’s the same thing that goes through my mind every time I step on the field, practice, or game,” he said. “What can I do in those six seconds to the best of my ability to help this team move the ball and help this team win?
“I just had a blast out there with these guys,” he continued. “We had a great week of practice and just executed at a really high level. To be able to go watch the tape and find ways to get better, that’s the No. 1 thing we’re focused on right now.”
McCarthy’s rise to the top of the Giants’ quarterback depth chart has been remarkable. Originally considered the third option behind then-starter Jameis Winston and scout-team quarterback Jake Haener, the ex-Viking quickly grasped the Giants’ playbook while showing comfort in coordinator Matt Nagy’s offense.
Though he was used only in select packages in the Giants’ 27-27 Week 5 tie with the Washington Commanders, McCarthy took the offensive reins with 11 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter of the team’s 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints, after Winston’s second interception of the day.
McCarthy finished the game having completed 11 of 21 passes for 243 yards and one touchdown. He logged the most passing yards in a fourth quarter by any player this season. For his efforts, coach John Harbaugh named McCarthy the Giants’ new starting quarterback.
As the Giants head into their Week 8 bye, one might assume McCarthy has extra time to rest on his laurels. However, the 6-foot-3, 219-pound quarterback understands that with his opportunity comes great responsibility. Despite the impressive stat sheet, McCarthy was sacked three times and also regretted some errant throws.
As Big Blue reconvenes to prepare for its Week 9 matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles, McCarthy will be ready to lead his team toward what Giants fans hope will be their first playoff berth since 2022.
“Just the overall complementary football that was on display today was very exciting,” McCarthy declared.
“There are obviously throws that I want back, and there are plays the defense wants back and special teams. That’s exciting because there are so many other areas and other ways we can get better and keep moving forward.
“But getting the win going into the bye is an absolutely great feeling,” he added. “We just have to keep staying humble and hungry.”

title: Giants Grades: Ground Force Rules in OT Win Over Texans
full_text:
The New York Giants delivered a big overtime win against the Houston Texans, a 27-21 thriller in which the running game, challenged this week by head coach John Harbaugh, answered the call against a Texans defense that came in with the league’s third-best run defense (83.0 yards per game).
Harbaugh challenged the running backs to step up and take the bull by the horns. They produced 188 yards on 34 carries (5.5 average), with 180 of those yards on 28 carries (6.43 yards per carry) by Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy Jr., and Devin Singletary.
Skattebo, who finished with a career-best 124 yards on 17 carries, and Singletary had the Giants’ two longest rushing plays from scrimmage this season in overtime on the game-winning drive. Skattebo went for 42 yards and Singletary for the 30-yard game-winner.
All four of the Giants’ touchdowns this week came on the ground, one each by Skattebo, Singletary, Tracy, and quarterback Jameis Winston on a tush push.
Here are a few other quick takeaways from the win.
Quarterback J.J. McCarthy, in his debut as Big Blue’s starting quarterback, had a fine afternoon, finishing 20 of 28 for 252 yards with no interceptions or touchdowns thrown (99.1 rating).
What especially stood out was McCarthy’s solid deep-ball play, completing two of his four attempts of 20-plus air yards for 69 air yards total. His two longest passes of the day went to rookie receiver Malachi Fields for 47 yards and receiver Malik Nabers for 42 yards.
Cornerback Deonte Banks’s bounce-back season continued this week as he allowed just three of six pass targets to be completed for 10 yards, only one of them after the catch.
Banks held his own against top Texans receiver Nico Collins, limiting him to one catch on four targets for four yards, one after the catch. The coaches wisely had Banks playing mostly man coverage, which is his strength, and he turned in one of his best performances of the season.
As Banks’s confidence grows each week, that can only help when the Giants return from the bye to face what should be a tougher slate of opposing receivers.
The media forgot to ask receiver Malik Nabers last week how much more he feels he has to go before he’s 100%. But if he’s not there by now after the devastating knee injury he suffered last year, then the sky truly is the limit for him this season.
Nabers recorded his fifth straight 100-yard game this season, this time catching seven of nine targets for 111 yards. He is tied with Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba for the most 100-yard receiving games this season.
This week’s Giants offense had it all, including the explosive plays it had been missing in both the passing and running games.
The offense also helped stifle league sack leader Will Anderson Jr., who was held without a sack, and credit should go to right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor, who pushed through a painful calf injury.
And how about the discipline? The Giants had only two penalties: a rather iffy unnecessary roughness flag against Skattebo and a deliberate delay of game by the punt team to give Jordan Stout more room to work with. Oh, and did anyone catch how Skattebo broke three tackles on his touchdown run?
Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson challenged his defense after last week’s lackluster showing in the loss to the Saints, and it responded. New York held the Texans to 84 yards on the ground and just 153 passing yards.
The defense also sacked Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud and covered Collins like a blanket. Tackling was better than last week, as more players ran to the ball and heeded their coach’s words to wrap up ball carriers rather than grab at them.
Kudos to Micah McFadden, who stepped in for Tremaine Edmunds and finished with a team-leading 10 tackles (all solo), two tackles for loss, and a quarterback hit.
Do the Giants have a kicking problem to worry about moving forward? After starting the season 9-of-9, Dominic Zvada has made four of his last nine field goal attempts. He missed two indoors this week, which thankfully didn’t hurt his team.
But it said a lot that in the third quarter, with the ball on the Texans’ 37-yard line, the Giants took a five-yard delay-of-game penalty and punted rather than try another field goal.
The punt coverage unit was shaky once again, allowing the Texans an average of 12.5 yards per return, with Tank Dell and Jaylin Noel having longs of 14 and 11 yards, respectively. If there’s a bright spot, it’s that the unit was better than last week.
The play calling was strong, but kudos to the coaching staff for challenging the players and to the players for answering. This was a classic example of how coaching matters, and it’s why one should never count out a team led by John Harbaugh.
From a tactical perspective, good job by offensive coordinator Matt Nagy in getting Malachi Fields more involved downfield. And what about the Giants’ version of the tush push, which faked everyone out on the last one they ran before Skattebo’s big run?
On defense, Wilson brought the heat against Stroud, who was blitzed on 44.8% of his dropbacks and faced pressure on 55.2% overall.

title: Giants Ride Cam Skattebo’s 124 Rushing Yards to a 27-21 OT Win Over Texans
full_text:
The New York Giants entered Week 7 of the NFL season needing a spark in their running game.
On their first overtime possession, running backs Cam Skattebo and Devin Singletary delivered an big bang, the duo combining for 72 ground yards in just two plays, as the Giants defeated the Houston Texans 27-21 at Reliant Stadium.
Making his first start for New York after being acquired via trade with the Minnesota Vikings on Sept. 28, quarterback J.J. McCarthy demonstrated calm composure while showcasing his skill set. The Michigan product finished the game by finishing 20-for-28 for 252 yards.
Skattebo rushed for 124 yards on 17 carries and one touchdown, in his return to the offensive mix after being held without a carry in Week 6 against the Saints. As for Singletary, his 41 total yards included the 30-yard game-winning score.
For the Texans, quarterback C.J. Stroud went 17-for-28 with 153 yards and two touchdowns, while running back Woody Marks ran 19 times for 66 yards.
With the win, the Giants improve to 4-2-1 through seven games in the 2026 NFL season.
The Texans used their home-field advantage on their opening drive, gaining 25 yards on six plays. New York’s blitz kept Stroud from logging big gains, and a four-yard pass to Xavier Hutchinson was ruled incomplete after officials determined Hutchinson trapped the ball rather than catching it.
Ultimately, the added yardage meant little to Houston kicker Ka’imi Fairbairn, who made a 58-yarder to give the Texans a 3-0 lead.
The Giants wasted little time in responding, as McCarthy led his team on a nine-play, 66-yard drive on the team’s first offensive possession of the day. Skattebo contributed a six-yard run to take the Giants near midfield.
Still, the drive was unquestionably highlighted by a 42-yard deep ball from McCarthy to receiver Malik Nabers, who beat Texans cornerback Kamari Lassiter in one-on-one coverage.
J.J. DEEP to LEEK!! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/djyIdZteKI
On the ensuing snap, running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. rushed for the two-yard touchdown, giving the Giants a 7-3 lead.
While the Giants couldn't add to their advantage before the end of the first quarter — due to a missed 56-yard attempt from rookie Dominic Zvada — the Texans earned the first points of the second quarter on a seven-play, 39-yard drive. The series ended with a 57-yard field goal from Fairbairn, cutting New York’s lead to 7-6.
Big Blue responded once again on the ensuing drive, as McCarthy led them 78 yards on nine plays for their second scoring drive of the afternoon. The Giants were paced by an 11-yard run from Skattebo and a 17-yard reception by Nabers.
The gem of the series took place on 1st-and-10 from the Houston 30, when McCarthy connected with tight end Thomas Fidone II. The 2025 seventh-rounder hauled in a 29-yard pass, his first NFL reception.
Thomas Fidone WIDE OPEN 🔥 #NationalTightEndsDay 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/iJYPOQbKfC
Two plays later, Giants quarterback Jameis Winston took a one-yard sneak into the end zone, extending the lead to 14-6.
Houston, however, was determined to prove itself beyond its 2-4 record. Stroud led the Texans on an eight-play, 90-yard drive as the clock wound down in the second quarter.
The highlight of the series came on a 43-yard strike to receiver Tank Dell, who was playing in his first NFL game since Week 16 of the 2024 season. Stroud capped the series by finding Marvin Harrison Jr. for a six-yard score, his first as a member of the Texans. Houston’s two-point conversion was successful, tying the game at 14.
With less than a minute remaining in the half, the Giants had a chance to take the lead — thanks in part to a 27-yard completion from McCarthy to Nabers. Unfortunately for Big Blue, Zvada missed a 44-yard attempt (his second misfire of the day), keeping the score locked at 14-14 at the half.
The Giants and Texans traded defensive stands and miscues before beginning a 14-play, 80-yard drive late in the third quarter. Despite a 14-yard completion from McCarthy to receiver Malachi Fields, New York’s ground game dominated the series — particularly Skattebo.
The second-year rusher sparked the drive with a 19-yard run from his team’s own 29-yard line. The Giants capped the drive with a 16-yard touchdown run from Skattebo, complete with a celebratory backflip. Following the Zvada extra point, the Giants took a 21-14 lead, while draining 8:18 from the clock.
HE WILL NOT BE DENIED 😤 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/ReAKg8Thp0
With a defensive stand needed to keep Houston in check, the Giants defense yielded 48 yards on nine plays. Texans receiver Xavier Hutchinson delivered an 11-yard carry, taking his team into New York’s red zone. Stroud capped the drive with a three-yard touchdown pass to Hutchinson. Fairbairn added the point-after to tie the game at 21 with 52 seconds remaining in regulation.
After winning the coin toss, the Giants chose to kick, giving the Texans first possession in overtime. New York held its ground against the home team, forcing a punt after only three plays. Linebacker Kayvon Thibodeaux nearly intercepted Stroud on 2nd-and-10, but couldn't secure the pass. Following that sequence, New York got its chance to score in the game’s extra period.
On 2nd-and-1 from their own 28-yard line, the Giants' run game took over.
Following a nine-yard pass completion from McCarthy to Nabers, Skattebo ripped the longest run for the Giants this season. The 42-yard run put Big Blue deep within Texans territory. Reserve back Devin Singletary showed why he is called “Motor” as he powered his way to the end zone for the 30-yard touchdown run.
SINGLETARY SEALS IT 🔥 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/NEB091GEyG
FINAL: Giants 27, Texans 21
Giants running back Tyrone Tracy suffered a hamstring injury in the second quarter after completing a seven-yard run. After limping off the field to the sideline, Tracy was deemed questionable to return. He returned to action in the second half.
Giants linebacker Zaire Barnes remains a force on special teams. The third-year veteran added one  special teams tackle against the Texans.
Barnes entered this Week 7 matchup tied for the league lead with 10 special teams tackles. Barnes has recorded at least 1 special teams tackle in every game this season and also forced a fumble in Week 3 on the opening kickoff.
The Philadelphia Eagles (2-4) will host the Dallas Cowboys (2-4) at Lincoln Financial Field for a Monday Night Football matchup. The final game of Week 7 will kick off at 8:15 p.m. ET.
The Washington Commanders (1-4-1) are on a Week 7 bye. They return in Week 8, hosting the Eagles for a Sunday Night Football showdown at Northwest Stadium.
The Giants will attempt to get healthy during their Week 8 bye. They will return to action on Nov. 8 for a Week 9 game against Philadelphia at Lincoln Financial Field. Kickoff is set for 1:00 p.m. ET.

title: Giants vs. Texans Live Updates: Score, Analysis and Highlights From Week 7
full_text:
The New York Giants (3-2-1) travel to Houston on Sunday to face the Texans (2-4), with redemption on their minds.
Last week, in their 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints (a game the Giants had no business losing but somehow found a way to), Big Blue did not play well in any phase.
The goal this week was to clean up a lot of the problems across all three phases, including defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson’s very direct characterization of players not running to the ball as “traitors” on defense , the embarrassing communication issues on special teams, and the lethargic rushing attack, which head coach John Harbaugh hopes someone will take the bull by the horns .
It won’t be easy. Despite their 2-4 record, the Texans are just starting to get into a groove. They’ve won their last two games, against the Titans and Jaguars, and have the league’s 10th-best offense and fourth-best passing offense. Their defense is probably the best the Giants have faced since their Week 2 loss to the Los Angeles Rams.
But the Giants, who this week made the switch to quarterback J.J. McCarthy, are hoping the offense, which has struggled since its Week 1 domination of Dallas, gets a much-needed injection of adrenaline.
McCarthy, who had a successful, extensive showing in last week’s loss to the Saints (albeit against a softer defense), more closely matches the skill set of injured starter Jaxson Dart.
That means the 20-30% of the playbook (the RPO and designed runs) that the Giants had to drop when they lost Dart will be restored. The hope is that bringing that element back will help the lethargic rushing attack.
There are other factors to consider. For one, the health of the team’s top three offensive tackles (Andrew Thomas, Jermaine Eluemunor and Marcus Mbow) is a big question mark, with the latter two listed as questionable for Sunday.
Suffice it to say, this is not a good week for the tackles to be gimpy, not with an afternoon against NFL sack leaders Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter and Jadeveon Clowney on the dance card.
On the other side of the ball, the Giants defense just lost another key starter in inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, the defense’s “quarterback.” That’s not good news for a run defense that ranks 29th in yards allowed per game (135.5) and 31st in average rushing yards allowed per play (5.05).
If there is a hint of good news for Giants fans to lean on, it’s that even if the Giants lose this week, they will still be in first place in the NFC East. Dallas and Philadelphia are playing each other, and Washington has a bye.
Still, it would make for a much better afternoon if the Giants can go into their Week 8 bye with an upset win, giving themselves and their division lead a little more padding.

title: Giants’ Tyler Nubin Active vs. Texans; Jevon Holland, Marcus Mbow Out
full_text:
The banged-up New York Giants defense got a bit of good news on Sunday as starting safety Tyler Nubin (neck) is active for the game against the Houston Texans.
Nubin, listed as questionable, was injured in the fourth quarter of last week’s loss to the New Orleans Saints. He had returned after missing the previous week’s game against the Washington Commanders with a neck injury.
Nubin, who has struggled this season, went through a pregame workout with a trainer to determine if he was well enough to play. He will presumably get the start alongside Jason Pinnock, who takes the place of Jevon Holland (concussion), who was declared out.
Ar’Darius Washington and Raheem Layne, the latter of whom was elevated off the practice squad, will rotate in on the sub packages.
Amid an otherwise injury-heavy day, Giants offensive tackle Jermaine Eluemunor (calf), who had a “questionable” designation this week, is active. Marcus Mbow (knee), also questionable, is inactive.
The Giants face a Texans team that ranks third in the league in sacks (18) and whose edge defender Will Anderson Jr. leads the league with 7.5 sacks.
Eluemunor, per PFF, is the Giants’ best-graded pass blocker with an 81.3 mark. According to the advanced analytics site, he has allowed three quarterback pressures, tied for fewest among the team’s offensive linemen with at least 10 pass-blocking snaps.
Mbow was a surprise addition to the injury report this week. He started last week for Eluemunor at right tackle and allowed only one quarterback pressure .
Left tackle Andrew Thomas, who has been laboring through a groin injury, did not receive an injury designation on Friday and is good to go.
Four of the Giants’ seven inactive players this week were on the injury report, and three were declared out on Friday.
With Newsome sidelined, Paulson Adebo, who was activated off IR, is expected to start opposite Deonte Banks.
Inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds (shoulder), who was also declared out on Friday, was placed on season-ending IR on Saturday.
Running back Cam Skattebo is expected to return to a normal workload this week after last week’s quasi-benching. However, Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy are likely to share the bulk of the carries.
Texans receiver Tank Dell, who was activated off IR this week, is active for the game. Otherwise, Houston’s inactive list consists mostly of injured players.
The Giants and Texans get underway today at 1:05 p.m.

title: Why the Giants Will Beat the Texans, Why They Won’t, and a Prediction
full_text:
The New York Giants might have a winning record (3-2-1) right now and lead the NFC East.
But let’s be honest. Aside from their dominant Week 1 showing against the Dallas Cowboys, have the Giants really looked as good as their record suggests?
We’re talking about a team where the phrase “A win’s a win” applies. The Giants barely beat the Tennessee Titans, 12-7, in Week 3. They also had to fight back in Week 4 against the Arizona Cardinals, who led 24-19 at one point.
The tie against the Commanders? That one was a gift. If Jayden Daniels and Dan Quinn don’t have that brain blip, the Commanders likely win, despite the Giants roaring back from a 19-6 deficit.
And last week? We’re sorry, but the Giants had no business losing to the New Orleans Saints as badly as they did. And again, make no mistake: the Giants lost that game because they were their own worst enemy, as shown by the sloppy play they put on film.
But it’s funny how the football gods work. The Giants, regardless of what they do against the Houston Texans this week, will remain in first place in the division.
They have a chance, albeit a difficult one, to get back to looking like the team they were in Week 1, even though they’ve since lost a lot of key personnel, all of whom played in that win: quarterback Jaxson Dart, returner/receiver Braxton Berrios, outside linebacker Brian Burns, and inside linebacker Tremaine Edmunds.
So what’s the goal this week if the Giants want to pull off an upset win over the Texans on the road?
“We’ve been practicing well the last few weeks,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “I think practice has been improving every single week, which is the mark of a team that has got a chance to do something. You’ve got to keep improving.
“So, we are on track to do that. I’m looking forward to it showing up in terms of consistency. If we’ve been anything, we’ve been inconsistent.”
It’s really that simple. The question is, will the Giants finally find the consistency that’s eluded them since that Week 1 game?
The Texans might be on a roll, having won their last two games, but they still have a few flaws that could work to the Giants’ advantage.
For one, the Texans’ offensive line ranks 27th in the PFF pass-blocking efficiency rating metric. The unit has allowed 71 quarterback pressures, tied for third-most in the league. Left tackle Aireontae Ersery has allowed 20 quarterback pressures, per PFF, tied for fourth-most in the league among left tackles.
Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has turned up the heat on opposing quarterbacks in recent weeks. This year, opposing quarterbacks have completed only 54.1% of their pass attempts against the Giants’ blitz, the fourth-lowest completion rate in the league.
Of course, the key is for the Giants to stop the run, something they haven’t done consistently in recent weeks. So we’ll see if Wilson’s calling out his defensive players for not running to the ball lights a fire underneath them.
Offensively, the Giants need to get their running game going, and the hope is that switching to quarterback J.J. McCarthy will help. This more mobile quarterback will discourage the Texans from loading up the box and start accounting for McCarthy as a runner.
More importantly, McCarthy’s ability to scramble away from trouble could help the Giants’ ailing offensive tackles, Andrew Thomas and, if he plays, Jermaine Eluemunor, against that Texans pass rush.
Per Next Gen Stats, since 2025, McCarthy has scrambled 19 times for 185 yards and three touchdowns, a 9.7 yards-per-carry average, which is a league high among quarterbacks with a minimum of 15 carries.
If McCarthy can buy time, he stands a chance at connecting with receiver Malik Nabers or tight end Isaiah Likely, both of whom have been the most frequently targeted players on offense for the Giants over the last few weeks.
I touched on it a bit above, but I’ll say it again here. The Giants have to stop the run.
Texans’ top running back, David Montgomery, has been sidelined with a groin injury, but Woody Marks has stepped up in his place. Marks is an explosive running back who has averaged almost four yards per rush over the last two weeks. He also has six catches for 47 yards over that span.
The Giants’ run defense? Not good at all. Big Blue has allowed opponents 135.5 rushing yards per game this year, and their 5.0 yards per carry allowed is the second-worst average in the league.
If the Giants can’t stuff Marks and the Texans’ running game, it won’t matter what pass-rush plan they have this week. And until the unit shows it has cleaned up the missed tackles (13 last week, seven against the run per PFF), that aspect of the game will remain the team’s Achilles heel.
At the start of the season, I had this game down as a loss and nothing — not even the Texans’ 2-4 record or the Giants’ 3-2-1 start — has changed my mind.
The Texans have been coming into their own lately, and the Giants, aside from their Week 1 win over Dallas, have barely gotten by in their other wins and in their tie against Washington.
The Giants will fight — that much I am certain of — and I hope this doesn’t turn into the ugly rout that I fear it could become.

title: How to Watch Giants vs. Texans: Time, TV, Radio and Referee for Week 7
full_text:
Ever since two-time Super Bowl MVP quarterback Eli Manning retired after a 16-year run with the organization, the New York Giants and their fans have had to come to grips with how spoiled they were to witness rare consistency at the sport’s most important position.
Manning finally hung up his cleats after the 2019 season, but even before that decision, the Giants had started testing the waters with other gunslingers around him. Since then, 12 different players have suited up to lead Big Blue and largely failed to live up to his legacy.
Those include Jaxson Dart, who the franchise believes is its long-term answer but who has run into injury problems, including a season-ending knee injury in Week 2, and his initial backup, Jameis Winston, who has assumed the role in the team’s previous four contests.
With head coach John Harbaugh electing to make a change at quarterback ahead of Week 7, J.J. McCarthy becomes the 13th man on the short list, and his first task at the helm won’t be an easy one as the Giants travel to Houston to face the Texans on Sunday.
The Texans’ 2-4 record might not be the shiniest in the league, but they have a few solid pieces that will test McCarthy and the Giants’ roster. Quarterback C.J. Stroud has started to heat up just in time for the Texans to get back one of their key offensive weapons in Tank Dell, who will line up wide opposite another All-Pro threat in Nico Collins.
On the defensive side of the field, Houston boasts what some might argue are the two best pass rushers in football. Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter are among the most productive duos in the league with 14 sacks and 60 pressures between them in six games, both stats to be feared by a Giants offensive line that has struggled under the weight of injuries.
The Texans’ two advantages have the football public leaning heavily toward the host team and doubting McCarthy, who has started only 10 games since being drafted No. 10 overall in 2024 and has gone through ebbs and flows in Minnesota.
For Harbaugh’s Giants, however, the switch to the former national championship signal-caller has created nothing but confidence throughout the locker room, especially on offense, where McCarthy’s strong arm and capable legs could reopen the full playbook once designed for Dart.
It’s certainly a big spot for McCarthy to prove himself once again. The Giants remain at the top of a very underperforming NFC East, where the three teams below have been crumbling in recent weeks, leaving the door wide open for them to chase a division title with a few more bold wins in the second half of the season.
Coming off a poor team performance against the New Orleans Saints, in which McCarthy entered the lopsided affair in the fourth quarter and nearly brought the Giants back from their  deficit, he has no better opportunity to help New York achieve that goal and change the image of his career.
The Giants got all they could squeeze out of the “Jameis Winston experience,” and the veteran deserves kudos for leading the organization into a 3-2-1 start that keeps them relevant in the postseason discussion.
After watching a few wild yet sharply executed drives by McCarthy at the end of a game that should have been an ugly blowout, Harbaugh and the Giants see there is another level they might be able to tap into with the third-year quarterback.
It’s time for the J.J. McCarthy experience for a full 60 minutes in Houston, where the Giants hope to escape with a much-needed win before their bye week.
Check in with New York Giants On SI for all the pregame, in-game, and postgame coverage.
Sunday will mark the seventh regular-season meeting between the Giants and Texans since the series began in 2002. New York leads the series 5-1.
The Texans captured the first game on Nov. 24, 2002, with a close 16-14 win over the Giants. Since then, Big Blue has dominated the series, winning the next five games, including the most recent in 2022, when it leveled Houston 24-16.
Most games have been tight, with only two separated by more than 10 points.
The game will air on FOX. For the second straight week, Adam Amin will call the game, former NFL quarterback Drew Brees will be the analyst, and Kristina Pink will report from the sidelines.
Giants fans can listen to the game on WFAN 101.9 FM. Bob Papa will handle play-by-play, joined by Giants legend Carl Banks as the analyst and Howard Cross as the sideline reporter.

title: Giants’ Run Defense Is a Problem, but D.J. Reader Is Not
full_text:
Through the first six weeks of the 2026 season, the New York Giants ’ run defense has once again been a glaring problem that has hurt the team’s overall performance.
Following their crushing 34-27 Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints, in which they allowed 175 rushing yards- the third time this season they have given up at least 163, questions have been rising as to whether the organization did enough to fix the defense’s biggest weakness, which ranked last in yards per carry last season.
Those concerns intensified in the offseason, when the Giants sent shockwaves by trading two-time All-Pro defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence to the Cincinnati Bengals.
The move shipped off a disgruntled star but left a gaping hole at one of the game’s most important positions.
With the money freed up by the deal, they signed two proven veterans, D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris, to man the middle of the defensive front.
Both have been promising, but it has been painfully obvious that the depth behind them isn’t holding up for Dennard Wilson’s group whenever either exits the field.
As New York heads into Week 7 with the league’s second-worst run defense , it has to find a way to strengthen its run response and give the pass rush and secondary more chances to dominate, as they did in the impressive wins in Weeks 3 and 4.
For now, the Giants can at least hang their hats on a workable foundation in the trenches with Reader, who is outpacing his talented predecessor.
Even with Lawrence’s decline in production amid injuries, which sparked a contract stalemate and his eventual trade, the Giants knew they wouldn’t easily replace a player of his caliber.
Not long ago, Lawrence was in the discussion as the NFL’s best defensive tackle, coming off a career-high 2024 season in which he had 9.5 sacks, 21 tackles (25 stops) and the second-highest run-defense grade among players at his position.
An untimely elbow injury cost Lawrence the final five games of that season. When he returned in 2025, both his production and his overall effort came into question as he finished the year with his lowest grade in five seasons and no sacks despite playing a full 17-game slate.
Even so, the move drew criticism of the Giants for shipping off arguably the best player on their roster, who had grown frustrated with the constant losing that engulfed the franchise for most of his tenure and led to the hiring of John Harbaugh.
In addition, some questioned the transition to Reader, the 32-year-old veteran whose recent stats suggested he might be past his prime and thus no more than a temporary rental for Big Blue.
Through six games with the Giants, Reader has been the lone bright spot on the team’s defensive front and, compared with Lawrence in Cincinnati, has proven himself the more productive player.
Reader got off to a slow start as a gap stuffer, posting no more than three tackles along the line of scrimmage in his first five games. His peak outing came against the Saints’ 30th-ranked rushing attack, when he logged a season-high seven run stops with no missed tackles.
With those numbers, Reader leads the Giants’ defense with an 85.3 run-defense grade. Among interior defenders with at least 100 run-defense snaps, he ranks in the top three in tackles (16), stops (14) and average depth of tackle (2.3 yards), while committing no penalties.
Lawrence has had a more impressive start with the Bengals as a pass rusher, generating 19 pressures, including three sacks and three hits. Against the run, he trails Reader with only 10 tackles, 12 stops and a missed-tackle rate of 14.3%.
It’s worth noting that Reader has been a two-down player throughout his career, compared with Lawrence, whose size made him an every-down weapon.
Reader has also commanded significant attention, holding the league’s highest double-team rate (71.7%) in 2025, which boosted his value on the free-agent market, where New York won the bid for his services.
It is still premature to crown the Giants the winners of the blockbuster deal that landed them the No. 10 pick used to select Francis Mauigoa and fortify their starting offensive line. The early returns suggest they have at least found the right replacement for Lawrence to build the rest of their defensive front around.
Building out that front will be one of the team’s looming offseason priorities, as some of its younger pieces need to develop into larger roles. Harbaugh also wants physicality at the line of scrimmage to be one of his team’s tenets.
