A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: Staff Predictions for Titans vs. Browns: Tennessee Puts Pieces Together for Second Straight Win... Mostly
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans are looking for their second straight win for the first time since 2022. At 1-5 overall, Week 7's matchup with the Cleveland Browns feels like yet another do or die contest for a franchise hanging on to optimism by a thread.
Call us wishful, but the Titans On SI staff predict that Tennessee will do just that tomorrow... well, mostly.
We've got one consistent reason to be positive popping up across the board, as well as a realist among us who doesn't expect the Titans to be so lucky. Here are our staff predictions for Week 7.
The Browns' offense has been on the downturn in the last few weeks. The Titans' offense has essentially been on a six-week downturn, but the difference I see here is in a Tennessee defense that just proved they're good enough to win football games by themselves.
In the case that Saleh's unit finds a way to make Deshaun Watson use his feet in the pocket, potentially forcing a few more turnovers, I like the Titans' chances at home. Give me a tight-knit, low-scoring brawl that sees Tennessee take their second straight win by less than a score,
After picking up their first win of the season over the Indianapolis Colts last week, I have the Titans pulling off the home upset against the Browns and get their season back on track. The defense has quietly been a functional unit, and though the offense is still finding their groove, they showed some promise in Week 6.
If the Titans can play clean football and force a few turnovers, a victory is definitely a possibility.
The Titans are looking to win consecutive games for the first time since 2022, and for the first time in over 60 games, I believe they’ll get it done. I expect another strong performance from Robert Saleh's defense while the offense ( which has have struggled mightily as of late ) does just enough to squeak out a close win.
This season the Titans and Browns share one common opponent, the Jets, and both teams lost. Cleveland is sitting at 4-2, but they haven't shown a whole lot of fireworks offensively. The up-and-down play by QB Deshaun Watson makes them somewhat of a wildcard from week-to-week.
After a Week 1 blowout loss to Jacksonville, every Browns' game has been settled by one score.Tennessee's offense still lacks consistency and has scored only seven offensive touchdowns in six weeks. I expect this game to be a low-scoring affair. Cleveland is deep with wideout talent and has an easier time scoring on offense than the Titans. I see the Browns earning the victory in Nashville.

title: Titans Red Zone Report: 1 Main Reason Drives Failed And How to Fix Them in Week 7
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans pulled off a win in Week 6, but that triumph had little to nothing to do with the offensive side of the ball.
Tennessee piled on 26 points, but a closer look at that number doesn't do the offense any favors. A blocked kick touchdown and four field goals complicate the kudos set to be handed out after a win. Once again, QB Cam Ward struggled to make his mark on a contest.
Ward completed only 11 passes in Indianapolis vs. the Colts, notching one touchdown and one interception on his way to an underwhelming outing from every angle. In this week's red zone report, we're taking a look at one of the main reasons Tennessee's drives continued to stall in Week 6.
In addition, I'll try and pose a solution as the Titans prepare to try and win two games in a row. The 4-2 Cleveland Browns are on deck tomorrow in a Week 7 homestand.
Not every issue with the offense can be pinned to Ward. For a look at the share of blame in that unit, check out our analysis of the group's struggles as they extend from Ward and OC Brian Daboll.
However, facing off with the Colts, Ward's passing chart reveals a major problem. Not only did the QB fail to complete a pass of 20 yards or more, but he refused to look over the middle to any impactful degree. Take a look, per Paul Kuharsky.
Cam Ward at Indianapolis. #Titans . pic.twitter.com/vhkCBeYvTy
Sure, Ward still found Carnell Tate in the end zone for a touchdown, and he led enough semi-successful drives in the second half to help eek the Titans to a win. But if the defense doesn't have three takeaways and six sacks, Tennessee doesn't win that game.
The Tiatns need Ward to take more risks. They need him to find guys over the middle and search for chunk plays.
Clearly, playing it safe vs. Indy didn't go far for Ward's numbers. 11/22 for only 102 yards hints at a QB just trying to survive in the pocket. Ward was less than a game manager in Week 6; he was throwing checkdowns and trying to avoid crucial mistakes.
I'd argue that Tennessee would embrace a few more mistakes if it meant Ward threw for more than 200 yards in a game again, which he's done only once through six weeks. The Titans need involvement out of more WRs than Carnell Tate alone. We need to see looks to TE Gunnar Helm, more work for Tyjae Spears in the passing game, and again, far more tries downfield.
Simply put, opposing defenses are no longer scared of Ward's big-play ability. Let's circle back to the aforementioned 20+ yard pass stat. Ward threw 40 of those balls in his rookie season. That was more than Bryce Young, Jaxson Dart, Aaron Rodgers, and Daniel Jones, per FantasyPros.
This season so far, Ward has only 10. That's less than any healthy starter in the league, save for Jacoby Brissett with the Arizona Cardinals. One statistic says it all, although Ward making the less surefire decision now and again may be the basic key to fixing this issue before it's too late.

title: NFL Fines Fred Warner $65,673 for Hits Officials Let Go Against Commanders
full_text:
The NFL announced its weekly list of fines for players on Saturday : among them were San Francisco 49ers linebacker Fred Warner’s two fines totaling $65,673 for two fourth-quarter hits on Washington Commanders tight end Chig Okonkwo. On one of the hits, officials threw a flag, talked it over, then picked it up . Referee Adrian Hill announced there was no foul on the play. The NFL fined Warner $17,911 for a hit on a defenseless player with 14:05 remaining in the fourth quarter and $47,762 for use of the helmet on a hit with 7:08 left. Both hits were against Okonkwo.
#49ers LB Fred Warner was fined $65,673 for two instances against the #Commanders — $17,911 for a hit on TE Chig Okonkwo (flag was thrown then picked up, with ESPN broadcast saying it should’ve stayed a penalty) and $47,762 for use of the helmet here that wasn’t flagged. pic.twitter.com/fxkApK6gLQ
The first infraction happened on the drive that ended with Rachaad White scoring a touchdown. The larger fine was for a hit on a possession that ended with Washington turning the ball over on downs. In a game decided by six points , those details matter. The NFL, as always, hides behind its blanket published review policy that basically says its officiating department reviews every play and refers potential violations for disciplinary review. That same process lets players be fined without an on-field penalty, but the process certainly shines a funky light on what were almost certainly two missed calls amid a sea of questionable officiating.
The NFL fined 49ers LB Fred Warner $65,673 for two unnecessary roughness violations last week — including $47,762 for this hit on Commanders TE Chig Okonkwo. Officials threw a flag on the play, but then picked it up. pic.twitter.com/Ro4ll4vtbX
One has to question how neither hit went down as a penalty, but one was flagged, then questioned and discussed, and somehow the refs on the field decided there was no foul, but then the league office feels he should pay for it. If safety rules are the standard and expected to be followed, the league needs to show that to all 32 teams. More importantly, getting it right the following Saturday afternoon, tucked away in a weekly report, still doesn’t explain why officials picked up a flag they had already thrown. The player took the hit, Washington got no penalty yardage, and the fine report offers no explanation for why officials picked up the flag. The entire incident is a really bad look for the NFL. title: 10 Commanders Quotes That Tell the Story of Washington's First Six Weeks
full_text:
The Washington Commanders entered the 2026 season with plenty of expectations, but six games in, things haven't gone as planned. At 1-4-1 heading into their bye week, Washington has dealt with injuries, inconsistent performances , and several missed opportunities. Each week, we've highlighted 10 quotes from the team's press conferences that helped explain where the Commanders stood at the time. With six games behind us, let's revisit 10 of those comments and see what they tell us about how Washington got here.
Week 1 — Before the Philadelphia Eagles game Question: “Speaking of moments, in terms of your own coaching journey, Sunday is going to be a big moment for you, your first time calling plays at the NFL level. In terms of emotions, butterflies, what do you think you’re going to be feeling on Sunday as you step into the Linc?” “I think we'll all be ready to compete. You know, I think you can trust your instincts when they're founded in hard work, and our whole group has done that. So that's kind of the mantra for us. We're going to go cut it loose and let it all out there.” At the bye : Blough was confident entering his first season as an NFL offensive coordinator, but the results have been inconsistent. Washington has shown flashes of what the offense can become, though penalties , third-down problems and situational mistakes have made it difficult to sustain success. The hard work Blough talked about before Week 1 still needs to translate into more consistent execution.
Week 1 — Before the Philadelphia Eagles game Question: “Looking at Sonny Styles — it’s just Week 1, understanding it’s a progression and you’re not going to see everything — how do you kind of temper those expectations when it’s your first-round pick, and it’s a top-10 pick, understanding that he’s going to be growing as the season goes on?” “I think the biggest one is the expectations are from inside the rooms, inside the building, and for teammates, the coaches, where we're at. And so that's where we want to see him grow and develop, from the people that see him every day and the things that he's so unique at. Each game, I think you're going to see Sonny grow. It's part of first-year players, where there's some of this — we would love all development to go straight across, but everybody who's been around just a little bit knows that's not really how it goes. “So when those are there, we've got people here to help him keep growing and develop. But I think he's got an unbelievable opportunity ahead with him here, some of the teammates that he's with. Already, in like six weeks, the growth that I've seen from him. So he's excited to get going. He's an excellent competitor. You can tell he's comfortable, even more comfortable now with the system, the people, the way it goes. But yeah, we're really pumped to unleash him.” At the bye : Of everything Washington's coaching staff talked about before the season, this is one of the things they've gotten right. Styles has already shown why the Commanders selected him seventh overall, including an interception and forced fumble against Seattle. There are still things he needs to learn, but he has been one of the bright spots in an otherwise disappointing start.
Week 2 — Before the Dallas Cowboys game Question: “When you're implementing a new scheme, at what point in the season does it usually click from your experience and kind of come to life in the way that you envision it?” “In the past, it varies. You would like, as a goal, to be the first quarter of the season, you know, in those first four games. Sometimes it happens faster, like that Game 3, because you're still working out some of the kinks. Sometimes you're trying to get the continuity together, especially if you have a lot of new guys. Some things that goes into that. But definitely by the first quarter of the season, you have a good beat on, ‘Okay, this is who we are. This is how our guys respond and how they play.’ And then you can kind of build even from a staff perspective in terms of, you know, we're still — I know I am — in terms of, you know, you watch these guys in practice and so forth like that, but also, you know, we say practice execution becomes game reality. So how they respond in games, you kind of understand, ‘Okay, this player is better at that than I thought he was, so let's utilize him more in that way,’ or, ‘He's not quite where we want to be in that particular space, so let's keep him out of those spaces.’ And so I think by the first four games, you kind of have a better idea of the team and the defense as a whole.” At the bye : We've passed that four-game mark, and the defense still doesn't look like a finished product . There have been encouraging performances, particularly when it comes to creating turnovers, but the consistency Jones discussed remains a problem. Washington has had stretches where the defense looks capable of taking over games, followed by others where it struggles to get off the field. That's something Jones and his staff have to figure out during the bye.
Week 3 — Before the Seattle Seahawks game Question: With Marcus Mariota taking over at quarterback and additional injuries affecting the offensive line and other positions, what challenges does that create for Blough as a play caller? “The same thing as when we were building the system. It's how do we put our players in a position to have the most likelihood of success? And so we evaluate our own roster and what we do have. We're not reflecting on what we don't right now. There's no time for that. Nobody cares. And so we are certainly going to do everything we can to put our guys in the best position possible to beat Seattle.” At the bye : That answer came before Washington earned its first win of the season against Seattle, but it has become even more relevant since. The injuries haven't stopped , and now Terry McLaurin is out for the year. Blough and the offense have had to deal with constant changes, but at some point, the players who are available have to produce. That's what made this quote stand out then, and why it still matters now.
Week 4 — Before the Indianapolis Colts game in London Question: Does Mariota feel he still has something to prove about his ability to play at a high level? “I think at the end of the day, like I've always had a belief in myself. So that prove it has never really crossed my mind. I just wanna be able to help these guys out and find ways to win. And if that means me playing well, great. If that means me managing the game and making sure that we're eating up clock, I'm taking care of the football, like I'll do whatever it takes to win. And I'm at that point in my career where that really is all that matters. So, I'm not here to prove anything. I really have just believed in myself all this time and the more that I can just help these guys out and win games, that's what's most important.” At the bye : Mariota gave Washington exactly what it needed against Seattle, helping deliver the team's only win through six games. He wasn't trying to replace Jayden Daniels or make a case for becoming the starter. He simply stepped in and did his job. Unfortunately, another knee injury against Indianapolis has complicated things for both Mariota and the Commanders, but his performance against Seattle remains one of the better stories from the first six weeks.
Week 5 — Before the New York Giants game Question: “For you guys, the second-half defense has not been there. The numbers are what they are. With that being said, you may be asked going into a game and say, ‘I'm only scheduled to play 25 snaps,’ and end up playing 40. We can't let that be a determining factor. title: Around the NFC East: Cowboys Talk Big, Giants Change QBs, Eagles Battle Injuries, Commanders Regroup
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have the weekend off. Their division rivals have plenty to sort out. The first-place New York Giants are changing quarterbacks, while the Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles head into Monday night with matching 2-4 records. America’s highest-profile cheerleading squad has won a victory of its own: The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders have formed a union. The union is believed to be the first in the nation among all pro-sports cheerleading squads, outside of a short-lived effort by the Buffalo Bills’ “Buffalo Jills” in the mid-1990s. The Dallas cheerleaders’ bargaining unit has already been recognized by the Dallas Cowboys, according to a brief joint press release issued Friday by the team and the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association. The agreement came after “meaningful discussion” between the two sides, the release said. The next step will be bargaining for an official contract for the cheerleaders. The squad currently consists of 36 active members, though it is not clear how many will be officially represented by the union. “The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for their talent and dedication they exhibit,” the two groups said in the release.

title: Commanders’ Defense Has an NFL-Worst Problem Before Third Down Even Arrives
full_text:
Against the Washington Commanders , opposing offenses have a 49.7% success rate on 169 plays run on first down, ranking the defense last in the NFL, according to HB Analytics. Looking for a fix to that should have been near the top of defensive coordinator Daronte Jones’ to-do list during the bye. That percentage doesn't mean opponents picked up a new set of downs on nearly half of those plays. Success rate measures whether a play improved the offense's expected scoring outlook. A five-yard gain on first-and-10 leaves a team with plenty of options for its next call. Hold the same run to a yard or force an incompletion, and the offense has more work to do.
Washington has played a lot better on second-and-long, and it also ranks second in expected points added allowed in those situations. Opponents have a 29.8% success rate across 57 second-and-long plays, the third-lowest in the NFL. That gives Jones something to build on. Better execution on first down would give his defense more chances to work from a position where it has played well. Washington still has a problem finishing possessions, though. Opponents have converted 36 of 81 third downs against the Commanders, or 44.4%. On third-and-long, HB Analytics shows opponents posting a 37.1% success rate across 35 plays, ranking Washington 24th. The weaker third-and-long results matter because they show the defense is struggling even when the distance should favor it. Jones needs better execution when his defense has already put the offense in a tough spot.
Head coach Dan Quinn talked about that Tuesday when asked how he could help Jones get more consistent play from the defense. He started with preparation before the snap and later singled out first and second down. “And that can mean urgency, call selection, and getting these guys' cleats in the grass to go play decisively and fast,” Quinn said. “So, that’s number one at the top of my list to make sure all the calls that we have are able to go and do that.” Washington has time to settle on the calls it can execute consistently before it returns against Philadelphia on November 1. I’d make getting everyone set and playing fast the starting point for that plan. Jones needs his defense to win on first down more often and create the second-and-long situations it has handled well. title: Washington Has 13 Days Between Games Before Eagles Rematch. They Can’t Waste Them — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders played their last game on Monday, October 19, and will return to action against Philadelphia on Sunday, November 1, 13 days later. The Eagles, meanwhile, will host the Dallas Cowboys this coming Monday night, then will travel to visit Washington six days later. These aren't the same teams that met in Week 1, with Washington losing 24-22 . The Eagles have gone through several things, including the retirement of long-time right tackle Lane Johnson and blood clots that put Jalen Hurts on injured reserve . The Commanders have had injury issues since training camp started and lost the face of their franchise last Monday night when Terry McLaurin went down. With Philadelphia and the Rams still on the schedule before the November 10 trade deadline, next weekend is the first of two games that could help Adam Peters decide what to do with this roster. The quarterback the Commanders will face that day is Tanner McKee, who went 26-of-45 for 215 yards, a touchdown, and no interceptions in Philadelphia's 25-14 loss to Carolina last week. Washington will get another look at McKee when the Eagles play Dallas on Monday. They can watch for adjustments Philadelphia makes after his first start this season and how he responds to whatever the Cowboys throw at him. Washington also has the bye week to settle into the reality that Terry McLaurin will not be back this season. We'll have to wait and see whether they use that time to develop a plan to get the other receivers more involved or if one receiver will shoulder Terry's entire load. The time off should give Washington an edge, even though they entered the bye week at 1-4-1 and gained only 90 yards in the first half of their last game. If the offense comes out better prepared and the defense has an answer for the Eagles’ adjusted passing game, you'll know the break was needed.

title: Where Does Mike Sainristil Fit in the Washington Commanders Defense Now?
full_text:
Mike Sainristil opened the season atop the Washington Commanders ’ cornerback depth chart alongside Amik Robertson , then played 54 of 55 defensive snaps against Philadelphia. Six games into the season, finding a place for him has become a much different conversation. Sainristil played seven defensive snaps against San Francisco . Robertson played all 62, while Rasul Douglas and Trey Amos played 36 apiece. That leaves Washington entering its bye with three corners getting considerably more work than a player it drafted in the second round just two years ago.
Amos’ return added competition, but Sainristil’s playing time had already taken a hit. He went from 54 snaps in the opener to 45 against Dallas, 26 against Seattle and five against Indianapolis. His workload jumped to 43 against the Giants before dropping again Monday night. The coverage has been a problem. Entering Washington’s bye, Pro Football Focus gave Sainristil a 29.4 overall defensive grade and a 28.5 coverage grade, both ranking 102nd among 102 qualifying cornerbacks. Those numbers make it hard to argue that Washington should simply restore his opening workload. The staff had already changed his assignment before the London game, moving Sainristil into the nickel while Robertson, Douglas and Fabian Moreau handled outside work. Dan Quinn described that arrangement as “that’s the best thing for right now.” Sainristil then played just five snaps against the Colts, so moving him inside hasn’t guaranteed much time on the field, either. Now Amos is back from injured reserve . Washington activated him October 19, and he immediately matched Douglas’ workload against the 49ers. The coaches still have to account for Amos working his way back, something defensive coordinator Daronte Jones acknowledged before his return, but they have an outside option they didn’t have during the first five games. Plus, Robertson has earned his place . Jones described him as steady during his October 16 presser, and Washington kept him on the field for every defensive snap Monday. There’s little reason to disrupt his workload to manufacture more opportunities for Sainristil.
Jones provided some useful context for Sainristil’s larger workload against the Giants. When asked about Amos’ return and whether he had considered Sainristil at safety, Jones pointed to the deep-zone assignments Sainristil had handled against New York . “The depth chart that we had in that game and who was available definitely had something to do with that,” Jones said. Jones went on to discuss finding the best combination of players and said Sainristil’s flexibility would help Washington down the road. He was explaining how the team could use him in different assignments, without announcing a permanent position change. That’s where I would keep Sainristil for now: situational nickel work and reserve duties that allow Washington to use that flexibility when needed. Robertson should remain central to the rotation, with Amos and Douglas handling the larger outside workload. Sainristil can still contribute without being handed his old job back. The next step is covering better in the opportunities he gets. If he does that, Washington can expand his responsibilities. His versatility gives the coaches options, but his performance has to give them a reason to use him more. title: Commanders’ Drew Stevens Owns Two Franchise Rookie Records After Just Six Games
full_text:
Washington Commanders rookie Drew Stevens already held the franchise’s rookie record for the longest field goal before Monday night against San Francisco. His 51-yarder in the first quarter brought him to three makes from 50-plus yards , extending the franchise rookie record he already held. The 57-yarder against Seattle set the distance record in Week 3, after Stevens had connected from 55 yards against Philadelphia in the opener. Both rookie marks are now his with 11 games still left to play.
DREW STEVENS FROM 51 THAT'S A GREAT KICK #PMSMNFonESPN2 pic.twitter.com/SJJVjhmmel
Stevens was 3-for-5 on field goals after the first two games, and he hasn’t missed one since. He made two apiece against Seattle, Indianapolis, and New York, then his lone attempt against San Francisco. That puts him at seven straight makes and 10-for-12 overall, or 83.3%, entering the bye. Both misses came from 50-plus yards during those opening two games. He’s also 7-for-7 inside 50 yards and 3-for-5 from 50 or longer. The long kicks are getting the records, but Stevens has taken care of the shorter field goals, too. His 57-yarder against Seattle came as the first half expired in a 33–31 win, so that range has already helped Washington pick up points in a game it barely won. The extra-point issues still need work, even after he made both attempts against the 49ers, bringing his season total to 10-for-13. Two of the three failures came under unusual circumstances, but Washington has still walked away without those points. That operation needs to become more consistent. Washington should feel better about its field-goal kicking now than it did after Week 2. Stevens has settled in since then, and six games into his rookie season, he's already established two franchise marks. That’s a good start, with plenty of season remaining. title: Washington Has Allowed Twice as Many Red-Zone Touchdowns as It Has Scored — Commanders Daily
full_text:
The Washington Commanders entered their bye week with a red-zone issue: opponents scored 18 red-zone touchdowns, while Washington scored 9. That's a problem on both sides of the ball for a team that has already seen close games slip away. The Commanders have scored nine touchdowns on 17 red-zone trips, or 52.9%, tied for 21st-best with the Bengals. Opposing teams have had five more trips (22 total) but scored nine more touchdowns (81.8%), which ranks Washington 31st in red-zone touchdown rate allowed through Week 6. Against San Francisco, Washington allowed touchdowns on three of four red-zone attempts. On the other attempt, K'Lavon Chaisson peanut-punched the ball out of Christian McCaffrey's arms. Washington wasn't able to get points off that takeaway, but San Francisco scored on its next possession to send it to halftime at 20-3. On the flip side, Washington scored touchdowns on two of its four red-zone trips Monday night. The other two ended on fourth down. Daniels threw the ball away from the 49ers’ 13 in the first half, then Treylon Burks couldn’t hold on at the pylon from the 17 in the fourth quarter. They climbed back in the second half, but those empty trips left points on the field in a 23-17 loss . Washington lost its first meeting with Philadelphia 24-22 , so it already knows how much one missed chance can matter. On November 1 against the Eagles, the test is whether the defense can force more red-zone trips to end without touchdowns and the offense can finish more of its own.

title: Commanders' K'Lavon Chaisson Exposes a Surprising 2025 Defensive Stat in Just Eight Days
full_text:
Washington Commanders edge rusher K'Lavon Chaisson did something over the last two games he's never done before. Chaisson strip-sacked Jameis Winston against the Giants, then eight days later peanut-punched the ball out of Christian McCaffrey's arms on Monday Night Football. Both plays resulted in takeaways, with Tim Settle recovering the first fumble and Frankie Luvu the second. Not only did Chaisson match his career-high of two forced fumbles, set last season with New England, but he also helped generate as many fumble recoveries in two games as Washington managed during the entire 2025 season. It's important to remember that Washington forced 11 fumbles in 2025 but recovered only two. This is in direct response to the staff's continued emphasis on creating turnovers throughout the offseason program.
K'Lavon Chaisson forces a rare Christian McCaffrey fumble pic.twitter.com/w65HUXM4wB
When Washington signed Chaisson in March , they were looking for a disruptor who could change things on the defensive front; in six games, he already has 2.5 sacks and two forced fumbles with 11 regular-season games remaining. Commanders HC Dan Quinn had already singled out Chaisson following the Cowboys game for trying to knock the football loose while sacking Dak Prescott. "So, we gotta continue to wreak havoc, cause disruption," Quinn said at the time . A few weeks later, those attempts are turning into actual takeaways. The real question for the Commanders moving forward is whether they can get the same production all across the unit after the bye, and how much of a difference-maker that will be in the win column. Up to this point, none of the individual accomplishments of any player have helped the unit overcome the defense's other problems .
